Make multi-island trips affordable with the right points strategy

Most visitors to Hawaii stick to one island because interisland flights add $100-$400+ per person to the trip cost. By using points for these short hops, you unlock a fundamentally different Hawaii experience — island-hopping from Oahu to Maui to the Big Island to Kauai without the airfare costs stacking up. This is a multiplier strategy: you are not just saving on one flight, you are enabling an entirely different type of trip. Combining a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight with points-funded interisland hops creates a nearly free (in cash) multi-island Hawaiian vacation.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Decide which islands you want to visit and in what order. The most common combinations are Oahu + Maui, Oahu + Big Island, or a three-island itinerary. Map out how many interisland hops you need so you know the total points required.

Check Hawaiian Airlines (7,500 miles each way), Southwest (variable, typically 4,000-8,000 points), and United (5,000-7,500 miles) for each interisland segment. Southwest often offers the best flexibility with no change fees and no blackout dates.

For Hawaiian Airlines, transfer Amex Membership Rewards. For Southwest, earn Rapid Rewards directly or transfer from Chase (transfer to Southwest is currently limited). For United segments, transfer from Chase or use Turkish Miles&Smiles for even lower pricing.

Book each interisland hop as a separate one-way award. This gives you maximum flexibility to mix airlines and optimize pricing per segment. One-way awards have no penalty compared to round trips on these short routes.

Align your interisland hops with your arrival and departure flights. Arrive on one island and depart from a different one (open-jaw booking) to avoid backtracking. For example, arrive Honolulu, hop to Maui, depart Maui to the mainland.

Hawaiian Airlines has the most extensive interisland network and offers the most daily frequencies. Southwest Airlines also operates key interisland routes (Honolulu-Maui, Honolulu-Kona, Honolulu-Lihue). United flies select interisland segments as well. Each airline has different award pricing and transfer partner access.

Hawaiian Airlines interisland awards typically price at 7,500 HawaiianMiles each way. Southwest varies by cash fare but generally costs 4,000-8,000 Rapid Rewards points each way for interisland hops. United interisland segments can be booked for 5,000-7,500 miles using various Star Alliance partner programs.

Yes, especially when booking multiple hops. A family of four making two interisland hops at $150 each way would spend $1,200 in cash. Converting that to points frees up significant cash for accommodations, activities, and dining. The per-point value (1.5-2.5 cents) is reasonable, and the trip flexibility gained is substantial.

A popular strategy is to fly into Honolulu (Oahu), hop to Maui for beaches and Haleakala, then continue to the Big Island (Kona) for volcanoes and snorkeling, and optionally finish on Kauai for dramatic scenery. Each hop is 30-60 minutes. Allow 2-3 days minimum per island.

This redemption was built for families and couples planning a multi-island Hawaii vacation — full stop. If you're visiting multiple islands (which most Hawaii first-timers and repeat visitors do), you're already mentally budgeting for interisland flights. This sweet spot simply redirects that cash budget back into your pocket and replaces it with points.

Families get a 5/5 Family Friendly score here for good reason: availability is wide open, booking is simple, and the economics scale beautifully. Four people, two hops = 60,000 miles to cover potentially $1,200+ in interisland airfare. That's an extraordinary displacement of vacation cash.

Beginners are explicitly welcomed by this redemption's design. There's no partner airline complexity, no fuel surcharge math to calculate, no routing rules to decode. You search on Hawaiian's website, you transfer points, you book. The 5/5 Beginner Friendly and Easy to Book scores reflect that this is genuinely one of the simplest award redemptions you can execute.

Minimum points needed: 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person per segment. For a solo traveler doing two hops, that's 15,000 miles. For a family of four doing two hops, that's 60,000 miles.

This is NOT for: Travelers who don't have an Amex MR or Bilt account and no path to earning HawaiianMiles quickly. It's also not ideal for travelers who only need a single interisland flight — the opportunity cost of setting up the transfer relationship for 7,500 miles may not be worth it unless you're already accumulating MR points for other redemptions.

This redemption earns a **Beginner** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. In a world of waitlists, fuel surcharges, routing rules, and phone-only bookings, Hawaiian interisland awards are refreshingly clean. **What makes it easy:** Award availability is consistently excellent (5/5). The booking portal is functional and user-friendly. There are no fuel surcharges to calculate. Miles never expire, so there's no pressure. You can complete the entire redemption — from transfer initiation to confirmed booking — in about 48 hours. **The one genuine friction point:** Earning HawaiianMiles isn't as straightforward as earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex MR. Hawaiian doesn't have a widely-used co-branded credit card for most people's everyday spend. This means you're dependent on transfer partners, and the Amex MR and Bilt paths are your primary options. If you don't have either, this redemption becomes harder to access. **Tip 1:** Start with an Amex card that earns Membership Rewards — the Amex Gold is the ChooseFI community favorite for everyday earning. Once you're accumulating MR points, you have a direct path to Hawaiian via a 1:1 transfer. **Tip 2:** Always search award availability before transferring. It takes 30 seconds and protects you from the one mistake that could derail an otherwise smooth booking. **Tip 3:** Don't overthink the merger situation. Hawaiian and Alaska remain separate programs today. Book what's in front of you. If you can earn Amex MR points, you can execute this redemption. It's the perfect first award booking for a ChooseFI member who wants to see how the system works without risking complexity.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Interisland awards are the key that unlocks multi-island Hawaii vacations without the stacking airfare costs that keep most travelers on a single island. At 7,500-10,000 miles per hop, the points cost is modest, and the trip transformation is significant. Whether you use Hawaiian Airlines miles, Southwest Rapid Rewards, or United partner programs, the strategy is the same: let points handle the short hops so your cash stays in your pocket for experiences. Combined with a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight, interisland awards make a multi-island Hawaiian vacation one of the most achievable aspirational trips in travel rewards.

#8934. 13 Black Women Share How They Found the Strength to Survive—and Thrive—With Breast Cancer

When it comes to Black women’s breast health, the statistics rarely tell a hopeful story. Black women are diagnosed with breast cancer at a younger median age (60, compared with 62 for white women) and are 38% more likely to die from the disease. They have the lowest survival rate for every known stage of breast cancer. And about one in five Black women with breast cancer are diagnosed with hard-to-treat triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), more than any other racial or ethnic group.

But here’s what the numbers will never capture: the phone calls at 3 a.m., the head-shaving parties, the therapy sessions that cracked something open, the moment a woman looks at her daughter or granddaughter and decides they are reason enough to fight. Black women have always been more than a data point, and perhaps nowhere is that truer than in the way they face, survive, and remake their lives after a breast cancer diagnosis.

The stories below belong to 13 Black women who refused to be reduced to a statistic. They are individuals with careers, children, humor, faith, rage, and joy whose experiences with breast cancer changed them in ways both devastating and profound. In finding their own paths through treatment and beyond, they’ve built something the data can’t quantify: community, purpose, and a hard-won blueprint for survival they’re passing on to every woman who comes after them.

Monique Bass, 53, had always been proactive about her health. A single mother of twin sons and grandmother of four, she started getting annual mammograms at 40. But it was a self-exam at 47 while lying in bed one night that changed everything. She found a lump that didn’t feel right.

What followed were three tissue biopsies of the lump over three years, each coming back benign. Doctors wanted to keep monitoring. Bass pushed back. The lump was growing, and she knew her body well enough to realize something was wrong. She insisted they remove the lump (a procedure called a lumpectomy) and test it. The diagnosis: stage 1 invasive ductal carcinoma that was aggressive enough to require immediate chemotherapy.

Bass got the call while sitting in a car wash. “I felt like I was in The Twilight Zone,” she says. “Not in a million years did I think I would ever hear the words, ‘You have cancer.’” The timing made everything harder. It was 2020, the height of the pandemic, so she navigated much of her journey alone. Adding “another emotional layer,” she was also going through a divorce. Treatment included four rounds of doxorubicin, four rounds of paclitaxel, and 21 radiation treatments. Losing her hair hit the hardest. “But the silver lining is that it grew back even more beautifully after treatment,” Bass says.

Throughout it all her faith anchored her. “I’m not a deeply religious person, but I believe in God, and I knew he had me in the palm of his hand,” Bass says. On the other side of treatment, she founded What’s Behind the Bra?, a New Jersey nonprofit that distributes comfort care packages to breast cancer patients year-round and hosts a weekly podcast of the same name every Sunday at 7:30 p.m. ET.

Jaqueline Beale, 64, comes from a family with a long history of cancer, including her mother, who had breast cancer. That’s why it wasn’t a huge surprise when, at 40, she found a lump during a breast self-exam. Even though a sonogram and mammogram came back clear, it was obvious that something wasn’t right, so Beale got a biopsy.

When the radiologist called with her result—stage 1 breast cancer, which means the cancer hadn’t spread beyond where the abnormal cells had developed—she could hear a lot of noise in the background. He said, “I’m in New York trying to hail a cab, but you have breast cancer. You need to find a breast surgeon.” Despite the bluntness, Beale says she couldn’t help but find the humor in the situation, which is something she carried with her through treatment.

“I made sure that I surrounded myself with laughter and love,” she says, “and I told my family that I knew they loved me, but I also needed a lot of laughter to get through it.”

She recalls one incident in an elevator after her sister had taken her to a chemo treatment. “I had been sick as a dog after, and a woman got in and asked if I was okay. My sister said, ‘Oh, she’s fine. She’s just got a little bit of cancer.’ The woman looked horrified, but I laughed. My family knew that their sense of humor is what I needed.”

Annita White, 51, was five months late for her mammogram. As a single mother of two boys, a higher education administrator, and a first-year PhD student, she always had something more pressing. When she finally went, she expected the usual letter in the mail saying everything was fine. Instead, she got a call. There was a mass that hadn’t been there before.

By the time the biopsy came back, she already knew. A technician had commented on how hard the mass was, and White felt the diagnosis in her spirit before the words were ever spoken. The confirmation came the next day. “When I got the call, I fell to the floor and cried tears of desperation,” she says. “My first thought was, ‘Lord, I can’t do this.’”

What followed was hard in every way: chemotherapy, losing her breasts, losing her hair, which had always been full. “Being bald left me feeling vulnerable and insecure,” White says. “Physically, losing my breasts and going through chemotherapy made me feel like my body was no longer my own.” Through it all the fear that drove her was running out of time—time to see her sons become men and to meet her grandchildren someday.

Her faith, which she’d been privately wrestling with for years, met her exactly where she was. She’d been asking God to truly show up in her life. “He did,” she says. “In the middle of one of the hardest seasons of my life, he carried me through.”

Three years later White is cancer-free, her hair is back, and she recently finished her PhD. She now walks in her purpose as Dr. Nita, a member of the African American Breast Cancer Alliance survivor network, sharing her story and those of others facing the disease. “What once felt like the end became the beginning of something greater,” she says.

Marylande Regis, 38, had been in her new Georgia home for four months when everything changed. A registered nurse, realtor, wife, and mother of three, she had just stopped breastfeeding her nine-month-old when she found the lump. Her baby had never latched well on that side. When she messaged her provider, the on-call response was that it was probably a clogged milk duct and that she was too young to worry about it being something more serious. Regis didn’t accept that. She called back and left a message, insisting that something was wrong. “Another ob-gyn saw the message and encouraged me to make an office appointment immediately,” she says. Within two weeks she had a diagnosis: aggressive stage 2B, BRCA1-positive breast cancer. Within two more weeks what had been one tumor and one impacted lymph node had become three tumors and four impacted lymph nodes. Regis was 36.

“I was relieved that I advocated for myself,” she says. “I was proud that fear didn’t factor into my decision.”

What followed was relentless. Regis went through six months of chemotherapy, a bilateral mastectomy, six weeks of radiation, a total hysterectomy (to eliminate her body’s main source of estrogen), and breast reconstruction, all over a span of roughly 18 months. She lost friends to cancer along the way, as well as a cousin diagnosed around the same time. Her faith was, as Regis describes it, “shaken and stirred and flipped every way possible.” She wrote the important letters. She wrote her own obituary. She was practical about it. “I wanted to be positive, but I am also very realistic,” Regis says.

The hardest part wasn’t any single treatment—it was losing control. As her family’s go-to planner for everything from doctor’s appointments to vacations, she found it foreign to ask for help. But when she told her parents, her mother showed up and never left. “We joke, but my mom never went home,” Regis says. “This is her house now.” Her husband, Kory, came to every appointment and held steady even through both of them losing their jobs. “He deserves a trophy,” she says.

As the daughter of Haitian immigrants, raised to be everything her parents couldn’t be, Regis says the fight was never just medical. Today strength looks different than it did before cancer. It looks like making it to the bus stop with her son, who has autism. It looks like seeing her oldest finish nursing school and work toward becoming an ob-gyn. It looks like watching her youngest hit milestones like learning to talk. “I would have missed that if I didn’t fight,” she says. “The clouds are moving. The sun has decided to show itself. I can’t wait to soak it all in.”

Illness had always been an afterthought for 75-year-old Judy Fambrough-Billingsley. Why would it cross her mind? She walked three miles every day, swam laps all summer, took Zumba classes, and played soccer for 30 years. Judy Fambrough-Billingsley had never smoked or drank, and she didn’t even need to take medication. Being healthy wasn’t something she worked at; it was just who she was. A naturalized American citizen born in Germany, she traveled back to her home country regularly to visit family. Her life was full and active.

So when she felt a lump—and then another six months later—she ignored them. After all, she’d had a clean mammogram earlier that year. But when she noticed them growing and multiplying, she went back to her doctor. The results were not what she expected.

“I was shocked,” Fambrough-Billingsley says. She suddenly found herself navigating an entirely new set of experiences: prescription bottles, hospital procedures, lab processes—the whole medical system. “Being a part of a world where sickness exists had never been my world until now,” she says.

What carried her through was far older than her diagnosis. She grew up during the Civil Rights Era, the daughter of a successful Black entrepreneur who built his business during tumultuous years in US history. Both her parents were lifetime members of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). She was president of the NAACP Youth Council and an active member of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Fambrough-Billingsley knows something about fighting for your life in systems that weren’t built for you.

“Growing up during the Civil Rights Era contributed to this era of fighting,” she says. “Never giving up.” That same spirit—the one her parents modeled, the one she fell into during her work as a community organizer and across decades of a life fully lived—is the one she’s bringing to this too. She may still be on her breast cancer journey, but this is not her first fight.

Taylor Johnson was nearly 30 when she found the lump on her left breast. A mom and content creator who loves trying new things and staying active, she went to her primary care doctor, who referred her for an ultrasound and a mammogram. Johnson was denied a mammogram—she was told she was too young. She pushed anyway, got a biopsy (in lieu of the mammogram), and days later, had a diagnosis: stage 2 triple-negative breast cancer.

“My reaction was a very deep pause, trying to process what my doctor had told me,” Johnson says. “It then hit me, and all I could do was cry.”

She’s in the middle of her treatment plan, which includes six months of chemotherapy, followed by surgery and three weeks of radiation. After finishing chemo Johnson felt confident that would be the hardest part of her journey, both physically and emotionally. But her own health wasn’t her only concern: She knew her five-year-old was watching her every move, and she wanted to stay stable for her daughter. “I was so used to always being the strong one,” Johnson says. “This definitely tested that.” She held it together not because it came easily, but because she understood what her daughter was absorbing.

She is grateful for the community that rallied around her while she waited. Weekly prayer calls, rotating visits from family and friends, and a medical team at Mayo Clinic in Arizona that went above and beyond carried her through.

Though Johnson hasn’t finished treatment yet, completing chemo clarified something for her. “It has reassured me how strong I truly am,” she says. Strength, she’s learned, isn’t just physical. The emotional and mental muscle it takes to keep going counts just as much.

Jessica Ncube, 41, built her life around caring for others. A licensed clinical social worker, the co-owner of a mental health practice, and a mom, she was always in motion. Her life revolved around showing up for others and helping them navigate their hardest moments. “Looking back I do not know that I was always receiving,” she says.

Her diagnosis came quietly. A routine mammogram caught it; nothing in her body had felt amiss. That silence, Ncube says, is exactly why early detection matters. When she got the news she went into survival mode. “You hear the words, but it takes time for them to land,” she says.

Ncube’s journey started with a lumpectomy. When her margins came back unclear, meaning the pathologist could not determine whether all the cancerous cells were removed, she made the decision to move forward with a double mastectomy with reconstructive surgery. “Losing a part of your body, even when it is lifesaving, is still a loss,” she says. “The hardest part was learning how to sit in both gratitude and grief at the same time.”

As someone professionally wired to be strong for others, letting that tendency go was its own kind of work. “Strength became less about holding everything in and more about being honest about what I needed,” Ncube says. Her faith grounded her, and her community showed up, but she also had to unlearn something deeply familiar. “As a Black woman there is a resilience that is almost ingrained in us,” she says. “I had to learn how to balance that resilience with softness.”

After completing treatment Ncube has become more present and deliberate. Her definition of strength has changed entirely. “Strength today is softness. It is honesty. It is allowing myself to receive, to rest, and to not have all the answers,” she says.

Ameiko Newman, 40, didn’t learn of her diagnosis through a routine screening. She was rushed to the hospital for abdominal pain, and that’s when she learned she had breast cancer. Life before her diagnosis had been stressful, uncertain, a season of not quite knowing where she was headed. In a strange way, cancer gave her direction.

“For me, cancer saved me,” she says. “It made me a better person. It made me fight harder, push through the hard times and know what I want in life.”

Newman is still in treatment, receiving chemotherapy and immunotherapy every week, and she is honest about what that looks like: There are good days and bad days. She goes to church faithfully, prays every day, and tries to stay positive through it all.

What has surprised her most is that in the middle of fighting for her own life, she found her purpose: helping others fight for theirs. Newman rebranded her business entirely around that mission and started designing scarves with chemo patients in mind. “I started making them mainly for my Black women because you know we love having style,” she says. But a wide variety of women from all over have since bought them.

She wakes up every day, gets her kids ready, works out, and moves through life. Faith, she says, is what makes that possible. Her message to any Black woman who’s just gotten diagnosed is both simple and hard-won: “Cancer doesn’t define you. You define you. Even though you’re fighting for your life, help someone else fight for theirs.”

Charlotte Connor, 38, had just undergone a breast augmentation when she felt a lump in her breast. “When I saw my doctor, they weren’t concerned, in part because of my young age,” says Connor, who was 30 years old at the time. She had a mammogram and ultrasound to check for signs of cancer, but no MRI. “Looking back now I wish I would have asked for that MRI,” she says.

At the first checkup six months later, they told her she was fine. At the second—one year after the original lump was found—the lump had tripled in size. Her doctor ordered a biopsy, and her diagnosis was confirmed: stage 2A ductal carcinoma, which means the cancer was growing but contained to the breast and surrounding lymph nodes.

“When they told me I had cancer, I was calm,” she says. Her mindset immediately shifted from a sinking feeling to being optimistic about the future. “I focused on getting healthy again,” says Connor, who started fantasizing about what she would do after treatment.

She remembers thinking, I may be feeling sick and throwing up from chemotherapy, but what restaurants am I going to go to after all this is over? It’s an outlook that didn’t necessarily come naturally to her, either. “I’m not even overly optimistic in life—I think I’m a realist—but in this situation, I shifted to being overly optimistic.”

Part of that mindset shift was for her young daughter. “I couldn’t be pessimistic; I had to be strong for her,” she says. “And I knew that how I acted in this situation was how she was going to mirror things and react to stressful situations when she got older.”

Connor’s other pillar of support came from a tight-knit circle of friends and family, who threw her a head-shaving party before she lost her hair due to chemo. “Making things fun and lighthearted like that got me through my darkest, saddest moments,” she says.

It was 1999, and Donna Culmer had just received a clean mammogram. A few months later she felt a stone-size bump on her right side, so she went back to her ob-gyn to get it checked out. They redid the mammogram on both breasts, and while what she’d felt was actually a fibrocystic lump, the imaging found a small, not palpable spot on her left side that turned out to be a stage 1 cancer. “I was stunned,” Culmer says. “I didn’t even know what questions to ask.” She drove back to work in a daze and told her boss what had happened.

At 46 she was serving in the Navy as an instructor and trainer to personnel who were working alongside the Marines. She was married to a Marine and raising three children. There was no good moment for this. There never is.

Four months of chemotherapy followed, with nausea and exhaustion that never quite let up. Her doctors were concerned that the chemo might not work, so she had a mastectomy. Through it all her community refused to let her go through it alone. Her father drove her to every session and sat with her. Her church came to her, literally; services were held at her house.

Twenty-seven years later, Culmer, now 73, has had time to reflect. “As Black women, we have been through challenges our whole lives,” she says. “This is just one more.” Her advice is practical and clear. “Don’t panic and ask questions, even if you have to write them down,” Culmer says. “The treatments available now are so much better than what I had.”

One morning, Patricia Fox, 38, woke up with a lump in her right breast that wasn’t there the night before—she was just 26 years old at the time. Fox scheduled an appointment with her ob-gyn that day. “They told me that I was a young Black woman and had dense breasts, and it was likely a cyst,” she says. “They were ready to turn me away.”

The lump, which was a little smaller than a golf ball, seemed strange to Fox. Thankfully, she listened to her intuition. “There was something telling me to get it checked out,” she says, so her doctor did a biopsy just to be sure.

Her results came back as estrogen receptor-positive stage 2A breast cancer, meaning her cancer had estrogen receptors that would respond to hormone therapy drugs. Fox says she’ll never forget her doctor’s words: “Patricia, you’ll be a breast cancer survivor.” That sentiment set the tone for her mindset as a fighter. “It made me think that I could face this and survive this,” she says.

Still, cancer treatments quickly overwhelmed Fox, and soon she faced her lowest point: crying on the floor for hours, feeling like having cancer at such a young age was a punishment for being a “bad person.” But she pulled herself out of it with hard work in therapy.

“I found that talking to a therapist helped me process my diagnosis and examine the areas of my life—certain people and my own behavior patterns—that were cancerous for me that I needed to do something about,” she says. “While therapy didn’t make the pain go away, it did make how I coped with it much better.”

In the Black community, therapy is often taboo, says Fox, but it’s become her mission to dispel that belief. “Therapy fortified me to get through cancer,” she says, “and I tell everyone that they don’t have to suffer in silence.”

Annette Colden, 63, was sitting at her sister’s bedside during the last days of her final battle with breast cancer when the conversation turned to screenings. Her sister had been through cervical cancer and two bouts of breast cancer before passing away from the disease. “She made me promise I’d get my mammograms,” Colden says.

Colden’s first two yearly mammograms were clear. On the third there was a spot, but she was told by her doctor that things looked okay and it wasn’t cancer—she just had lumpy breasts.

“There’s this inner feeling you have,” she says. “Something was inside me saying, That’s not right.” Her sister’s doctor had told her the exact same thing, but Colden was so happy to hear she didn’t have cancer that she didn’t follow up.

A year later she went back for a mammogram, and that’s when her doctors found it: stage 0 breast cancer, meaning only abnormal cells had been found. She was 42. “Now, looking back, I always tell women that if something doesn’t feel right, get a second opinion.”

Despite the diagnosis Colden remained calm. “I’m a religious person,” she says. “In my prayer I said, ‘Lord, if you will be my pilot on this journey, I’ll be your copilot.’” She immediately felt a sense of peace.

After her recovery she decided to share that calming presence with other women going through breast cancer at a support group through Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, where she had treatment. “I say, ‘It’s going to be a long road. If you don’t want to travel it alone, I’m right there with you.’”

And she means it. Sometimes that involves talking with someone at 3 a.m. when the pain from chemotherapy hits. Other times it means sending food delivery boxes to the homes of people with breast cancer who can’t muster the strength to leave. “My sister did a lot of support work before she got really sick,” she says. “This is her vision.”

Ricki Fairley, 69, was in the security line at the airport for a work trip when she got a call from her doctor. They’d found a peanut-like lump under her nipple that turned out to be cancer.

Fairley, who was 55 at the time, said, “I don’t have time for this right now. I’ll call you when I get to my destination.” A couple days later she found out she had stage 3A TNBC, and it was really aggressive. Compared with other breast cancers, TNBC has fewer targeted-therapy treatment options, often spreads beyond the breasts, and is more likely to recur. Black women have nearly three times the risk of developing triple-negative breast cancer.

Her diagnosis woke her up. “It made me realize that I needed to get all of the ‘cancers’ out of my life,” Fairley says. During treatment that first year which involved a double mastectomy, aggressive chemotherapy, and radiation, she quit her job and started her own company. Then she filed for divorce and later sold her house. “I quit my life and started a new one, and changed everything,” she says. “I had to learn that my peace is nonnegotiable. I really think that stress caused my breast cancer.”

A year later her life changed again. Fairley was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer and told she had two years to live. After finding out her current doctor had only treated two previous cases of TNBC and both women had died in eight months, she found a new doctor, who was well-versed in current research and treatments for the disease. She beat cancer a second time. “I remember sitting at my daughter’s graduation thinking, Okay, I made it. What’s next for me?” Fairley says. The answer: helping others. In the years that followed, Fairley cofounded The Black Breast Cancer Alliance, which works to reduce the mortality rate for Black women.

#8933. 11-Minute Stretch and Breathwork Routine to Soothe Your System

Radiance Basden is a certified yoga teacher and passionate advocate for stress reduction, mental resilience, and restorative wellness. Here, she guides readers through a gentle movement and breathwork practice that’s even better when done outside.

It’s a beautiful day to breathe on purpose.

Incorporating grounding practices—including breathing exercises, yoga, and mindful stretching—into your daily routine is one of the the simplest ways to teach your body that it’s okay to relax.

If you have the opportunity to do this sort of breathwork outdoors, the experience can be even more beneficial. When I need to regain my equilibrium, I spend time in nature. After all, outdoor spaces are scientifically proven to soothe your system. Listen to the sounds, notice the world around you, breathe in the fresh air, and embrace the power of simple movements done with intention. You’ll be surprised by how quickly you can come back to yourself.

Begin in a comfortable seat, preferably on the edge of something supportive, whether a chair, couch, bench, even a rock. Place your feet flat on the ground. Both before you start and throughout your practice, check in with yourself and make sure that your shoulders, face, and hands are relaxed.

Rest your hands on your knees—palms facing up to receive energy, facing down for extra grounding. If you feel called to do so, gently close your eyes. Start with 3 deep breaths, slowly inhaling through your nose, slowly exhaling through your mouth.

Now, it’s time to bring in humming breath. Inhale through your nose, and as you exhale, make a humming sound. Continue to hum for the entire length of your exhalation, however long that might be.

Repeat this 5 times or however many you’d like.

Take 3 deep breaths, allowing yourself to sit in stillness while mentally checking in with your body.

Can you still feel the vibrations of your humming?

Make sure your feet are planted about shoulder’s-width distance apart. When you’re ready, begin to move through some hip circles. Circle toward the right, leading with your shoulders and guiding your torso forward, around, and back.

When you’re ready, switch directions and enjoy 8 more circles.

As you move through your hip circles, pay attention to any parts of your body that feel particularly tense or tight and spend some time there. Pause to rock, deepen your stretch, or bring in whatever movement or breath you might need to relax the area.

Next, embody your breath with a seated flow through Cat-Cow. With your inhalation, arch your back and lift your chin toward the sky, bringing your hands to rest on the sides of your hips in a seated variation of Cow Pose.

With your exhalation, round your spine and tuck your chin and bring your hands to rest on the front of your knees in a seated variation of Cat Pose.

Repeat this pattern of movement 10 times, moving with the pace of your own breath.

With your next exhalation, clasp your hands and extend your arms forward in a variation of Seated Forward Bend.

Take 1 full breath here before inhaling your arms up to the sky and exhaling them down at your sides.

Stand up and prepare for a variation of Breath of Joy. Inhale through your nose to throw your arms up overhead, taking a slight backbend in the process.

Exhale through your mouth, making a whooshing sound. Bend forward, bend your knees, and throw your arms back behind you.

Repeat this pattern of movement for 1 full minute.

With you next exhalation, come into Mountain Pose. Stand tall here for 5 cycles of breath through your nose.

Now, for your last bit of breathwork, take 3 more slow breaths, inhaling through your nose and exhaling through your mouth.

#8932. 5 Ways to Build Yoga Into Your Winter Arc

Calin Van Paris is a YJ editor and longtime wellness writer. Here, she shares some suggestions for incorporating elements of yoga and mindfulness into your winter arc.

The last leg of the year means only one thing: you’re in your winter arc. This approach (or, for some, challenge) is all about leveraging the final months of the year—a time historically associated with parties, scrambling, and saving anything pressing (and perhaps wellness-related) for January 1—as an ideal time for “locking in” and practicing self-care. That way, by the time the new year rolls around, you already have a regimen of helpful habits to hone, rather than feeling the pressure to commit to a series of rushed (and often ill-fated) resolutions.

In our opinion, the best winter arc focuses on mindfulness above all else. Sure, you could prioritize things like productivity. But slowing down is an innate part of winter, and honoring the part of you that wants to similarly take it easy is very human. With that in mind, the following yogic practices offer simple shifts to improve your life—or your experience of it.

Be patient with yourself as you acclimate to new patterns and intentions—that counts as mindfulness, too!

Morning meditation is always a good idea. But if sitting in stillness isn’t your thing (or you already have an established practice), try incorporating savoring into your morning routine. We all know that the way you spend your a.m. tends to set the tone for the vibes of your entire day. So rather than rushing through breakfast, getting ready routines, workouts, and practices like journaling, why not revel in them?

Instead of going through the motions, whatever they might be, make sure you’re engaging each of your senses. Stay present and see how each aspect of your morning grind makes you feel. This sort of noticing helps keep you in the moment and helps you get honest about what parts of your morning are feeding you—and which ones might need some adjusting.

Even setting a slightly earlier alarm and gifting yourself an extra five minutes in the morning can create enough space to release the need to rush.

The midday slump is a near-universal experience. You kick off the day with a full cup and as responsibilities quickly come your way, each chore, task, and errand takes a sip of your energy until you’re feeling depleted. If you’re searching for ways to boost your vitality (and refill your cup), turn your attention to your breath.

Breathing exercises, such as lion’s breath and breath of joy, invite you to physically release some stagnant energy and stress while stimulating circulation and leaving your mind feeling a little clearer than before. Plus, these breathwork practices are playful, encouraging you to make silly faces and let your body get loose, respectively. After all, having fun is among the most restorative activities there is.

As you’re standing at your sink doing dishes, typing away at your standing desk, or pacing around on a phone call, pause for a second (or even a full minute) and pop into a balancing yoga pose to practice your single-pointed focus.

We’re not suggesting that you randomly take Dancer Pose (although you might!). Lifting your leg and arms in Tree Pose, or sending one leg back and hinging at your hips in a quick Warrior 3, are enough to subtly challenge your body and mind in an unexpected way. Need to pick something up off the ground? Make it a Half Moon!

Discovering balance in your body might inspire you to find it in other areas of your life. Find a point of focus, concentrate on your inhalations and exhalations, and discover the presence and resilience that’s already within you.

Getting a certain amount of steps in each day is undeniably beneficial for you, but that’s not the entire point of taking a long walk. Just like opting for the scenic route home, walking is about forgoing convenience in favor of honoring your experience of the world.

Walks are a time for noticing what’s around you—the sights, scents, sounds, textures, even tastes that make up your environment. When done with intention and attention, your walk can be an act of full-body presence.

So, if your everyday walk has become more of a chore or fitness endeavor than act of wonder, now is a great time for a reframe. And if you’re not currently walking, there’s no better time to bundle up and begin than the present.

This isn’t about adding yet another step to your bedtime routine (we’re not into that). It’s about the quality of your thoughts as you drift off to dreamland. Rather than cuddling up with your phone, invite your sleeping state by spending some time in Savasana.  Just take a few minutes to tune into your breath and attempt let your racing mind slow and then still. See how the quality of your rest improves after a few nights of practice.

#8931. Triathlon News, October 2026: Ironman Crashes, NYC Tri Returns, Middle East Racing

Tim Heming highlights the biggest news in triathlon in October 2026. (Photo: Triathlete)

In October, the triathlon world turned its eyes to the Big Island for another epic edition of the Ironman World Championship, but that didn’t stop the rest of the multisport world from serving up its usual mix of drama, debate, and headline-grabbing news.

From analyzing the sparse participation numbers at New York’s long-awaited race return to tackling safety, transparency, and course caps following a scary collision on the Queen K, October delivered plenty of food for thought. And, as always, contributor Tim Heming is here to digest it with you.

The first line of Sarah Wassner Flynn’s article about the return of the iconic New York City Triathlon, published earlier this year, reads: “For more than two decades, the New York City Triathlon was one of the sport’s most iconic races. Debuting in 2001, it quickly became a bucket-list event for age-groupers and pros alike.”

The piece previewed this year’s race return, renamed the Big Apple Triathlon, under new ownership of Alpha Win, formerly known as HITS Endurance, with Tommy Struzzieri taking over the company from his father, Tom.

Alpha Win, based in Saugerties, New York, is no novice when it comes to race hosting. They have put on over 200 races, but making a success of this one offered the sternest test of their credentials to date.

Held on October 10, the day when most eyes in the triathlon world were focused almost 5,000 miles west on the Big Island of Hawaii, would it prove enough of a draw to justify the set-up costs of a swim in the Hudson River, a bike up the closed West Side Highway, and a run through Central Park?

Since its halcyon days, the event has been beset by problems, with participation tumbling from a peak of almost 4,000 during its time as part of the Life Time Fitness Series in 2010. In 2024, it was canceled by new owner Supertri before registration even opened, with organizers saying they couldn’t find a suitable date. It didn’t return in 2025 either, which, given Supertri’s focus on producing stylish, short-course events in major urban areas, had to be a worrying sign.

“We’re just trying to bring back something that athletes have been asking for,” Struzzieri said in March, noting that numbers would be capped at 2,500. If that felt optimistic, a New York Post piece on the eve of the event recounted its troubled history and asked: Is this time the charm? stating that around 1,300 athletes were expected to start, with prices ranging from $350–$650.

The results, however, show fewer than half that number: only around 600 finishers across all formats, the lowest the event has seen since it began in 2001. “Every year that there’s an issue with this event, it hurts the event the following year,” Scott Nilson, Supertri’s U.S. general manager of events, told us in 2024. Perhaps this year it will be the simple economics of numbers.

Registration for the 2027 event is now open with early-bird pricing (including processing fees) at $548.90 (Olympic distance) and $383.90 (sprint distance). Triathlete reached out to Alpha Win for comment.

For the majority, the Ironman World Championship is a day of celebration and achievement. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience, the ultimate triathlon dream. For Trish Byron, that dream turned into a nightmare.

Byron was struck by a male cyclist from behind almost 30 miles into the bike leg, leaving her with seven fractured ribs, a broken collarbone, a punctured and partially collapsed lung, a concussion, a laceration requiring stitches, and extensive road rash.

It’s understood the cyclist stopped and spoke with volunteers before continuing the race, but Byron’s daughter Cassie Anne put out a plea on Facebook for more information, saying: “We’re hoping to gather firsthand accounts, identify the cyclist involved, and better understand what happened.”

Accidents happen, but the incident raises questions about transparency when serious collisions occur during races. Should such incidents be publicly reported, both to demonstrate that appropriate safety protocols and follow-up procedures have been followed and to help triathletes better understand the risks involved in signing up?

Cassie Anne’s post received a response from Judy Daggett, who said: “This exact scenario happened to me on the bike about mile 85, causing me to crash also. The guy who hit me kept going. Another athlete helped me to my feet.

“I immediately had double vision and said, ‘Yes, I need help,’ but there was no one around. I managed to get back on the bike and ride to T2, praying my vision didn’t completely leave.

“When I got there, they took me by ambulance to the ER for a CT of my head, thinking I could possibly have a brain bleed. Thankfully, I did not, but I also have fractured ribs, a hip and shoulder injury, and a concussion.”

Daggett went on to say she’d reached out to Ironman but was yet to hear from them, stating it was her first DNF in 30 years and that the “men were so aggressive, they need to let them go first”.

Her final point relates to the questions raised about the scheduled swim start waves that interspersed the men’s and women’s age-group divisions in Hawaii, whereas previously, the men had been started earlier in one cohort, followed by the women.

It also brings into focus the broader question (that has continued to surface since the announcement of the return to one day of racing) of whether Ironman should cap numbers on the course for both fairness and safety reasons.

While it might seem that Trish Byron’s family shouldn’t have far to go to find answers, as Anna Grosz, who also responded to the post, explained, it might not be that simple: “I provided medical support for the race. We are bound by patient confidentiality laws. You should reach out to Ironman through official channels. The medical director may be able to communicate directly with the affected athlete, but course volunteers cannot do so.”

Triathlete has contacted Ironman for comment.

Championship season is not quite over in the world of triathlon. The T100 Tour still has three events on the calendar, with Dubai and Saudi Arabia in November ahead of the T100 World Championship Final in Qatar. The action in the Middle East will also continue with the 2026 World Triathlon Multisport Championship in Abu Dhabi.

The headlines will be the professional races over 100K where Hayden Wilde looks to be the odds-on favorite to retain his title, and it’s wide open on the women’s side. But there is also shorter-distance racing and representative age-group competition throughout.

Despite conflict in the region and the cancelation, postponement or relocation of other major sporting events, particularly in Saudi Arabia, both World Triathlon and the Professional Triathletes Organization are, for now, proceeding as planned. That’s perhaps to be expected, with contingency decisions often left until the last possible moment. But if the events do go ahead, it will be interesting to see how much appetite international athletes have for traveling to the region.

Conversations around weight can be a sensitive topic: triggering to some, frustrating to others, and almost irrelevant to others. And Susan Kitchen’s article on why we shouldn’t be concerning ourselves with post-race weight gain will no doubt grab the attention of athletes who might have concerns about how they can be heavier after doing all that exercise.

While Kitchen spells out the reasons here (which, spoiler alert, can be perfectly natural as your body recovers), it also made me think that perhaps the concern shouldn’t be how much you weigh, but why, in the days following an incredible endurance feat, you’re not off celebrating somewhere, rather than hopping on the scale.

You may not find an answer as to which is better, but there is plenty we can learn from Jordan Blanco’s roundtable discussion with triathlon legends Flora Duffy and Jan Frodeno when it comes to their appreciation for the pinnacle events in our sport – including that the 2008 win in Beijing was Frodeno’s first-ever elite victory!

But if there is one takeaway, then it’s probably that following your heart is the first step, and the financial rewards will follow. Doing it the other way around might just be a little tougher.

What do we learn from the Kona bike mechanics recounting tales from the Big Island?

Number one: That most of us should probably invest a bit more time in understanding how to fix our own bikes.

Number two: That whatever daft mistake you’ve made, it won’t be the dumbest thing they’ve seen (one athlete rolled up with two front wheels and no back, another with two back wheels and no front).

Number three: If you do have a problem, get to the mechanics early (the day before race day was the busiest).

And number four: Have a little patience. “That’s really the hardest part of Ironman week – managing athletes’ timeline expectations,” Taylor Bushong, a traveling race mechanic working out of Bike Works Kona, told Sara Stover. “Managing the unrealistic ‘can you just’ requests. The understanding of the level of the request seems to be outside the scope of recognition.”

But while being a bike mechanic sounds like a thankless task, it has some upsides. The real kicker, featuring five carbon wheels and the town’s dump, is cleverly left until the final line.

Some charitable sporting endeavors fall flat while others just fly, and often there seems to be no logic as to which cause will capture the public mood.

Thankfully, for Ethan Hunger, the idea to complete a world-record number of super sprint triathlons within 24 hours to raise money for his local food bank in Bellingham, Washington, really took off.

If ever there was a classic case of nominative determinism, then this is it. Hunger v. Hunger actually started following the COVID pandemic, but as Travis Mundell found out, this year’s challenge was the most ambitious yet, helping push the initiative’s total fundraising beyond $1.2 million.

It’s life-affirming to see such dedication in action, not just from Hunger, but from the community that rolled out to support him, where putting all the proper procedures in place so the record could be ratified by Guinness reads as more grueling than all that swimming, biking, and running.

There’s probably not much more that needs adding to one of the most dramatic Ironman World Championship races in living memory. Having written a reaction piece on how the house (in this case, the Big Island) always wins versus the gambler, I’ve reflected more on how it just seems such a difficult race to get right. My first thought: If the pros can’t do it (see the DNF files here), what chance do the mere mortals have? Follow-up thought: Nobody racing here could ever be described as a mere mortal anyway.

#8930. Is it too late to start strength training at 70? (No. Here’s what happens when you do.)

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.

You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.

Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.

A reader wrote me this week. Her whole email was one sentence:

That hits deep. That fear of: have I missed my window?

I want to share with you what I shared with her, because the science behind this is actually super cool and empowering.

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s still get stronger when they start lifting. And it meaningfully improves how they move through their lives.

And if you’re someone who hasn’t trained before, or hasn’t trained in a while, I have even better news.

As a beginner, your body is even more sensitive to training. Translation: you get even more reward for your effort!

In the first few weeks, most people feel stronger before they look any different.

That’s because a lot of early strength is actually your muscles and brain learning to coordinate. The movement gets smoother. Standing up from a chair feels a little easier. Etc.

Over a few months, muscle starts to build.

Your bones respond to the load too (strength training is one of the best-supported ways to support bone health as we age.)

You’ll start to feel some muscle in your arms that you didn’t notice there before, like this reader who’s been doing workouts 3x/week and kicking butt with it:

Is every body different? Yes. Does it also depend on sleep, nutrition, and what else life is throwing at you? Also yes.

But the direction is the same for everyone. No matter your age, you can make a meaningful impact in your overall health, fitness, and quality of life!

1) Don’t start with workouts. Start with practice.

Take a few minutes each day to learn and practice a couple of strength moves.

You’re not training yet. You’re getting acquainted.

Try some push-ups off of the wall or the countertop. ​ Sit down in a chair, slow and controlled, and practice keeping your weight evenly spread across your feet (that’s a squat right there!)

Grab a gallon jug, some light dumbbells or canned goods or whatever you have on hand, and practice a one-arm row. See if you can feel it in your upper back as you pull the weight up.

Work within whatever your ability level is, what feels safe and approachable to start.

You’re collecting information about what your body is ready for, and learning exercises like you’re learning a new skill.

30-60 minutes of strength training in TOTAL across the week goes a surprisingly long way.

You can break that up however works best for you. A short 5-10min session most days of the week, inserting some “movement snacks” throughout the day, or a couple of longer sessions 2x/week, etc.

It doesn’t require hours of your day to make serious progress.

3) It’s easier to level up than to cut down

Because your body is more sensitive to strength training, you’ll likely feel more sore in the beginning.

So in general, I recommend you err on the side of less is more.

If you do a few short sessions during the week, and wake up the next day feeling great with little to no soreness, great! You can add a bit more the next week.

Mentally, I’ve also just found it’s way easier to be “leveling up” than having to cut back, which really helps with building that early momentum.

Becky, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, is someone I immediately thought of when I read that initial email. She’s 77, and didn’t start going to the gym until she was 57. Here’s what she had to say:

I couldn’t have said it any better myself, Becky. 😊

No matter your age or where you’re starting from…YOU GOT THIS! 💪

Whenever you’re ready, here are more ways we can help

1) Here’s an article with a bunch of different bodyweight exercises and progressions you can do at home.

2) Our coaches build programs specific to you and your needs. Here’s the exact system we use.

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

Humans featured are exceptional examples and do not guarantee individual success. Your experience and results may vary.

Part Two: World of Hyatt's Fixed Award Chart Is the Unlock

Once your Bilt points are sitting in your account, you transfer them to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant. No waiting 3–5 business days. No points in limbo while availability disappears. You search, you find availability, you transfer, you book — in a single session if you want.

Hyatt's award chart is category-based, fixed pricing from 3,500 points (Category 1) to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. This is the inefficiency. When a Park Hyatt in a major international city costs $500 in cash but only 30,000 points (Category 6), you're extracting 1.67 cents per point at minimum — and in peak season when cash rates hit $700, you're at 2.3+ cpp. The chart doesn't move with cash prices.

What makes this particularly powerful for the ChooseFI community is the no fuel surcharges policy — Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award stays, so 15,000 points always means exactly 15,000 points out of your account. No surprise $75 "carrier fees" tacked on at checkout.

The transfer path is: Bilt Rewards → World of Hyatt at 1:1, instant. Chase Ultimate Rewards also transfers to Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, which means if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you have a second pipeline to the same program — an important redundancy for maximizing this sweet spot.

For 5,000 points — a single night at a Category 1 or 2 property — you're looking at a $100–$150 night that might cost you 2.5 months of coffee purchases on the Bilt card. That's the entry point. The ceiling is a $400+ night at a Category 5–7 property for 20,000–30,000 points. Both ends of the spectrum represent exceptional value, which is rare in any loyalty program.

Head to biltrewards.com and apply for the Bilt Mastercard (issued by Wells Fargo). The card has no annual fee. Once approved, add the card to your Bilt app and register your rent payment. If your building is in the Bilt Alliance (a growing network of partnered properties), setup is seamless. If not, you can still pay rent through the Bilt app via ACH transfer — Bilt mails a check to your landlord on your behalf, and you still earn points.

Key setup rule: Activate rent rewards in the app before your first payment cycle.

Before rent points post, you need five qualifying purchases on your Bilt card that statement period. Set up small recurring charges — a streaming subscription, a coffee shop, a weekly grocery run — and you'll hit this automatically. Don't forget this step; missing it means forfeiting that month's rent points.

Go to world.hyatt.com and use the award availability search. Select "Use Points" and search your destination and dates. Hyatt's search shows availability up to 395 days in advance — one of the longest windows in the hotel loyalty space. Identify your property, confirm the points price and availability, then — and only then — proceed to transfer.

Never transfer points without confirmed availability. Even though Hyatt availability is generally strong, you want to lock in what you see before moving irreversible points.

In the Bilt app, navigate to "Redeem" → "Transfer Points" and select World of Hyatt. Enter the exact number of points you need. The transfer is instant — points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes, not days. This is one of Bilt's most underrated features and means you can act on last-minute availability without risk.

Return to world.hyatt.com, confirm your points balance has updated, and complete your booking. You'll pay zero fuel surcharges — the points cost is the only cost. You can also call the World of Hyatt reservations line if you need help with a complex booking or want to stack a free night certificate.

If your first-choice property is sold out on points, try these tactics:

Hotel loyalty programs use "award charts" that assign each property a category level with a fixed points price. When a hotel's cash rate rises due to demand or location, the points price stays the same. This creates the value gap that makes points redemptions worthwhile. Hyatt's chart is considered the most generous among major hotel chains because it has resisted the aggressive devaluations that Hilton and Marriott have implemented. A Category 7 property might cost $500-$800 per night in cash but only 30,000 points. That gap is where your 4-8 cents per point value comes from.

Let's make this concrete. You've been paying $1,800/month in rent for the past year, diligently hitting your five monthly transactions. Your Bilt account holds approximately 21,600 points (1x on rent, plus some bonus earning on the card). You're planning a long weekend in Nashville with your partner.

The Property: Hyatt Place Nashville Downtown. Category 3, costing 12,000 World of Hyatt points per night. Cash rate for a Friday–Sunday stay: $189/night, totaling $378 for two nights before taxes and fees. With taxes, you're looking at roughly $430 out of pocket.

The Points Play: Transfer 24,000 Bilt points to Hyatt instantly, book two nights. Total points spent: 24,000. Total cash paid: $0 (Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges, no award fees).

The CPP calculation: $378 cash value ÷ 24,000 points = 1.58 cents per point at the conservative end. Factor in the taxes you're also avoiding (most properties don't charge taxes on award stays), and your effective CPP climbs closer to 1.8–2 cents per point.

Now scale up. Apply the same 24,000 points to a single night at Park Hyatt Chicago — a Category 7 property. Cash rate: $550–$700/night on a peak weekend. Points cost: 30,000 per night (you'll need to save a couple extra months). At $600 cash value for 30,000 points, you're at 2 cents per point — but if you hit a $700 night, that's 2.33 cpp.

The experience itself? Park Hyatt properties deliver: floor-to-ceiling windows, complimentary minibar items, a spa, and a level of service that genuinely doesn't feel like a "points hotel." You're not using a coupon at a budget chain — you're staying at the same property business travelers expense at full rate, experiencing everything they experience, funded almost entirely by the rent check you wrote anyway.

If you hold Hyatt Globalist status, suite upgrades on award stays are available based on availability — turning a 30,000-point redemption into a $900+ suite night. That's where the CPP ceiling of 8 cents per point becomes real.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

World of Hyatt awards include a fifth-night-free benefit on standard award redemptions when you book five or more consecutive nights. On a five-night stay at a Category 5 property (20,000 points/night), you'd normally pay 100,000 points — but with the fifth night free, it's 80,000 points for five nights. That's a 20% improvement in value with zero extra effort. Plan longer trips to unlock this.

Do: Book 395 Days Out for Peak Destinations

Hyatt opens award inventory at the same time as cash inventory — 395 days in advance. For high-demand properties (think Park Hyatt Maldives at Hadahaa or Alila Ventana Big Sur), availability at standard rates disappears quickly. Set a calendar reminder and search early.

If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, your Chase Ultimate Rewards points also transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. This means you have two separate point pools feeding the same program — Bilt for rent earnings and Chase for everyday spending. Together, you can accumulate Hyatt points significantly faster and take on higher-category properties.

Avoid: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

Bilt-to-Hyatt transfers are instant and irreversible. If you transfer 30,000 points and then can't find the availability you thought you saw, those points are now in Hyatt — and if you don't use them, they expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Always search Hyatt first, confirm dates and property, then transfer.

Avoid: Missing the 5-Transaction Monthly Minimum

This is the most common Bilt mistake. If you forget to make five purchases on your Bilt card in a given month, you earn zero points on rent — not reduced points, zero. Automate five small recurring charges to the card and never think about it again.

Do: Target Category 4–6 Properties for Best Value

Category 1–3 properties offer solid value, but the CPP accelerates meaningfully in Categories 4–6 (15,000–25,000 points/night) where cash rates are $200–$400 but points costs haven't kept pace. This is the sweet spot within the sweet spot.

Do: Watch for Hyatt's Points + Cash Awards

Hyatt offers a Points + Cash option at roughly half the standard award rate, combined with a cash co-pay. If your Hyatt balance is small, this lets you access properties without waiting to accumulate a full award.

This redemption was built for renters — specifically, renters who are already on the path to FI and feel the friction of paying rent every month with nothing to show for it. If you pay at least $1,000/month in rent, this sweet spot is generating meaningful Hyatt points from dollar one. At $2,000/month, you're accumulating 24,000 Hyatt points per year from rent alone — enough for two nights at a Category 5 property or a single aspirational night at a Park Hyatt.

Minimum to make it work: You need at least 5,000 Hyatt points for a Category 1 redemption — easily achievable after 5–6 months of rent payments on a $1,000/month lease. For aspirational Category 6–7 stays, you're targeting 25,000–30,000 points, which takes planning but is absolutely achievable.

This isn't the right fit if you own your home (no rent to earn on), if you're already deep into a competing hotel loyalty program, or if your primary travel goal is international business class flights — in that case, transferable airline currencies deserve more of your attention first. But for hotel stays, especially in the U.S., this is the single most frictionless on-ramp into the Hyatt ecosystem available anywhere.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness**, and that rating is accurate — but it helps to understand exactly *why* it's easy, so you don't accidentally make it harder than it needs to be. **What makes it easy:** - Earning is passive. Once your Bilt card is set up and rent is registered, points accrue automatically with no behavior change required (beyond five small monthly transactions). - The transfer is instant — no waiting, no uncertainty, no risk of availability disappearing while points are in transit. - Hyatt's award chart is fixed and transparent. You can see exactly what a property costs before you transfer a single point. - No fuel surcharges means no unpleasant surprises at checkout. **The one area that trips beginners up:** forgetting the five-transaction monthly minimum. This is the single most common Bilt mistake, and it's entirely preventable. Set up five small autopay charges on your Bilt card — a $5 streaming service, a recurring Amazon purchase, anything — and you'll never miss it. **Tip for the first redemption:** Start with a Category 3 or 4 Hyatt Place or Hyatt Regency for a domestic weekend trip. The points requirement is low (8,000–15,000 points), availability is widely open, and the booking process is identical to any other Hyatt stay. It's a low-stakes way to see the entire system work from earning to booking. If you can pay rent, own a smartphone, and make five purchases a month, you can execute this redemption. The ChooseFI community has embraced this one for good reason — it's genuinely the most accessible entry point into premium hotel travel rewards available today.

No. Bilt works with any landlord that accepts payment. If your building is not in the Bilt Alliance, Bilt processes the payment via ACH. The only difference is Alliance buildings may offer additional perks like bonus points or rent credits.

You will still pay your rent through Bilt, but you will earn zero points on that month's rent payment. The five-transaction requirement resets monthly. Set up autopay on small recurring charges to prevent this.

Yes. Bilt transfers to over a dozen airline and hotel partners including American Airlines, United, Air Canada Aeroplan, and IHG. However, Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value among hotel transfer partners.

Bilt caps rent earning at 100,000 points per month (equivalent to $100,000 in rent at 1x). For the vast majority of renters, this cap is irrelevant. There is no annual cap on total points earned.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Bilt-to-Hyatt pipeline is the most accessible travel rewards sweet spot available today. You are already paying rent. The Bilt card has no annual fee. Hyatt points deliver 2-8 cents in value. The transfer is instant. If you rent and you are not earning Hyatt points from that rent payment, you are leaving hundreds of dollars in annual hotel value on the table. Start with one Category 3-4 weekend stay to see it work, then scale up to aspirational properties as your balance grows.

#8928. How to Start a Workout When You Really Don’t Feel Like It (The Bridge Task Method)

If you can’t get yourself to start a workout after a long day, the problem might not be the workout itself. It’s the gear shift from “couch” to “go.”

A bridge task is a small, neutral action (not fun, not hard, just…meh) that you put in between the two so the jump is smaller.

Below is the 5-step version one of our coaching clients uses with her own students, plus a free worksheet to map your own.

A few weeks ago I was talking with Tabitha, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, about a challenge a lot of people face. ​ Some quick context: Tabitha is an executive function coach. She helps neurodivergent students and their families build the skills and systems that support their academic and personal goals. ​ And she noticed something: ​ The challenge of getting started on a workout is almost identical to the challenge her students face when trying to start homework. ​ This might sound familiar. You get home after a long day, mentally fried, and all you want to do is veg out on the couch. ​ In that state, getting up to cook a healthy dinner or go do a workout can feel really freaking hard.

Switching from a “YEAH!” task (chilling on the couch) to a “NAH!” task (workout/homework), is often harder than the task itself.

If we can make that gear shift less dramatic, it can make a big difference!

Instead of going from YEAH! to NAH!, you insert at least one task that’s just…MEH.

If you’re struggling to start your workout, don’t fight the gear change. Bridge it.

Add a little MEH to the mix and see what happens.

Tabitha put together a free worksheet that walks you through mapping your own task initiation sequence. Your personal YEAH -> MEH -> NAH.

Try it this week, and keep me posted on how it goes. ​ You got this. ​ -Matt

Whenever you’re ready, here are other ways we can help:

1) Not sure where to start? Take our Getting Started Quiz.

2) Want a coach who builds a plan and walks with you each step of the way? Learn about NF Coaching.

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

#8927. Does Soreness Mean a Good Workout? No. Here’s What It Actually Tells You

Soreness is not an indicator of a good workout, and not being sore doesn’t mean your workout didn’t count.

That day-after ache (DOMS) mostly tells you that you did something new, not something effective.

Progress is more reliably measured in your training log: more weight, more reps, more control over time, sore or not.

Rachael (a reader and all-around amazing person) sent me a question about this so well-organized it came with multiple choice answers. 😃

I LOVE this question, because almost everyone who’s getting started (or starting again) wonders the same thing:

Quick definition first. That achy, stiff, “why does it hurt to sit on the toilet” feeling that shows up a day or two after a workout has a name: DOMS, or Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness.

It usually peaks somewhere around 24-72 hours after you train.

Severe soreness is NOT an indicator of a good workout.

It’s a sign that you did something new that your body isn’t used to yet:

But it’s also not something to be afraid of, especially if you switch up your routine and are mildly sore for a day or two.

Your body is adapting quickly! And as you adjust to the new exercises, you’ll be less and less sore from it.

So when is soreness helpful, if ever? ​ Soreness can give us a useful signal that we worked a muscle we were trying to target and hadn’t felt before.

But if you’re SUPER sore? Like, can’t get out of bed the next day and have to waddle around like a newborn giraffe sore? That’s a sign the jump was bigger than your body needed.

And the real cost (beyond the discomfort) is that it gets in the way of your next couple of workouts. Either because your technique gets sloppy because everything hurts, or you’re so wrecked that you don’t want to show up at all.

The best way to lower your odds of severe DOMS is to ease into a new program slowly.

Start with fewer sets and lighter weights than you think you need, and build from there. 💪

Yes! You DO need to push yourself over time in order to make progress:

That’s the law of progressive overload, and there’s no getting around it.

Sometimes adding that extra bit will make you sore. Other times, it won’t.

But it’s the underlying principle that matters: are you asking a little more of yourself over time? Not: did it hurt afterward?

So why do we care so much about soreness?

Here’s what I think we’ve fallen into with fitness in general.

We as humans operate really well with feedback. If we touch a hot stove, we get burned and know not to do that again.

We want to know, immediately after doing something, whether it worked or it didn’t.

And with strength training, you don’t feel stronger the next day. It takes time to build up.

So we reach for proxies that close that feedback loop.

It’s exactly like the story of minty toothpaste.

As the story goes, toothpaste manufacturers had a hard time selling their product until they added mint.

Suddenly, there was a tingly clean feeling you could latch onto. “Oh, this IS working.”

The mint doesn’t clean your teeth. But it’s associated with the thing that does, and it gave people something to feel.

It’s not the REASON you’re getting stronger.

But it can be associated with the work you do, especially as a beginner who is new to exercise, so we’ve learned to chase the tingle.

✅ How much weight, how many reps, how many sets are you doing?

✅ Do you feel more stable and controlled with the exercise than you did last month?

Then great! It’s working. Doesn’t matter if you never get sore.

And if you do end up super sore after trying something new, it’s not that you “failed”.

Just take it as a cue to introduce things more gently next time. 😊

So, back to Rachael’s multiple choice question.

C is really close. But I’ll add an fourth option:

D) Soreness tells you what was NEW. Your training log tells you what’s WORKING.

No extra fitness points for being sore. No points off if you do end up sore, either.

All the points gently ramping things up over time, and showing up again next time. 🔥

Is it bad if I’m never sore? No. If your weights, reps, or control are improving over time, your training is working, sore or not.

How long does DOMS last? It usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after the workout and fades over a few days. If you’re regularly wrecked for longer, ease the jumps in your program.

Should I work out while sore? Mild soreness is fine to train through, and easy movement often helps. If you’re severely sore, target a different part of the body, scale down, or take another rest day; what we don’t want to do is have sloppy technique because we’re SO sore we can’t perform the exercise normally.

#8926. This Yoga Video on YouTube Is My Go-To Practice For Lower Back Discomfort

Laura Harold is a Yoga Journal editor who has practiced yoga for more than 10 years. Throughout her years as an editor in the health and wellness space, she’s spent a tremendous amount of time uncovering videos on floor stretches for lower back pain on YouTube. You can explore more yoga poses to help relieve back discomfort.

I often avoid my yoga mat as if I’m playing the “floor is lava” game from childhood. That’s typically due to my default state of caffeinated hyperactivity, wherein I’d rather scrub the baseboards and research water filters than slow down and ground myself for a few minutes. But as someone who’s experienced debilitating lower back pain on and off since I was a kid, I realized that sometimes there’s another reason for my avoidance.

Debating whether to stretch while experiencing pain can feel like a catch-22. The last thing I want to do after triggering my injury is over-stretch and incite more pain. But I’ve learned that after one to two days of requisite rest, the discomfort will circle back with a vengeance if I return to desk-sitting, driving, and couch-surfing without moving my body at least a little.

I’ve tried to search YouTube “gentle lower back yoga,” but I’ve either gotten overwhelmed by the thousands of options or, after finally choosing one and starting a practice, been disappointed by the seemingly inevitable cue to come into Down Dog or Cobra or some other pose that I knew my body wasn’t ready to try. Until the thought occurred to me that maybe “gentle yoga” wasn’t a specific enough search for me.

I did some more digging, instead searching “yoga for older adults,” and came across this 16-minute practice. I didn’t quite realize what I had been missing in the other videos until I experienced this one. The sequence moves at a slow pace, and includes clear and specific cues for mostly reclining postures that can be dialed back if needed, depending on how I’m feeling. For instance, if I’m tending to intense lower back pain, I usually avoid the supine spinal twists in favor of a few Windshield Wipers.

There’s also something about the moments of silence the instructor offers throughout that allow me enough space to hear my own thoughts and determine whether I’m feeling enough of a stretch, too much of a stretch, or need to skip it altogether. Some days, the few core-strengthening exercises in the video are just what I need to feel more supported in my lower back. Other days, I opt to close my eyes and take a few deep breaths instead, which feels equally important.

I think the biggest relief I’ve experienced after finding this practice wasn’t even physical. It was the mental burden it took away—namely, endlessly scrolling videos and debating whether I should even tempt fate by moving my lower back too soon. I’m all too familiar with that dreaded post-injury feeling of knowing that my body needs to move but wondering, “Where do I even begin?” Lately, this practice has been my starting point.
