#8925. The 67-Year-Old Who Raced Two Full Ironmans a Week Apart

Mary Mitchell won her age group in Kona and eight days later raced Ironman California, where she also won her age group. Here's how she did it. (Photo: Mary Mitchell, FinisherPix)

Fresh off a sixth-place finish at the Ironman World Championship in Kona, American professional triathlete Sam Long recently took to Instagram to ask his followers a question. Should he race Ironman Florida on November 7, or give himself another two weeks to recover and race Ironman Cozumel on November 22?

Long wants to secure his qualification for the 2027 Ironman World Championship early, but the question of how quickly to return to racing after Kona is a serious one. Among the responses to his post were plenty of suggestions that he take the extra recovery time and race Cozumel instead.

After all, Kona is no ordinary Ironman. Its combination of heat, humidity, unpredictable winds and exposed terrain takes a major physical toll, even on athletes who have spent their careers preparing for those conditions. Racing another Ironman just four weeks later is ambitious enough. What about racing one eight days later?

For 67-year-old Australian age-grouper Mary Mitchell, that was precisely the challenge.

On October 10, Mitchell won the women’s 65-69 age group at the Ironman World Championship in Kona, finishing in 13:11:46. Eight days later, she lined up at Ironman California in Sacramento, where she crossed the finish line in 11:32:45, more than 90 minutes faster than her Kona performance.

And she won her age group again. Even more remarkably, her husband, Andrew, 66, who had also raced in Kona, joined her in Sacramento and won his age group too.

What began as a somewhat improbable endurance experiment ended with three age-group victories between them.

The idea wasn’t actually Mary’s. Earlier this year, Mary and Andrew traveled to Morocco to spend time altitude training in the Atlas Mountains with a friend. During the trip, their friend floated an intriguing challenge. What would happen if a bunch of athletes in their 60s attempted two full-distance Ironmans a week apart?

“He persuaded us that it would be a good human experiment to do, to see whether, at our age, you could do two Ironmans in eight days, and what would that be like?” Mitchell explains.

The plan was for all three to qualify for Kona, race the World Championship, and then travel to Sacramento for Ironman California the following weekend.

There was just one problem. Their friend subsequently suffered a knee injury and withdrew from the experiment. But Mary and Andrew had already committed. Their flights and accommodation were booked and the race entries paid for.

“We thought, well, we might as well go,” Mitchell recalls. “How bad can it be?”

They also had the encouragement – or perhaps bad influence – of American friends Jill and Dougin Walker, serial Ironman competitors who have completed around 100 Ironmans apiece.

“We’ve fallen in with a bad crowd,” she jokes.

For Mitchell, who has completed around 30 Ironmans since her first in 2004, racing twice in eight days was uncharted territory. The closest she had previously come was roughly a month between Kona and Ironman Malaysia.

But Mitchell also had another reason to make the most of Kona.

Mitchell had previously won her age group at the Ironman World Championship in 2019. Since then, however, her attempts to return to the top of the podium had been repeatedly derailed.

In 2022, she was hit by a car while riding on the Queen Ka’ahumanu Highway just 10 days prior, preventing her from starting the race.

In 2024, at the women’s World Championship in Nice, she developed food poisoning the night before the race and abandoned roughly 140 kilometers into the bike.

Then in 2025, she returned to Kona, only to discover that what she initially believed to be a cold was COVID. She struggled throughout the race and eventually withdrew on the run.

“I had three years of thwarted attempts to do the World Championship,” she says.

Heading into 2026, Mitchell and her husband had decided this would be their final Kona appearance. They wanted to experience other races and destinations rather than continue returning to the Big Island.

And for much of the race day, Mitchell’s final Kona appearance looked unlikely to deliver another world title.

Mitchell had hoped to swim around 90 minutes, but the ocean conditions and what she admits was insufficient swim preparation conspired against her. She eventually emerged from Kailua Bay in 1:57:06.

“I had an appalling swim,” she says. “I hadn’t done enough long swimming, didn’t have enough endurance, just because swimming’s not my favorite thing.”

By the time she reached transition, Mitchell had effectively written off her chances of winning: “When I stood up out of the water, I thought, a competitive race is off the table now.”

Rather than chase positions, she decided to enjoy what she believed would be her last Ironman World Championship. Her mantra became simple: “Look after yourself and just keep chipping away at it.”

Despite the heat, wind, and particularly oppressive humidity, Mitchell began making steady progress through the field. She completed the bike in 6:38:10 and started the marathon feeling surprisingly good. She settled into a sustainable pace, making sure to take in adequate fluids and calories at every aid station.

With her husband, Andrew, also competing, there was nobody on the sidelines feeding her information about her position. It wasn’t until she reached the top of the Energy Lab, with roughly 12 kilometers remaining, that an acquaintance delivered some unexpected news.

“She said, ‘You’re first and running faster than anyone else in your age group.’ And I’m like, ‘What? No, come on.’”

Mitchell completed the marathon in 4:23:23, the fastest run in her age group, to secure her second age-group world title.

Ordinarily, the next few days would have been devoted to celebrating, recovering and enjoying the satisfaction of a long-awaited victory. Instead, she had another Ironman looming.

Following the Kona awards dinner and a celebratory glass of wine, Mary and Andrew flew to Sacramento, arriving on Monday with less than a week remaining before their next race.

There was no elaborate recovery protocol, no special preparation, and definitely no attempt to squeeze in additional fitness.

“We rode our bikes for an hour to an hour and a half along the river trail a couple of times, which was really nice,” Mitchell recalls.

The rides were deliberately easy, simply turning their legs over while enjoying the scenery and wildlife. She also completed a couple of short runs no longer than 30 minutes or demanding.

Her only swim was a brief dip in the river to test the water temperature and a new wetsuit, purchased after her previous one split during a 70.3 race in Leipzig, Germany, earlier in the trip.

More surprisingly, Mitchell wasn’t experiencing any crippling muscle soreness she remembered from her earlier Ironman days.

“It’s strange. They sort of ached, but they didn’t actually feel sore,” she explains.

She believes advances in running shoe technology have made a meaningful difference to how her legs feel after an Ironman. She raced in “super shoes” but suspects recovering from back-to-back marathons would have been considerably harder in the shoes available a decade ago.

Still, there was plenty of uncertainty. When asked whether she questioned the wisdom of attempting another Ironman, Mary laughs: “Oh, I thought about that just about every day.”

“If they’d had a half [Ironman] race, I probably would have dropped down to that distance.”

She reasoned that California’s current-assisted, wetsuit-legal swim would be far less demanding than Kona’s ocean swim. The flat, relatively straightforward bike course also appeared manageable.

But the marathon was another matter entirely.

“My big concern throughout the whole week was the run. Can you do two marathons in eight days with having raced in Kona with the conditions that are notoriously one of the more difficult races that you can do?”

Mitchell had trained specifically for Kona and made no adjustments to prepare for the double. Whatever happened in Sacramento would simply happen.

As expected, the California swim was a very different experience. Thanks to the river current and wetsuit, Mitchell emerged from the water in approximately 55 minutes, effectively halving her swim time from Kona.

But the bike wasn’t entirely without incident. Early in the ride, Mitchell developed significant pain in her quadriceps muscle and her shin. By the end of the first 90-kilometer lap, she was seriously considering pulling out.

“I was thinking, should I stop? It’s really quite sore,” she recalls. “Am I causing damage?”

She decided to continue to the next aid station and reassess, knowing she could stop at any point. Eventually, the pain subsided.

With no expectations, and already holding her Kona qualification for the following year, Mitchell approached the rest of the race with an unusually relaxed attitude. She chatted with volunteers, stopped when necessary, and enjoyed the atmosphere.

“I was just chilled the entire race because I didn’t have anything to prove,” she explains.

The marathon, her greatest concern, proved surprisingly manageable. Rather than experiencing the crushing fatigue she had anticipated, Mitchell found herself settling into a rhythm. The crowds were enthusiastic, the aid stations welcoming, and she passed the kilometers chatting with other competitors.

Her marathon time, 4:23:30, was almost identical to the one she had run in Kona eight days earlier. When she crossed the finish line in 11:32:45, she had not only completed the experiment but had also won her age group again. Andrew had done the same.

“To our astonishment, we both won our age groups,” Mitchell says.

Perhaps even more surprising was how they felt afterward.

“When we first started this sport, you do an Ironman and basically couldn’t walk for three days. Getting up out of a chair was really difficult and painful.”

This time, within 24 to 48 hours, both felt remarkably normal.

Mitchell discovered triathlon in her 30s, partly because Andrew was already involved in sport and she was tired of being left at home while he trained. She bought a cheap bike, started entering local short-course events and quickly fell in love with the sport and its community.

Her first Ironman came in 2004 at Busselton in Western Australia. Like many newcomers, she initially assumed it would be a one-off experience. More than two decades later, she’s still going.

Now retired and living in Adelaide, Mitchell trains up to 20-25 hours per week during her biggest blocks. She has worked with a coach for many years and increasingly recognizes the importance of strength training and nutrition, particularly in preserving muscle mass as she ages. Around five years ago, she also began working with a sports dietitian to improve her fueling, gut training, and overall nutritional approach.

But Mitchell is quick to point out that endurance sport doesn’t consume her entire existence. She enjoys good food, wine, socializing, reading and traveling with Andrew. And while she is competitive, she says curiosity is an even greater motivation.

“I just want to see how far I can push myself,” she explains.

Since retiring, Mitchell has challenged herself to do “at least one thing each year that takes me out of my comfort zone.”

Last year, that meant racing Patagonman in Chile, confronting her dislike of cold water by jumping from a ferry into a freezing cold fjord to start the race. This year, it was the Kona-California double. Next year, she’s already entered the 100-kilometer Tarawera ultramarathon in New Zealand.

For Mitchell, the biggest reward of the double wasn’t another age-group victory. It was discovering that, at age 67, she could still surprise herself.

“I think it resets your mind. It resets your thinking about what your body can achieve. And what mentally you can achieve,” she reflects.

The experience also reinforced what she loves about triathlon: the places it takes her, the friendships it creates, and the opportunities to challenge assumptions about her own limitations.

“It’s taught me that you’re stronger than you think you are, mentally and physically.”

Would she ever attempt two Ironmans in eight days again?

“No. Absolutely not. There’s no need to repeat the experiment!”

For all the satisfaction of the achievement, Mitchell admits she would have liked more time to savor her second Kona world title. Instead, almost immediately, she was packing up and preparing to race again.

“It would have been nice to just chill and enjoy it a little bit more,” she explains. “Have a couple more glasses of wine, soak it in.”

But the experience did change one thing: Despite initially declaring that 2026 would be their last Kona, Mary and Andrew have both accepted qualifying slots to next year’s World Championship.

#8924. How Fast Do You Actually Lose Strength? Slower Than You Think

You lose strength much more slowly than you probably think.

A few days off changes basically nothing, measurable losses take roughly two to four weeks depending on the quality (muscle endurance fades first, maximal strength last).

Muscle memory makes rebuilding faster than building the first time, and maintaining takes a fraction of the training that building did.

Here’s the timeline, and how it can inform your training.

Has this question ever crossed your mind:

This was an awesome question that Charles sent my way. (Thanks Charles! 🙌)

When life gets crazy and you find yourself skipping workouts, there’s a voice that says:

I had that exact thought the first time I had to take significant time away for a back injury.

And heck, just recently my kiddos brought home the “crud” from school and I missed a full week of workouts.

So, let’s look at what actually happens, and what it means for your training.

Short version: a few days off doesn’t impact your maximum strength or muscle size basically at all.

Your muscles may look or feel “flatter”, but that’s because stored water and glycogen decrease, not because you are weaker.

And this “pump” comes back quickly once you start training again. 💪

Here’s a rough timeline of when we start to see the effects of detraining:

Highly trained folks and older adults will notice detraining faster than new or younger lifters (so they’ll sit towards the beginning of these timelines.)

But you don’t lose your progress in any meaningful way after a week or 2 away from the gym. 😊

And if you DO have to spend significant time away for whatever reason, I have good news for you, too:

1) Your nervous system remembers how to do the movement.

The first session or two in the gym after time away may feel a bit clunky, but you’ll quickly regain the technique.

And a big component of strength is neuromuscular coordination (i.e. your brain and muscles firing together more efficiently, which improves rapidly.)

2) The muscle itself seems to hold onto some of the machinery it built, so it rebuilds faster the second time.

A general rule of thumb is about 50% as long as you were away (so if you were away for 12 weeks, it may take ~6 weeks to rebuild your strength.) Take this with a grain of salt as there is a LOT of variation here. This isn’t a hard and fast rule.

(And you don’t want to jump right back in at 100%. Use the 50/50 rule to get yourself going again.)

The point is, it’s generally easier to rebuild than to build the first time.

Building muscle and strength? It takes time and effort.

No one wakes up a day after a workout and has just magically put on 5 pounds of muscle.

That takes only a fraction of the volume.

When you keep intensity the same (i.e. how hard the exercise is), doing 1/3 the number of sets maintains your strength for a loooong time. ​ The point being: doing ANYTHING during a period where you aren’t able to consistently work out is still really really helpful!

When life throws you off track with your fitness goals, you’re not starting back from square zero.

And even a single session each week with a couple challenging sets is enough to hold what you’ve built until things calm down.

There’s that old saying that: “The best time to invest was 20 years ago. The next best time to invest is today.”

I think the same holds true for building up your fitness.

Every session you put in now is strength you get to keep later.

This is exactly why we built our coaching program. Because having a coach makes both of those so much smoother. ​ We take the thinking off your plate so it’s easier to get going.

We direct your limited time and effort toward the stuff that actually moves the needle. ​ AND when life pulls you away (sick kids, a work deadline, etc.) we help you maintain and get right back at it. ​ If that sounds like the kind of help you’ve been looking for, here’s how NF Coaching works. 💪 ​ -Matt

#8923. Why You Keep Falling Off Your Fitness Routine (and the 2-Minute Plan That Fixes It)

Expecting yourself to stick to the same fitness routine, no matter what, is why it fails.

Because the only predictable thing about life is that it’s unpredictable.

A kid gets sick. Sleep falls apart. The to-do list explodes.

You can’t know which one is coming or when, but you can know something is, and you can build your routine to expect it.

That’s the whole trick: take two minutes and decide, in advance, exactly what you’ll do the next time life goes sideways.

Here’s the coaching conversation that shows how it works.

I want to let you in on one of my biggest lessons from the last 15 years of coaching.

Once you know it, it will feel like you can see the future. 👀

On a live Q&A, George (not his real name) told me about a pattern he kept running into.

Then a kiddo would get sick, or some other responsibility would pop up, sleep would fall apart for a bit, and the whole routine would go with it.

And he got this look like “Oooooohhhhhhhh…no. No I haven’t.”

He’d been treating the sick kid as something that happens to the plan.

So we talked through it right there. Here’s what we came up with:

Now, he wasn’t just reacting in the moment, trying to “gut it out.”

He knew exactly what to do and it fit what he needed.

Here’s the thing: these moments don’t come out of the blue. They are predictable.

You’ll have WAY too much on your to-do list.

I don’t know which one, or when exactly, but I do know that it’s inevitable.

Once we accept that the only predictable thing is that life is unpredictable, we can use that to our advantage.

Take two minutes right now and finish this sentence:

First blank: the thing that knocked you off track the last time you were trying to get into a fitness routine.

Second blank: the best version of your plan you can still commit to on one of THOSE days.

Sometimes, life will throw something at you that you REALLY didn’t see coming.

But the more of these you’ve been through, the clearer the crystal ball becomes.

And the better you get at navigating it. 💪

Hit reply and send me your crystal ball plan. I read every one, and I’ll tell you if I’d tweak it.

-Matt ​ ​P.S. This is exactly the type of stuff we work on in our coaching program. My job as your coach is to look into my crystal ball, and help you plan ahead so you don’t get blindsided. 🔮👀 Learn more about how coaching works [HERE].

#8922. Triathlon Gear Our Editors Used and Loved in October 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

It’s officially the off-season. In Ohio, we’re having the best fall, where no one complains about the weather (rare for Ohioans) and no wind or rain storms have blown through, robbing us of the vibrant change in the leaves. Hiking is a staple way to enjoy the crunchy leaves, swimming has moved fully indoors, and biking has a sort of leisure to it that it doesn’t have when the landscape is green.

As we slow down and explore other outdoor hobbies in the coming months, here’s a look at the gear our editors are reaching for.

This might seem like an unusual choice for a triathlete, but as the race season winds down and we transition from workouts to just-getting-out, I find myself blasting all of my tempo trainers to the back of my closet in favor of this pair of Jeep-wheel-level all-terrain crushers. For those unfamiliar with Norda, the Canadian brand hit the scene in 2021 (bad timing, sorry) with the release of their ultra-premium — read: ultra-expensive — $285 shoe dubbed the 001. Folks had a field day with the high price, but few could deny that the 001 was something different than what was out there already.

Fast forward to today, and Norda is still (crazy) expensive, but they also still offer shoes that are entirely novel in the increasingly crowded trail running shoe world. The 055 was released earlier this summer as a maximal take on the well-loved, but race-focused 005. For me, I love how you can point your foot at literally anything and the thick-but-stable base will eat it up. Better yet, the woven gaiter adds another layer of stability and protection, meaning you don’t really have to think much about where you put your feet, allowing me to, quite simply, zone out and enjoy the view. And that’s what fall “training” is all about, anyway.

Winter is coming, which in Phoenix means two things: socks come out of storage, and they better be day-glo. Because I live and train downtown, where traffic is abundant and drivers are always (always!) distracted, I dress as obnoxiously as possible to make sure they see me. That means neon fabrics, reflective materials, and LED lights on as many points as possible.

Years ago, I interviewed a safety expert who said you especially want these materials on the parts of your body that move he most when you ride or run, as movement is more likely to catch the eye of a driver. These bright socks have reflective yarn woven into the fabric, making my legs easier to spot on rides and runs. They’re comfortable, they stay up, and they stand up to multiple runs and laundry cycles each week.

Do I look like a 90s fever dream in my neon wardrobe? I sure do. But you’ll see me coming from a mile away, and that’s the whole point.

I haven’t had long hair in the 14 years I’ve been a triathlete — until now. I hate the feeling of hair skimming my neck or swishing back and forth as I run, so it has to be all the way up in the ugliest messy bun. Basically, I’m the opposite of Marjolaine Pierré.

I found that the Goody ComforFlex holds my hair well without pulling, no matter the intensity of workouts. And I don’t end up with tons of hair wrapped around them, which leads me to believe they are keeping my hair at least somewhat healthy despite regular chlorine exposure and frequent washes.

They’ve also held up well, so I can use the same one for at least a month before replacing it.

I’m ashamed to admit I’ve been one of *those* triathletes showing up at the local bike shop, frazzled and looking for the nearest mechanic, then frantically explaining how my seat clamp fell down my downtube and lodged itself somewhere seemingly impossible to reach. Yes, this happened to me at Ironman Chattanooga last year. As someone who prides myself on fixing my own bike issues, this was and still is my worst nightmare.

But I know I’m not alone. Between packing and trying to fit in final workouts ahead of travel, we triathletes can make some poor choices. Add to it that we’re limited in what tools we can bring to fix the problems we create, and it’s a recipe for disaster. Even when we have room and enough weight left to throw them in the bag, we often rush the pack job and toss them in without much organization.

After Chattanooga, I vowed to be more prepared. That’s when a friend showed me this trusty little roll-up tool bag that they use for camping. Small enough that it doesn’t take up all the room, big enough to fit what I need, and cheap enough to buy one for myself and a friend. It was the perfect recommendation.

And the best thing is you don’t have to travel for triathlon to get use out of it. Mine hangs in the garage when I’m home, and I use it every time I work on my bike.

— Travis Mundell, social media strategist

#8921. This Seated Twist Stretches Your Spine, Engages Your Core, and Enhances Your Awareness

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about a seated twist first appeared in the March-April 1994 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

To encourage new perceptual skills in my students, I like to ask them from time to time to practice in a new spot in the yoga studio. If you’re like most people, after a few classes you find yourself regularly gravitating to the same location, often within a few inches of accuracy.

The mere suggestion to place your mat in the front of the room instead of the cozy corner may make you decidedly un-comfortable. Changing positions enables you to see yourself and the world from a different vantage point, much as a photographer might circle a subject to get pictures from different angles.

It’s not surprising, considering the propensity of our species to form habits, that we tend to perceive our bodies from one perspective, including some aspects of ourselves while leaving others out.

Thus our perception of our body may become like a two-dimensional sketch, deprived of the volume, form, and texture that would extend our awareness into the three-dimensional realm. While Eastern cultures have investigated and honored the inner layers of the body as the key to our physical, mental, and spiritual health, most Western cultures have concerned themselves primarily with the body’s superficial layers. Because of this bias, most of us have come to view our movements as entirely dictated by the muscles and bones, unconsciously deleting other systems from our awareness. Keeping the mind on the outer layers, we become unable to feel or act from our deeper selves.

One of the body systems that brings us most succinctly into a deeper sense of self are the organs, the contents of the musculoskeletal container. Awareness of the organs gives our movements volume, form, and a sense of ripe fullness. Through the health and vitality of the organs, the outer layers gain their strength and form.

Just as we might bring our attention to the sensation of a muscle stretching, we can bring our attention to the sensation of an internal organ. When we change the vantage point of our awareness to bring the inner body into the foreground (an inner adjustment analogous to moving to a different place in the yoga studio), the way we experience ourselves and the quality of our movement will be quite different.

For most of recorded history, yogis have been engaged in just this kind of research, exploring the effects that the asanas (as well as pranayama and meditation) have on the deeper, subtler bodily systems. The ancient practitioners noted which movements and practices stimulated, purified, sedated, or neutralized the energy currents moving deep within the body, correlating these phenomena to health, longevity, and the elevation of consciousness. By contrast, they were not terribly interested in the state of their hamstring muscles, and traditional texts make few references to such structures.

Movements that twist the body compress, elongate, and massage the inner organs. Unfortunately, twists are often practiced exclusively from the perspective of the musculoskeletal system; we use the strength of the muscles and the leverage of the bones to force the body into rotation without ever inviting the soft inner contents along for the ride. Focusing on the internal organs not only reduces the possibility of injury, but stimulates and tones these deep structures by bringing our attention to them, just as electrical activity is created in our muscles simply by visualizing them flexing.

In this article, we’re going to look at how changing the vantage point of our awareness affects the practice of Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi (Marichyasana III), a seated twist.

Bringing attention to the inner body is a way to physically organize our presence on this center. Knowing that there is nowhere to “get to,” we can proceed with the full knowledge that we are on our way.

The following exercise was adapted from Sensing, Feeling, and Action by Bonnie Bainbridge Cohen. Sit on a cushion or blanket with your legs crossed. Close your eyes and let yourself settle. Bring your awareness to the soft inner contents of the torso surrounded by the musculoskeletal container. Imagine your body as two concentric cylinders with the soft internal organs on the inside and the harder musculoskeletal system surrounding them. Feel how the rise and fall of the breath swells from the core and communicates itself to the outer layer.

Now gently bring your awareness to each of your major organs. In the chest is the heart, slightly to the left of center, with the lungs on either side. In the upper left quadrant of the abdomen is the stomach; in the upper right quadrant of the belly is the liver, which extends up underneath the rib cage. The small intestines occupy most of the central and lower belly. In the lower right quadrant of the belly, the small intestine becomes the large intestine, which makes a hairpin turn to run up the right side of the belly (the ascending colon), across the top (the transverse colon), and down the left side (the descending colon), finishing as the sigmoid colon and rectum.

You may want to refer to an anatomy text for a more in-depth discussion of the internal organs. For now, sense their general position and volume, using your breath to palpate them. The kidneys lie on either side of the spine above the waist. The uterus is deep in the abdomen above the pubic bone.

Now bring your attention to your skeletal structure, as if you were seeing the body with X-ray vision. Extend your right arm over your head and bend to the left, focusing your attention on the bones moving. Repeat this to the other side.

Returning to the first side, initiate the side bend from the skeleton and then Shift your attention to the underlying organs, focusing on elongating the organs on the right side of the body and compressing the organs on the left. Did you go further? How did the quality of the movement change as your focus shifted?

Now initiate the side bend as a movement that arises from the organs. Breathe into and elongate the organs on the right side of the body, letting the skeleton follow. How did this experience differ from the one in which you had your mind on the skeletal system alone?

The organs are the seat of our deepest emotions; we physically experience strong feelings as sensations in the viscera (for example, the butterflies of fear or the tight knot of anger). Therefore, many people find that when they initiate movement from the organ system, the movement seems to arise out of their deepest self—that is, there is not a dualistic sense that the mind is “doing something” to the body. By contrast, when you perceive the body as nothing but a skeleton, it may feel as though your mind is manipulating your body like a puppet on a string.

Now integrate this new awareness of your organs into a simple twisting posture.

Some preliminary suggestions may make your task easier. One of the obstacles to twisting freely is the inability to sit upright with the normal curves of the spinal column intact. When the legs are extended, this problem may be further exaggerated because the hamstrings may pull on the base of the pelvis, causing the back to round (Figure 1: Incorrect). In this position, you are actually sitting on the base of the spine rather than on the sitting bones, and the collapse of the outer body makes it difficult to breathe freely.

To make sitting—and therefore twisting—a little easier, this first variation calls for both legs to be folded. By deactivating the hamstrings, we allow the pelvis to move more freely into an upright position.

Sit cross-legged with the buttocks elevated on a blanket or cushion. Place the right leg so the shin is upright, with the sole of the right foot directly in front of the left ankle. Inhaling fully, allow the abdomen to expand freely. On your exhalation roll the abdomen to the right, guiding the abdomen back against the spine to encourage the twist. Bring your left elbow onto the outside of the right knee (Figure 2).

With each breath, allow the soft inner body to move circularly in the direction of the twist, very much as if you were doing a belly dance. Once the lower torso is turning freely to the right, direct the breath more fully into the right side of the chest. Expanding the right lung with the inhalation, encourage the thoracic spine to move in and up. As you exhale, release the left lung from the center of the chest out into the shoulder, allowing the muscles along the back of the body to follow the changing shape of the lung.

As this occurs, the shoulder blade and then the arm will move further around.

Replace the elbow against the knee as necessary. When you feel you have reached your limit, stay for a few more breaths, simply letting the inhalation and exhalation oscillate the body slightly to and fro. Release on an exhalation and then repeat on the other side.

Now extend both legs in front of you, placing a blanket underneath your buttocks if necessary to create an erect sitting position. Sit with your back one arm’s length from a wall. Bend your right knee, placing the heel of the right foot in line with the sitting bone of the right side of the pelvis. Extend downward through the length of the left leg, simultaneously pressing the right foot down into the floor. Feel how this groundedness through the bones rebounds up through the body as the energy flows through the soft organs and the bones to support the erect carriage of the torso. When you release the downward movement of the legs, notice how the spine sags and the whole torso wilts.

Sense how the movements of the muscles and bones affect the shape of the internal organs, and vice versa.

As you inhale, direct the breath into the mid and upper chest. With each exhalation, successively turn from the lowest part of the belly to the head. Bring your elbow onto the outside of the right knee and place your hand against the wall, making sure that you are far enough from the wall that the shoulder is not elevated toward the ears (Figure 3). Use your arm to lift and support the torso, but do not overpower the soft movements of the inner body by using the arm to forcefully turn the outer muscles. Instead of using the arm as a “dictator,” let your arm become a “guide.” In the same way, wait for the inner body to yield to the movement, then encourage it with the guiding arm.

Take a few more full breaths before releasing and repeating the movement on the second side.

In this exercise you will focus on the contents of the spine—the spinal cord—to bring deeper awareness to your movement. Begin by sitting in Staff Pose (Dandasana) with both legs extended. Bend the left knee and place the heel of the left foot in line with the sitting bone. Now place the left hand immediately behind the left buttock and use it to support the trunk.

Before beginning the twist, take a moment to bring a few central images to mind. Start by bringing your awareness to the contents of the skull. Sense whether the brain is balanced equally between the front and back of the skull. Exiting the brain is the brain stem; then the spinal cord runs through each vertebrae like thread running through a string of beads.

Think of your spinal cord as the tail of your brain and the vertebrae as individual beads, each with its own size and shape.

As you bring your awareness to the brain stem, notice how the spinal cord curves inward so that the cervical vertebrae stack up underneath the head. As you continue your mental journey down the back, the soft spinal cord curves outward, following the convex curve of the thoracic spine. As you move your attention down toward the base of the rib cage, the spinal cord loops back in and the five lumbar vertebrae stack directly under the center of the chest. Continue on down to the massive sacral bone which curves outward and articulates with the two wings of the pelvis.

Having established this anatomical map, begin to sense how the bones of the spine are positioned in relationship to the soft spinal cord. Are there any areas of the spinal cord that feel compressed, perhaps even red and sore from being pressed and rubbed by the bodies of the vertebrae? Are there vertebrae that feel as if they were glued together, or areas where the bones feel rotated or collapsed on one side? Use your breath to gently move your vertebrae as if you were rearranging very precious antique furniture in a room. Adjust the vertebrae so they glide over the spinal cord easily.

As you enter the twist, continue to gauge your movement to avoid any irritation to the spinal cord. (While the brain is insensitive to pain, the outer sheath of the spinal cord is richly supplied with sensory nerve fibers.) Imagine that you are initiating the movement from the level of the spinal cord. If you overpower the spine with the strength of the arm, the result will often be irritation in the spine during the twist and an ache in the back long after your practice is finished.

Once the torso has rotated so the chest is facing the left knee, you can take the “hand lock” by bringing the right arm around the outside of the left shin. Link the fingers or, if possible, hold the left wrist with the right hand. Exhale and draw the hands away from the shoulders, allowing the spine to lengthen strongly upward.

If taking the hand lock compresses the front of the abdomen and collapses the spine, you are moving your skeleton further than the organs can support. Be conscious of using your breath to shape the internal organs. Keep the front of the abdomen open and draw the base of the left rib cage in toward the waist to encourage full spinal extension. Turn the head to look back at the foot of the extended leg (Figure 4). Take a few more breaths and then release. Repeat on the other side.

To clarify the distinction between initiating movement from the inner body and dominating with the outer muscles, you might try the previous exercises again, this time exerting force with the outer body by using the arm as a strong lever. Notice the tone in the muscle tissue when you exert force from the outside, as opposed to the quality when you allow the inner body to give to the movement in its own time. Also notice how the two different ways of initiating movement create different psychological states.

Within each of us is a longing for wholeness. Like the spiraling shape of the twist, our spiritual path must constantly turn back toward the still center within us. The longing to “get somewhere” through yoga is a distortion of our true urge to return back to the undifferentiated, unchanging core from which all life expands.

#8920. Overwhelmed by Fitness Advice? You Need an Action Plan, Not a Perfect Plan

Do you ever feel like you’re stuck at the starting line?​ ​ You want to improve your health and fitness. But there’s so. much. going. on.

Every time you try to make a plan, you get 1,000 opinions on the “perfect” workout. The “perfect” diet. The “perfect” routine.

You’re not sure where to start or what to do.

I hear this story so often that I gave it a name. And a face. 😅

(h/t to Leo, our awesome illustrator who makes these images for us from scratch! 🙌 ) ​ Meet Major Overload.

He’s every fitness voice on the internet at once.

Do this. Never do that. Fasted cardio. Never fasted cardio. Carbs are fine. Carbs are the enemy.

The Major loves it when you have 100 tabs open on your browser, but haven’t done a workout yet.

He wants to keep you plugged in to The Matrix. He feeds off of you staying stuck in planning mode while he drains your batteries.

My client Eric ran into him a few months ago.

He’d spent weeks searching for “best at-home workouts to lose fat”. ​ In his words:

It’s the way I felt when I tasked myself with running Nerd Fitness’s Instagram.

A million different opinions on how to do it. Hours spent researching. And weeks later, I still hadn’t filmed an actual video yet. 😅

I was firmly stuck in analysis paralysis.

Same boss battle as Eric. Different rabbit hole.

What got me unstuck was the same thing that helped Eric.

It wasn’t finding the “perfect” strategy or plan.

1) Follow one plan and block out everything else for now.​ ​ ​2) Commit to taking some small action, most days of the week.

The first one turned Major Overload’s volume down.

I didn’t need every voice. I needed a simple starting point. One that didn’t have a gajillion hoops to jump through.

The second one is where the learning actually happened.

I didn’t have to be perfect. I had to commit to imperfect reps.

I’ve learned more from a couple of weeks of posting than from all the agonizing I did beforehand.

Here’s what I told Eric, and what I’d tell you, too:

Unless you’re Doctor Strange, scrubbing through 14 million possible futures to find the one where everything works out, you can’t know what perfect looks like. Neither can I. Nor anyone on the internet, no matter how loud they get.

Enough structure to get out there and do the thing. Not so convoluted that you never get started.

That’s why we built the Beginner Bodyweight Workout and our Strength Training Templates.

So you stop getting stuck at the starting line, and start putting in the reps.

Moving from planning to action does two things at once.

It breaks the inertia, and it teaches you what fits in YOUR life.

It’s where you learn that, actually, training later in the evening works better for you than trying to force yourself up at 5AM.

It’s how you discover that splitting your workout up into two 15-minute chunks works better for your schedule.

Or that you prefer training with weights to training with bands.

You won’t know those things until you get out there and try.

It’s just as important to learn what DOESN’T work for you as what does.

Three weeks of taking imperfect action will tell you more about what works for you than three months of listening to Major Overload ever could.

Instead of searching for the “perfect” plan, build your action plan.

1 or 2 actions you can take this week, small enough to test and see how they feel.

That’s exactly what we did with Eric. ​ We mapped out his first few action steps. Things that fit his life, and he felt confident doing.

#8919. How to Hold Yourself Accountable Without Beating Yourself Up

Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.

When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.

Someone standing over you going “What were you thinking? Why did you skip that? Do you even want this?“

(And if there’s no drill sergeant handy, we do a pretty good job of beating ourselves up all on our own.)

Here’s the thing: if being hard on yourself worked, it would have worked by now.

Great accountability isn’t built on being a hard-ass.

It’s built on forward momentum and honest feedback.

The drill sergeant questions YOU. Your motivation. How much you want it.

Real accountability helps you try again quickly.

Then helps you see what you’re doing well and what can improve.

A client of mine had a hectic week. Travel, out of their routine, workouts missed.

The drill sergeant move is “why didn’t you do your workouts?!” at the exact moment they were already struggling.

“Hey! I know this has been a hectic week. Let’s do some push-ups together. Do a set next chance you get and shoot me a 👍. I’ll do one too.”

This got a 👍 and a “Thanks for the encouragement! This week has been so hectic my schedule got away from me.”

Then we build off of that by looking ahead to the next few days.

“How’s the rest of this week looking for strength training? I went ahead and put together a few variations in case you’re short on time.”

When you’re already struggling, the question isn’t “hey, why didn’t you do that?”

Then looking ahead to what’s coming up after that.

But forward momentum is only the first part of the equation.

The second step is giving honest feedback on both the wins AND the challenges.

To be a neutral observer. To point out what’s going well, what’s not, and suggest how we can improve it moving forward.

Based on the actual human in front of me: their unique goals, motivations, and whatever flavor of chaos they have going on in their own life (work, family, travel, illness, injury, etc.)

“Hey! I reviewed the strength workout on Friday. Solid work all around here. I can see from your form check video that you’re doing a better job staying balanced across your whole foot on the squat. 💪

I also noticed that the middle of the week has been tougher to get consistent workouts in. You’ve hit 2 out of the last 4 midweek workouts. I know work has been crazy with the project deadline you have coming up, so my guess is you’re getting buried and it makes it hard to get to the gym. Am I on the right track? I have some ideas for how we tackle that next week that I’ll drop down below in a video for you.”

This is the honest part. It didn’t go anywhere!

But instead of berating you for missing a workout, the goal is to look at all the evidence and suggest next steps.

Including if the evidence says that something BIG needs to change. It’s all on the table.

Accountability isn’t punishment for what you didn’t do.

It’s helping you decide what you do next.

If your week went haywire, before you beat yourself up, take this approach:

#8918. Bored With Your Workout? Try a New Level, Not a New Program

This was the first thing a new client said to me.

When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:

Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.

Nerd Fitness Coaching was the latest in a long line of fresh starts.

And here’s the thing: all of it was GOOD.

She was moving. She was trying new things. She was having fun (at least at first).

She felt like she kept starting over and never getting anywhere.

And she wanted help figuring out what to do.

Let’s be real: trying something new is exciting.

A new program, a new class, a new challenge. There’s a buzz to it.

And that buzz isn’t bad. Enjoying it is a big part of what keeps people moving.

The catch is that most goals need some repetition.

Getting stronger, running farther, learning a skill. You get better at the things you practice again and again.

So the question isn’t “how do I stop getting bored?”

It’s “how do I keep some of that new-thing fun AND repeat things enough to see progress?” 🧐

When I built her program, I kept its overall shape the same week to week.

But inside it, a few key exercises got a target. Something like:

“Once you can do 12 reps with 25 pounds, we level up.”

The targets were far enough away to stretch her, and close enough that she could hit them in 2 to 6 weeks of focused practice.

When she hit one, we leveled up that exercise: new reps or weight, or a new variation. Everything else stayed put.

There was always a target she was closing in on and a level she’d recently beaten.

But the frame stayed the same. We were still working on the same overall qualities.

And that’s what let her progress stack up instead of resetting every few weeks.

She was able to stay really consistent with her program.

But when she came back, she wasn’t looking for something new.

She was excited to pick up her program and keep progressing.

And sure, sometimes her goals would change.

We spent 6 months training for her first half marathon, then switched gears to focus on building muscle.

If you love bouncing between things and you’re happy doing it, keep bouncing.

This is for when the bouncing starts to feel frustrating.

Before you reach for a new program, try a new level.

✅ Set a target you could reach in 2 to 6 weeks (a rep count or a weight)

✅ When you hit it, level up that one exercise with new reps, a new weight, or a new variation. Leave everything else alone.

I’m excited to see what you come up with. 😃

#8917. Veterans Who Turned to Yoga Are Now Teaching It—And Not Always in the Places You’d Expect

Veterans yoga has been in existence for decades, with several organizations providing free classes. But what has been changing is the number of veterans teaching yoga, both to their peers and the general public. Writer “Chez” Chesak explores how his former platoonmates and other former military personnel are introducing others to the practice.

When I was deployed to Iraq with the U.S. Army in 2005, me and the rest of my platoon were constantly jumping in and out of Humvees, ascending uneven stairs in buildings, climbing ladders in guard towers, and generally finding ourselves in constant motion—all with more than 80 pounds of armor, ammo, night vision goggles, and other combat load sitting on our shoulders. And then there was the tremendous and relentless emotional and psychological stress. Needless to say, we were all very wired and very, very tight.

One proactive and thoughtful soldier in our platoon, Jake Smith, suggested that yoga could probably help and offered to download some instructions and lead us through a class. For some reason—quite possibly to stay out of sight from other soldiers, who would have likely ridiculed us—we thought it best to climb onto the roof of our building in Kirkuk for an ad hoc yoga session. Jake, who was definitely not a certified instructor but certainly did his best, led us through various poses and we attempted to follow along.

Somewhere in between making shapes with my body and concentrating on my breath, it registered that there were dozens of buildings in plain view of our patrol base. And if we could see the surrounding buildings, anyone in those buildings could see us. Realizing that we could be in the sights of a sniper, we quickly wrapped up class and made our way back inside.

For most of us, it was our first attempt at yoga. Despite the fact the class was well-intentioned and received well, none of us continued practicing during our time overseas. Instead, we succumbed to more shoulder pain and mental duress.

But in the years since, some in my platoon—as well as active military personnel and veterans everywhere—have been getting past our initial biases against such a “hippy” activity and turning to yoga for an array of reasons, including support with lingering physical and mental health challenges. I’ve heard the quote “Yoga saved my life,” from numerous military veterans who expressed the sentiment with zero embellishment, exaggeration, or hyperbole.

With nearly 16 million veterans in the U.S., there are more who could benefit from yoga. A survey of 300,000 veterans and service members registered with the Wounded Warrior Project found that more than half of respondents struggled to manage their pain, with 95 percent experiencing pain in the previous three months and 76 percent acknowledging that pain interfered with their ability to enjoy life. Additionally, more than 50 percent experienced anxiety symptoms in the previous two weeks.

Many of the veterans who proselytize about yoga know firsthand its role in supporting individuals through the repercussions of surviving combat zones. Some proceed to take yoga teacher training and introduce others to the practice, sharing it every conceivable style and practice space, including studios, gyms, and corporate offices. And among them are also those helping fellow soldiers and veterans explore how yoga might help them navigate the complexities of PTSD.

Mike Cappel used to hate yoga. He served 12 years in Military Intelligence in the Army Reserve and three years as a Combat Engineer in the National Guard and readily admits his past loathing for the practice.

Thanks to doctor’s orders, he tried yoga, fell in love with it, and then took a summer class at the University of Cincinnati (U.C.). Cappel now teaches yoga to the Reserve Officers Training Corps cadets there, beginning with cadets who participated in his yoga warm-ups before the Army Combat Fitness Test (ACFT) swearing that they scored higher thanks to the practice.

“They all say they love it now,” says Cappel. “And I can see that they really do. We’ll have a whole battalion of people out there in the stadium first thing in the morning, all doing yoga.” The officers that run the program eventually decided to try his classes as well,and these days everyone does yoga together before taking the ACFT.

His yoga instruction isn’t limited to students in uniform. Cappel also teaches at the offices of corporate clients, local independent yoga studios, and chain gyms, and leads a total of 16 classes a week.

In contrast to exposing those new to the military to yoga, Chris Smith brings it to those who have come back from their tours of duty and struggle to reacclimate to everyday life. After serving as an Engineer in the Army for eight years and being deployed three times, including during the 2003 Iraq invasion, Chris separated from the military and from his wife. He was unhoused and struggling with substance abuse when he was committed to an involuntary five-day psychiatric hold at a hospital.

Eventually, Chris landed in a rental assistance program through Veteran Affairs (VA), used the GI Bill to get a degree from Marywood University, and then started a veteran resource center. In researching benefits, he learned about Warrior Strong, which provides free wellness services, including yoga, to veterans across 33 states.

Chris explains that after taking his first yoga class, he was hooked. He soon signed up for training to become an instructor. He and other Warrior Strong instructors currently deliver nearly 100 classes spanning yoga, fitness, meditation, and breathwork to veterans each month. The classes are conducted online as well as in-studio at the Scranton, Pennsylvania, location as well regional VA medical centers. He also volunteers his teaching time to a weekly breathwork class for the depression group at a local veterans center and a monthly meditation class at the drug and alcohol unit at a VA Medical Center.

“Yoga is what’s really helping me manage my PTSD symptoms,” says Chris. “It’s helped me reconnect with people because for a very long time I was isolating myself a lot. I credit it with helping me continue the journey that I started nine years ago.”

Other veterans take elements of how yoga best supports them and share it with a more generalized student population. Jessica Armendariz spent 21 years in the U.S. Army, serving in the Airborne, completing all four levels of the Amy’s Combatives hand-to-hand combat training, and deploying to Afghanistan. When she retired, her body was experiencing severe physical wear, joint pain, and elevated cortisol levels. She eventually found that practicing rigorous vinyasa yoga helped alleviate chronic pain and quiet her racing mind.

Armendariz currently teaches studio classes at Hot Asana in Southern Pines, North Carolina, and tries to share the same benefits with others. “I am trying to challenge you physically,” says Armendariz. “That’s not to say that the rest of the yoga goes out the window. Of course we do breathing, we do centering, and all those critical things, but for me, for it to work to feel authentic to me as a teacher, there has to be that challenge.” She also has training in yoga nidra as well as yin and restorative yoga.

Sometimes the adaptability of yoga and its built-in community become as much a part of the yoga experience as the poses. After Jeremy McMullen left the Navy, he became severely sedentary. That’s when his wife gifted him a yoga lesson. The retired Chief Petty Officer instantly found that it benefited his sleep as well as his physical and mental health. Now a yoga instructor, McMullen teaches in a studio, performs yoga on mountain passes during long-distance hikes, has led online classes, and teaches “beer yoga” at breweries, where the participants indulge in a beer or two together afterward.

McMullen sees a correlation between his role in the Navy and his role as an instructor. “The chiefs at work [in the Navy] are always trying to teach sailors the right way to do everything. I do the same thing as a yoga teacher, making sure to teach you your left and your right and your breathing and your mindfulness.”

Military veterans are no strangers to working in unexpected and remote places. Jared McKenzie, a medic in my platoon when we deployed, currently teaches yoga at studios, so it wasn’t entirely a surprise when he was inspired, during a recent multi-day whitewater rafting trip, to lead others through early morning stretches along the shore. He’ll be resuming his beach yoga classes on the outfitter’s 2027 River Soul Journeys whitewater rafting and yoga trip in Idaho.

McKenzie is looking forward to teaching yoga within the solitude and serenity of Idaho’s river canyons. “I love the juxtaposition of this trip where everyone will be blasting whitewater through the day and then slowing down in the evenings with riverside yoga and breathwork,” he says.

There are surely more vets out there who are just now trying a class and starting their own experience with yoga journey. Those who take the next step and become instructors can deploy out to studios and VA facilities, teach online, and maybe even lead a class in a river canyon or other backcountry location. And I choose to believe that none of them will be so foolish as to attempt a class on a rooftop in a combat zone.

Veterans interested in trying yoga will find free resources for veterans-focused, in-person and online classes and teacher trainings through the VA’s Whole Health program and various organizations, including Wounded Warrior Project, Veterans Yoga Project, and VEToga.

#8916. The Best Bike Lights for Triathletes in 2026, Tested and Reviewed

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Bottom Line: Each of the bike lights in our Best Bike Lights of 2026 list below has been tested on long rides by an experienced triathlete for many miles. Our reviewer is unbiased, with no brand relationships, meaning no brand has paid to appear in our list.

It’s that time of year again. You glance at your training plan, realize your post-work ride slot will now be taking place in the dark, and suddenly “bike light” jumps to the top of your shopping list. The good news is that bike lights in 2026 are significantly better than offerings from just a few years ago. You could even say they are light-years ahead (pun intended) of the bike lights from the 20th century. They are brighter, lighter, and – critically for triathletes – easier to mount on your bike than ever before.

But before you order the cheapest bike light on Amazon, there’s a bit more to think through. The cheapest option is far from the best, but you also don’t need to take out a second mortgage to buy a bike light either. Here’s what actually matters when buying lights as a triathlete, followed by the best options on the market right now.

As a light-toting triathlete, your goal isn’t just to see the road ahead of you; it is also to be seen. Public roads are far from perfectly safe, especially in today’s phone-addicted world filled with distracted drivers. But thankfully, having a bike light is one of the best ways to gain the attention of nearby drivers, reminding them to slow down and give you space as they pass by.

When shopping for a bike light, you want to consider two different design priorities, and pay close attention because most lights optimize for one or the other. First, you want a bike light that shines a powerful beam down the road, illuminating your path at speed in the dark. Second, you want a light that is designed to be seen. These lights use wide-angle optics, lateral emission, and attention-grabbing flash patterns to make you visible to cross-traffic and drivers approaching from the rear. Ideally, your bike light(s) do both.

For triathletes specifically, the lighting challenge runs deeper than a single unit on your bicycle. You might actually want three different lights for the corresponding sports. The ideal setup might include front and rear coverage on the bike, a headlamp or chest light for early-morning runs, and some form of visibility for open-water swims, especially those before sunrise. Each sport requires different hardware, but in this guide, we’ll focus on bike lights. Let’s help you figure out how to sort and sift through the hundreds of options on the market.

The standard brightness unit for sports lights is lumens. The higher the number, the brighter the light. But brighter isn’t always better. Some brands love to advertise max lumens at maximum output, but that can drain the battery in under two hours. Always check the light’s runtime at the mode you’ll actually use.

Consider the type of darkness you’ll be riding in, and how much light you’ll need. Not every triathlete will train in pitch darkness, so here is a quick reference of what you’ll find on the light market:

A pinpoint beam aimed straight ahead is great for one thing, and that’s seeing directly in front of you. But if you’re riding in the dark, you also want to have side visibility, not just from your own perspective, but for other riders and drivers to see you. The best bike lights have a wide spread beam that alerts drivers approaching from angles, not just head-on. Some lights now use multiple LEDs, which is worth considering if you ride in the dark year-round.

This is one of the most important aspects of a bike light because if the battery dies while you are riding in the dark 20 miles from home, you are SOL. Most bike lights are USB-C rechargeable, but runtime varies enormously. If you don’t get a light with a low-battery warning (ideally with several minutes of reserve before shutdown), make sure you keep tabs on how long you’ve been running it before it’s time to recharge.

This is where triathletes diverge from road cyclists. Aero bars, clip-on extensions, and non-standard cockpit shapes make standard clamp mounts useless in many setups. When shopping for lights, you’ll want to look for options that come with flexible silicone straps, GoPro-style mounts, or Garmin quarter-turn compatibility. Silicone straps cover the widest range of setups and are easy to transfer between bikes.

In the 2026 bike light market, there are a number of smart features that come with some of the more pristine options. Some of the features are just bells and whistles, but a few are genuinely helpful, especially for triathletes. Radar integration (Garmin Varia), ANT+ connectivity, automatic brightness adjustment, and brake-sensing technology are popular features that help improve function and safety on the bike. These are not marketing gimmicks – radar in particular can dramatically improve your confidence when riding on open roads with traffic.

Front light placement can be the trickiest part of lighting your tri bike. You can choose between below the basebar (the most aerodynamic option), midway down the aerobars (if the light rotates that direction), and arguably the best solution: adding a computer bridge to your aerobars and mounting the light on top or below it. Whatever you choose, test it on a bumpy road during daylight hours before relying on it in the dark. Remember that you’re not only looking for the light to stay attached, but also for the angle to remain stable as the light illuminates the road in front of you.

Rear lights are much more forgiving, with the seatpost being the most ideal spot for a rear-facing bike light. If you have limited seatpost access, you can mount a light on the seatstay. Just make sure your light is pointing backward rather than toward the sky or floor. If you have bottles or other gear mounted under or behind your seat, make sure they don’t block the bike light when they are fully loaded.

Output: 1,300 lumens front; 90 lumens rear

Battery life: 1.5 hrs front; 4.5 hrs rear

The Ion Pro and Flare bike lights do much more than illuminate through darkness. The paired set uses ANT+ to link the front and rear lights together, and you can control both from a compatible Garmin or Wahoo head unit. Up front, the Ion Pro has up to 1,300 lumens, which is more than enough for most low-light situations. It also has a clean beam pattern with solid front and side visibility, with a few hours of battery life across various power settings. In the rear, the Flare can be used with a 16-degree offset mount option that helps solve one of the most common triathlete problems: mounting a rear light on an angled seatpost or seatstay. The mount is sold separately, but it only costs $5.

Pros: ANT+ integration, offset rear mount solves tri-bike seatpost issues ($5 cost), strong front output Cons: Pricey for a set; front light only has 90 minutes of runtime at max output

Output: 130 to 1,000 lumens with six different modes

Battery life: 120 hrs on ECO FLASH; up to 2 hrs at max output

The Blinder has earned its spot on best-of lists for years, and the 2026 version is no exception. IP67 waterproofing and six different light modes make the Blinder 1000 suitable for a wide range of weather and light conditions, including midnight rain-riding. At low outputs, the Blinder 1000 lasts for days on a single charge. GoPro-style and standard handlebar mounts are both included, making it versatile on almost any tri cockpit.

Pros: Fully IP67 waterproof, versatile mounts, solid build quality, side window visibility

Cons: Heavier than some competitors at the same lumen output

Battery life: 1 hr at max output; up to 60 hrs at minimum output

If your friends call you “Nightrider,” then the AMPP 2200 might be the perfect bike light for you. With a max output of 2,200 lumens, the AMPP 2200 obliterates darkness in a way that can make you feel like you’re riding during the daytime. This is the light for those who ride in pitch darkness at speed, or those who live in extreme daylight climates such as Alaska or Iceland. While its top-end output is impressive, the AMPP 2200 includes different light modes that are ideal for riding in the dusk rather than the pitch black. At 500 to 800 lumens, the AMPP 2200 becomes a practical all-night light with sufficient battery reserve. Its included mount is quite secure, even on rough pavement. The trade-off is weight; at 211g, it’s the heaviest option on this list.

Pros: Exceptional max output, wide runtime range, secure mount, high-quality build

Cons: Heaviest light on this list; 2,200 lumens if overkill for those who don’t ride in complete darkness

Battery life: 4 to 80 hrs (front); 3 to 60 hrs (rear)

If you’re only looking for a pair of lights that will help you be seen, the Knog Frog combo could be the perfect fit. The front light output isn’t enough to illuminate a dark road, but not every triathlete wants to ride in the dark. Sometimes, you just want to be seen by drivers and cross-traffic, especially in low-light conditions. The combo’s battery life is fitting for the price point, and the pair is so light that you won’t even notice them. They come with a flexible silicone strap that wraps around virtually any tube shape, including aero bars. While they won’t light up a country road, the Knog Frog combo is great for being seen in the city, on the bike path, or on a foggy training loop.

Pros: Aero-bar compatible, extremely lightweight, very affordable, easy to use

Cons: 40 lumens won’t illuminate a dark road; not a standalone solution for night riding

Battery life: 16 hrs (day flash mode); 6 hrs (solid mode)

The Varia is a rear light that also functions as a vehicle radar. In terms of safety and security, it is one of the best bike lights on the market. When paired with a compatible Garmin head unit or Varia app, the light alerts you to vehicles approaching from behind, before you can even hear them. It is an incredibly useful safety feature, especially if you frequently ride in groups or on busy roads. If you get nervous riding on open roads, the Varia RTL515 could be the best option for you. While the light function itself isn’t anything special, the radar is the reason to buy it.

Pros: Vehicle radar is a game-changer on open roads; lightweight, impressive battery life, pairs with Garmin ecosystem

Cons: Expensive for a single rear light; radar requires a compatible head unit or phone mount

Battery life: 12 hrs constant; 30 hrs flash

In terms of bang for your buck, it’s hard to beat the Gravity Plus, which uses an accelerometer to detect braking and automatically increases brightness when you decelerate. It is effectively functioning as a brake light, and it is one of the cheapest options on this list. For triathletes who ride out of town, train with unpredictable stop-and-go conditions, or frequent group rides, the brake-sensing rear light is surprisingly effective. Runtime is excellent for a budget light, and you probably won’t even notice the added weight.

Pros: Brake-sensing technology, outstanding battery life, lightweight

Cons: 100 lumens is modest; a brighter light is necessary for riding in complete darkness

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

This detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.
