#8789. The Best Advanced GPS Running Watches of 2026, Tested by an Ultrarunner

I tested these premium running watches on city streets, mountain trails, and at ultra distances to find out which features are worth paying for.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I review a ton of running watches, cycling through all of the various features and idiosyncrasies to find which watch would suit which runner best, which watches deserve a place on our lists, and which don’t measure up. Sometimes, there are watches that are really cool, and do a lot of work, but they offer more than what the average runner needs to log their daily miles and monitor their fitness. But for backwoods adventure runners, ultrarunners, or runners who put a lot of demand on their machines, advanced GPS running watches like the ones on this list offer a bit more of everything—from cellular and satellite connectivity to off-road trail mapping to sturdier cases, more multisport functionality, and all around just more.

As an ultrarunner, I am frequently testing watches for 50, 75, or even 100 miles at a stretch. Often these miles are spent deep in the woods in Upstate New York on trails that are poorly marked and pretty treacherous. Sometimes, there simply isn’t cell service to be had—anywhere. On top of that, I routinely test them during Hyrox, kayaking, paddle boarding, weight training, hiking, and even skiing—when there’s actually snow on the ground. My daily runs tend toward miles spent in New York City, which you wouldn’t think is an issue, but the tall buildings can thwart GPS pretty hard.

Looking for more running tech? Read our reviews of the best wireless headphones for running, headlamps for runners, and basic running watches.

The Fenix 9 is not flawless, but dang, it is as close to it as I’ve ever tested.I’ve put over 300 miles on the Pro Solar, so I’ll get my little nitpicks out of the way first. Annoyingly, there’s a lag of about half a second to a second when you start a workout, and again when you switch between laps that the 8 did not have. It’s not the most annoying thing in the world, but alas. Also, the app is still the Garmin Connect app. (I will beat this drum until they fix it.)

Now? My happy place, the good stuff. The solar ring on the Pro Solar model puts this watch so far ahead of every other run watch on the market that it can’t even see the others from the rearview. The 51mm is rated for up to 57 days in smartwatch mode with solar, and the 47mm gets up to 34. In the 51mm’s max battery GPS mode, that stretches to 186 hours, or up to 1,000 with solar. I took this out in the backwoodsiest of backwoods Adirondack trails, where I forced it to rely wholly on satellite, and I ran it for 12 solid hours, and it barely ticked the battery.

And that multiband GPS with SatIQ? It’s the best in class, and it locks you down in a hurry. The inReach satellite connectivity lets me run those backwoods and feel safe about doing so. (Though, I still bring a SatCom.)

It’s built like a beast without feeling like one. This is the first Fenix with a titanium case, plus a sapphire lens and a 10 ATM water rating, so rain, sweat, and my early morning postrun ocean swims don’t screw it up.

It’s chockablock with performance and training metrics, and with Epic, their new multiday activity tracker, it’s better than ever. It’s light on the wrist, and it’s easy to use even with sweaty or sea salty fingers.

My favorite little bonus is the flashlight. It’s dimmable and comes in white, red, or green, so it’s great for visibility on early morning runs and also for finding crap at the bottom of my purse.

The base Fenix 9 is a solid watch too, but the Pro Solar is the one I’d get. It’s simply a very fine watch.

You might not be familiar with this brand, but when I tell you, they are punching so far above their weight class with this watch that you would think a 10-year-old just knocked out Floyd Mayweather, I’m not kidding.

The Amazfit Balance Ultra costs $599.99. For that you get a Grade 5 titanium case, a sapphire lens, and a 10 ATM rating that also covers freediving and recreational scuba. It weighs 57 grams without the strap, which is a lot of watch for so little weight. It’s a bit on the thicker side, but not so high profile it’s going to get caught on doors.

Battery is where things start to get unbelievable. The 780 mAh cell battery is rated for up to 30 days of typical use and 10 with the always-on display. In accurate GPS mode you get 50 hours, and power-saving GPS stretches to about 90 in our testing. Unless you’re running through the weekend, you’ll hit your limit before the watch does.

For tracking, it uses dual-band GPS across six satellite systems that ends up acting just like a typical multiband GPS on par with a Coros or a Suunto. That is clutch when you run between tall buildings or under tree cover and your watch would otherwise decide you swam across the Hudson. The 1.5-inch AMOLED screen is bright enough that it can be read in direct sun for the most part.

I will say that the dang buttons on the side are far too easy to depress, leading to accidentally starting activities, but overall, it’s incredible.

The Garmin Enduro 4 is a light upgrade from the 3. It has increased storage, an upgraded band, and introduces some more in-built activities like rucking and rowing alongside Garmin’s multiday training tool Epic. The Enduro line is built for multi-day trekking. Everything about it is engineered for endurance—the rugged design, precise tracking, and especially the solar-powered battery that seems to last forever. You don’t even think about charging most days; it just handles your training, races, and long trail days without missing a beat. The safety and satellite coverage give you extra peace of mind when you’re out alone, far from cell service or the nearest trailhead.

Two features stand out on every serious run. The Pack Weight tool adjusts your effort estimates based on how heavy your gear is, which makes your performance data feel more real—especially on long mountain efforts. And the Next Fork guide keeps you on track, showing how far it is to the next junction so that you don’t have to stop and fumble through maps. Add Garmin’s multiband GPS with SatiQ tech that automatically switches between the best systems into the mix, and logs routes that are spot-on, no matter how deep into the woods you go.

For ultrarunners or anyone training big, the Enduro 4 is reliability wrapped around your wrist—with battery life that feels almost unfair.

I’ve been using the Suunto Vertical 2 off and on for a while now, and I’ve come to see it as a true multisport powerhouse rather than an everyday watch. It’s the one I pull out when training or adventures get serious—long runs, big mountain weekends, or backcountry routes where accuracy and endurance matter more than aesthetics. What sets it apart immediately are its maps—they’re crisp, easy to read, and fully offline, which makes navigation seamless even in the most remote terrain.

Battery life is another standout feature. The Vertical 2 easily lasts up to 60 days in smartwatch mode and delivers exceptional runtime with dual-band GNSS tracking, something that still amazes me every time I scroll through my recorded routes after multihour training blocks. The titanium and sapphire glass construction give it a premium, expedition-ready feel, and the watch itself feels built to handle harsh conditions without flinching.

It’s definitely not what I’d wear every day—it’s large, rugged, and purpose-built—but that’s exactly the point. For athletes who bounce between cycling, running, skiing, hiking, and more, the Vertical 2 is a multisport dream, offering a level of mapping, tracking, and battery endurance suited for endless exploration.

The Garmin Forerunner 970 has been my daily watch for months, and it feels like the perfect blend of lifestyle usability and serious athletic performance. It’s light, comfortable, and sleek enough to wear all day—but underneath that understated design is a fully loaded training tool built for racing, coaching, and multidiscipline endurance work. Whether I’m tracking an interval session, planning an ultra-block, or guiding athletes through structured workouts, the 970 handles it all seamlessly.

GPS precision is exceptional thanks to its multiband GNSS system, locking on quickly and maintaining accuracy even through tree cover and narrow streets. The built-in coaching and training readiness tools have become part of my daily routine—providing recovery insights, suggested sessions, and race forecasts that actually feel tailored. For multisport training, it transitions modes smoothly, syncing effortlessly with sensors and Garmin Connect data.

As someone who loves to spend their hard-earned money on running in a pack of fellow weirdos at races, the pace predictor and race features are a big draw for the Garmin Forerunner 970. I sync my races from Garmin Connect, and the watch spits out predicted times for 5K up to marathons based on my VO2 max, training load, and recent runs, updating as I log more miles. What seals it for me are the race markers overlaid on the course profile, showing projected splits and elevation-adjusted pacing so I can visualize where to surge or conserve energy without second-guessing midrace. It's like having a personal coach whispering realistic goal times right before the gun goes off, turning pricey pack running into a heart-thumping hunt for a PR.

Battery life remains solid, though not as extreme as Garmin’s solar or expedition-focused models, lasting up to 20 days in smartwatch mode. Add in smart notifications, music storage, contactless payments, and wrist-based navigation, and it becomes a rare hybrid—a true performance watch that fits effortlessly into everyday life.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a vast improvement over the Ultra 3, which is a polite way of saying the Ultra 3 had room to grow.

GPS now locks on fast. Apple says there’s no change here, but other members of my team and I noticed a difference. It might be in the software updates, but it’s better. I'm no longer starting runs before the watch has made up its mind. Once it has locked on, though, it commits to a story that isn’t quite true. Distance runs consistently one to one and a half percent long. During a marathon, that’s a few tenths of a mile I didn't earn.

Battery, thankfully, is finally impressing me. It’s leaps and bounds better, and it charges absurdly fast. I top it up while the coffee brews and I take my shower, and by the time I’m done, it’s fully loaded and ready to go.

Heart rate is the big jump. Against a Holter monitor, it stayed within two to three bpm on steady efforts. Run hard and it drifts to five to seven. I do wish it sampled my heart rate every second of every day instead of every five, but overall I don’t think the difference is huge, and when you combine that with the beauty of their apps, it’s hardly a thing.

What’s missing for me is lactate threshold. I can live without many advanced run metrics, but I like knowing my threshold for training runs.

In their new and improved health app, the ECG and hypertension alerts are useful, the cycle insights are spot on, and the morning report doesn’t make me feel graded. Transit pay, apps, and phone integration are unmatched. Satellite calling is extremely easy compared to any other watch I’ve tried. It’s a freaking great watch, overall.

When you step into the world of high-end GPS running watches, the sheer number of options can feel overwhelming—until you see the immense power packed into these bad boys. The essentials are non-negotiable: rock-solid multiband GPS precision, exceptional battery life (no one wants to lose tracking on a 50K run), accurate heart rate and recovery metrics, and seamless integration with your training plans. Every watch on this list delivers on those core requirements.

Where they start to spread their wings is everything layered on top. The bells and whistles are kinda wild. Things like dual-frequency GPS for navigating deep woods (or mountaintops), topo and trail maps that actually make sense when you’re lost, and multisport modes that keep up whether you’re running, swimming, skiing, triathlon training, or rolling through a Hyrox circuit. Barometric altitude readings, pulse ox sensors, and training readiness scores just round out the “how cooked am I?” data we’ve all come to both love and loathe in equal measure.

Some watches, though, don’t just tell you about your fitness—they could save your butt in a sticky situation. The Garmin Fenix 8 Pro works with Garmin’s inReach satellite system, letting you text or send an SOS nowhere near cell service. The Apple Watch Ultra takes a slightly different route with built-in satellite SOS and cellular, so if you’re off-grid and something goes sideways, you’re not shouting into the void. These are the kinds of features that make the difference between just tracking a run and actually trusting your gear if things go sideways.

Let’s be honest—most runners don’t need a watch this powerful. But if you’re out there chasing hours instead of miles, exploring trail networks that don’t even show up on Google Maps, or toggling between swim intervals, mountain climbs, and winter ski sessions, these make a world of difference. Basically, if you’re a runner like me with electricity in your veins and the ADHD that drives you toward multisport or off-the-beaten-trail running, these watches are for you.

One of the quietest but most important reasons these watches shine is safety. With incident detection, live tracking, fall alerts, and SOS tools that actually connect you to help, they turn your wrist into a mini rescue hub. The Garmins can ping your emergency contacts automatically or connect through inReach. The Apple Watch Ultra fires off emergency signals via satellite if you end up out of range. And even the Suunto Vertical and Coros Vertix 2S earn their stripes here with detailed offline maps and batteries that cruise through multi-day efforts.

Basically, these aren’t just training tools—they’re peace of mind on your wrist. When you’re 10 miles deep in a trail system and the forest gets quiet, it’s nice knowing your watch is smarter about directions and safety than your phone or maybe even you.

## Flying Qatar QSuites for 70,000 Miles: The Redemption That Feels Impossible Until You Do It Imagine settling into your own private suite — a door that actually closes, a fully flat bed measuring 80 inches long, a 21.5-inch 4K screen, and a meal service that rivals the best business-class restaurants at 40,000 feet. Qatar Airways QSuites isn't just the best business class product in the sky right now; it's the product that frequent flyers describe as the moment they understood why people obsess over travel rewards. And you can book it for 70,000 American AAdvantage miles one-way. Let that sink in. The same seat — Washington Dulles to Doha, with the ability to continue to dozens of destinations across Asia, Africa, and beyond — retails for **$5,000 to $9,000 in cash**. At 70,000 AAdvantage miles, you're extracting between **7.1 and 12.9 cents per point**. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5 to 2 cents per point. This redemption is *three to six times that*. This is what the FI community means when we talk about travel rewards as a genuine wealth multiplier. If you've been stockpiling points wondering whether they're actually worth something, this is your answer. A cash ticket that costs more than many people's monthly take-home salary becomes nearly free with the right points strategy. The inefficiency exists because AAdvantage still prices partner awards — flights on airlines like Qatar, JAL, and Cathay Pacific — on a **fixed partner award chart** rather than the dynamic pricing it uses for American-operated flights. Qatar, as a oneworld alliance member, is required to make award space available to partner programs. American prices that space at a flat 70,000 miles for business class, regardless of what Qatar itself charges in cash or its own Avios currency. The result is a structural arbitrage opportunity: you're using a fixed-price chart to book a premium product that Qatar prices at whatever the market will bear — and the market bears a *lot* for QSuites. The ChooseFI community has long understood that the highest-leverage use of points isn't domestic economy upgrades. It's premium international cabin redemptions where the gap between cash price and points cost is widest. On that spectrum, QSuites via AAdvantage sits near the very top.

The core insight here is understanding two separate pricing systems operating simultaneously. Qatar Airways prices its QSuites cabin dynamically in cash — demand surges around holidays, business travel seasons, and major events can push that $5,000 base price to $9,000 or beyond. But American AAdvantage doesn't care about any of that. As a oneworld alliance partner, AAdvantage uses a fixed partner award chart for Qatar redemptions: 70,000 miles one-way in business class, full stop.

This means the more expensive the cash ticket gets, the better your CPP becomes — without you doing anything differently. Book during peak travel periods when cash prices spike to $9,000, and you're extracting 12.9 cents per AAdvantage mile. Even at the floor — a $5,000 cash ticket — you're at 7.1 cents per point. Both numbers are extraordinary.

AAdvantage periodically runs "Web Specials" — discounted partner awards where pricing drops significantly below the standard chart. On Qatar routes, these have historically appeared at 50,000 miles one-way for business class. At 50K miles against a $5,000 cash ticket, your CPP jumps to 10 cents per point. These specials are unpredictable and availability is limited, but if you're flexible on travel dates, checking AA.com regularly for Web Specials on Qatar routes can yield an even better deal.

AAdvantage doesn't have a direct credit card transfer relationship with most major bank currencies the way Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards do. Your primary transfer paths are:

One of the most important nuances of this redemption: AAdvantage has a low fuel surcharge policy. When you book Qatar metal through AAdvantage, you pay government taxes and carrier fees, but AAdvantage does not pass through the fuel surcharges that Qatar would charge if you booked through its own program. This can save hundreds of dollars compared to booking QSuites through Avios or Qatar Privilege Club directly. Always verify fees at checkout, but expect to pay $50–$150 in fees rather than the $500+ you might see through other programs.

Doha isn't just a destination — it's Qatar's hub, and connecting through DOH opens the entire Qatar network. A flight to DOH becomes a connection point for onward travel to destinations across South Asia, Southeast Asia, the Indian Subcontinent, and East Africa, all on the same premium aircraft and the same 70,000-mile award. The IAD→DOH route is one of the best-documented entry points into this system.

American Airlines and Qatar Airways are both members of the oneworld alliance, which means AAdvantage miles can book any Qatar-operated award flight at AA's published partner rates. The sweet spot here is that AA uses a fixed award chart for partner bookings rather than dynamic pricing, so the cost is predictable: typically 70,000 miles one-way in business class from the US to the Middle East. Compare this to AA's own Flagship Business product on the same routes (which often prices at 60,000-85,000 miles with dynamic pricing) and you are getting a dramatically superior product — QSuites — for a comparable or lower mileage cost. AA does not impose fuel surcharges on partner awards, keeping out-of-pocket costs to taxes and fees only.

Let's run the numbers on a concrete example.

The Route: Washington Dulles (IAD) to Doha (DOH) on Qatar Airways QR 22, operating a Boeing 777-300ER with QSuites. This is a nonstop flight of approximately 13 hours — exactly the kind of long-haul journey where your seat product matters enormously.

The Cash Price: A business class ticket on this route typically runs $5,500 to $7,500, and during peak travel windows — think spring break, summer, or major holidays — it can reach $9,000. Call it a realistic average of $6,500.

The Points Cost: 70,000 AAdvantage miles + approximately $80–$120 in taxes and fees.

The Math: At $6,500 cash value against 70,000 miles, you're getting 9.3 cents per point. Against a $9,000 peak ticket, you're at 12.9 cents per point. Either way, this is among the highest-value AAdvantage redemptions available anywhere in the program.

You arrive at Dulles and proceed to the Qatar Airways check-in counter, where you're processed as a business class passenger. At Doha, you'll have access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge — one of the most celebrated airport lounges in the world, featuring a full à la carte restaurant, shower suites, and a calm, spacious environment that makes a layover feel genuinely pleasant.

Onboard, your QSuite is a private cabin with a door that slides closed. The bed extends to a full 80 inches. You'll be offered a genuine dine-on-demand service — no scheduled meal times, no "chicken or pasta" announcements over the intercom. The wine list is serious. The bedding is from The White Company. The 21.5-inch screen is 4K.

For the ChooseFI community, the most powerful part of this isn't the luxury itself — it's the ratio. You're experiencing a $6,500–$9,000 product for the cost of points you earned on everyday spending and a small tax outlay. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: maximum experience per dollar (or point) deployed.

Do this: Book as far out as possible. AAdvantage allows bookings up to 331 days in advance. Qatar releases its best award inventory to partner programs at the time of schedule opening — not closer to departure. If you have a target travel window, search at the 331-day mark. Availability genuinely deteriorates as departure approaches.

Do this: Watch for Web Special pricing drops. AAdvantage's Web Specials have historically offered Qatar business class awards at 50,000 miles instead of the standard 70,000. These appear without warning on aa.com under the "Web Specials" tab. If you're flexible with your dates within a week or two, checking this section regularly (or signing up for AAdvantage email alerts) can save you 20,000 miles — a meaningful difference.

Do this: Use Citi ThankYou for same-day transfers. If you find award space and need to transfer points immediately, Citi ThankYou → AAdvantage transfers are instant. This is the fastest transfer path and eliminates the risk of space disappearing while your transfer processes. Keep Citi points in reserve as your QSuites "strike fund."

Avoid this: Transferring Marriott points unless absolutely necessary. The Marriott Bonvoy → AAdvantage transfer at 3:1 is deeply inefficient. You're spending three Marriott points to create one AAdvantage mile. Marriott points are worth roughly 0.7–0.8 cents each, meaning you're paying effectively 2.1–2.4 cents per AAdvantage mile — still potentially worth it for QSuites, but exhaust your Citi and Bilt options first.

Do this: Treat DOH as a hub, not a destination. Doha is Qatar's base, meaning a 70,000-mile award from the US to DOH can be the first leg of an onward journey to destinations across Asia, South Asia, or East Africa — all on Qatar metal. A trip from IAD to Singapore (SIN) routing through DOH, for example, puts you in QSuites for the transatlantic leg and potentially a narrowbody for the shorter DOH-SIN segment.

Avoid this: Booking round-trip when one-way is more flexible. AAdvantage allows one-way partner awards. Book your outbound and return separately — this dramatically expands your availability options and lets you mix partners or return on a different airline without being locked into a single itinerary.

Do this: Build AAdvantage miles through Bilt's monthly rent payments. Bilt Rewards is the only major program that earns points on rent. If you're paying $1,500–$2,500/month in rent, a year of Bilt earning generates 18,000–30,000 Bilt points — transferable to AAdvantage at 1:1. That's a meaningful contribution to your 70,000-mile target from a spend category you have anyway.

## Honest Difficulty Assessment: Moderate This redemption scores **moderate difficulty** — and that rating is accurate. It's not a click-and-book process like domestic awards, but it's not the multi-step puzzle that some ultra-premium redemptions require either. The difficulty is concentrated in **two specific areas**. **Challenge #1: Finding Available Award Space** Qatar releases QSuites award inventory to AAdvantage, but not generously. Availability scores a **2 out of 5**, which means you will sometimes search for weeks before finding the right date. This is the primary bottleneck. The fix: search early (331 days out), be flexible within a 1-2 week window, and use ExpertFlyer alerts to get notified when space opens. Midweek departures and shoulder-season travel windows (late January through March, September through November) tend to surface more space. **Challenge #2: Building 70,000 AAdvantage Miles** AAdvantage's transfer partner list is narrower than Chase or Amex ecosystems. Your best paths are Citi ThankYou (instant transfers) and Bilt Rewards (1-2 days). This earns a **3 out of 5** for ease of earning — achievable, but requires intentional card strategy rather than casual accumulation. **The booking process itself** — once you have miles and availability — is straightforward on aa.com. AAdvantage's award search tool clearly displays partner availability and pricing. **The encouragement:** Every traveler in the ChooseFI community who has navigated this redemption consistently describes it as worth every minute of the search process. The moment that QSuite door closes, you'll understand exactly why. If you're willing to invest the time to find availability and build your miles intentionally, this redemption is entirely within reach — and the payoff is extraordinary.

Log into your AAdvantage account and search for one-way business class flights on your desired route. Filter for partner-operated flights and look specifically for Qatar Airways (QR) flight numbers. The search results will show the mileage cost alongside availability.

If aa.com does not show availability, search the same route on Qatar's own website using a Privilege Club account. Qatar sometimes releases space that AA's system takes 24-48 hours to reflect. If you find space on Qatar but not AA, check back the following day.

Not all Qatar business class flights operate QSuites. Check the aircraft type listed in the search results — A350-1000 and select 777-300ERs have QSuites. Verify on SeatGuru or Qatar's fleet page to ensure you are booking the premium product.

Once you confirm QSuites availability, complete the booking on aa.com using your AAdvantage miles. The process is the same as booking any AA award flight. You will see the mileage cost plus taxes and fees before confirming.

American Airlines charges approximately 70,000 AAdvantage miles one-way for business class from the US to Doha on Qatar Airways-operated flights. Taxes and fees are typically $30 to $80. A round trip comes to roughly 140,000 miles total plus minimal fees.

Both options cost roughly 70,000 points one-way. The main differences are earning sources and booking experience. AAdvantage miles are earned through Citi cards and Bilt, while Avios can be earned through Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt. AA offers web booking while BA may require phone calls. Check availability through both programs — they sometimes see different award space.

Yes. The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select earns bonus miles on purchases, Bilt Rewards transfers to AAdvantage at 1:1, AA's SimplyMiles program earns miles on everyday purchases linked to your credit card, and the AAdvantage shopping portal earns miles at online retailers. You can accumulate 70,000 or more miles without taking a single AA flight.

Airlines control how much award inventory they release to each partner. Qatar may release seats to BA's Avios program but not to AA, or vice versa. AA's search engine also has known inconsistencies with partner availability display. Always cross-reference qatarairways.com and ba.com if aa.com shows no availability on your desired dates.

At 70,000 miles for a product that retails at $5,000 to $8,000, the value per mile is outstanding. The web-based booking experience on aa.com removes the friction of phone calls, and the lack of fuel surcharges keeps your cash outlay minimal. #8787. 7 Common 5K Training Mistakes Runners Make

Everything you should avoid for a faster 3.1 miles.

The 5K is a staple in many runners’ racing schedules, and training for one comes with its own unique strategies for interval workouts, long runs, nutrition, and recovery. All of these factors are bound to leave room for error, so you’ll likely run into some pitfalls as you prep for 3.1 miles.

Some common missteps runners face might even lead to injury, explains Maya Ellison, C.P.T., RRCA-certified run coach and owner of P.A.C.E.D. Coaching Services. If you don’t optimize your training method, you’re also likely to keep getting the same results, which may not lead to that PR you’re vying to achieve, she says. Even if you’re a seasoned runner with dozens of 5Ks under your belt, there’s always room for improvement. “Doing it before doesn’t make you an expert,” says Ellison.

So you can surely take a couple notes from run coaches in order to run your best 5K yet. To better prepare for all your favorite seasonal 3.1-milers and help you feel confident at the start line, we spoke with run coaches to unpack the most common mistakes runners make when training for a 5K.

For many runners, 5Ks are easier to jump into compared to a marathon, which requires a solid block of training time to adjust to high mileage and fueling demands. With a 5K, you might tag along at a friend’s race or sign up last minute. Because of this, you might squeeze in a bunch of speed workouts within a few weeks before the race, which can leave you feeling tired or flat come race day, says Sam Renikoff, USATF- and RRCA-certified run coach.

While you can get away with a shorter training block for a 5K, it’s still important to give yourself enough time to absorb your training, recover, and feel 100 percent going into the race, Renikoff explains. For example, rather than tapering for three weeks before race day like you would training for a marathon, Renikoff recommends tapering for a week to 10 days before a 5K, keeping intensity high with speedwork but cutting back on volume.

Plus, going from zero to 100 can lead to getting sidelined, according to Debbie Woodruff, USATF- and RRCA-certified run coach and certified personal trainer. That’s because runners who increase mileage too quickly—rather than taking small steps toward more volume—are more likely to face injury, according to a study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.

To mitigate the risk, Woodruff recommends beginners follow a couch-to-5K plan or a run/walk training plan to ease into training with a gradual buildup, while more seasoned runners should follow an eight-week-long plan that also allows you to build mileage, add speedwork, and prioritize the prerace taper.

Sticking to an expert-backed training plan, like Runner’s World’s 5K training plans, allows you to have structure and give yourself time to adjust to the demands of the distance.

Renikoff explains that even though 5Ks are much shorter than a marathon or half, the long run is still crucial. It allows you to get comfortable with being uncomfortable, an important part of the 5K. It also prevents you from giving into fatigue by building your endurance, which allows you to hold onto your pace through the entire 3.1 miles. Plus, the long run often acts as a confidence booster, making the 5K less intimidating all around.

The long run is one of the best ways to increase your aerobic capacity, Renikoff explains. This is important even for shorter race distances because you need to use oxygen to efficiently produce energy for any run lasting longer than just a few minutes.

Long runs during 5K training will typically range anywhere from 4.5 miles (for more beginners) to 12 miles (for advanced runners with time-based goals like breaking 20 minutes). That means some plans may triple the distance of your race, which will only make you more prepared to conquer 3.1 miles.

Seasoned runners in particular might struggle to keep their easy runs easy, Ellison explains, because of their experience, fitness levels, or overall ambition. But these easy days give your body a chance to recover from hard days, allowing you to get stronger throughout your training cycle, she says.

You should feel relaxed throughout your easy runs, like you’re able to have a conversation with someone. Some runners find it helpful to check in on their effort level with the ABC test: Chant the ABCs out loud and try to get to the letter G without having to take a breath. If you falter, that’s your cue that you need to slow down.

If you make a habit of not taking easy pace seriously, you might even find yourself running a speedy first mile during an easy run or tempo run, only to falter by mile two, progressively getting slower and more fatigued by the end. This happens when runners struggle to find an effective pacing strategy, Renikoff explains.

This makes it more likely you’ll go out too fast on race day, which could sabotage your goals. “If you go out and run the first mile [of the race] 20 seconds faster than your average 5K pace, you’re a lot more likely to have that pace balloon to 30 seconds or more slower [than goal pace] in the second and third miles, which is not only not fun or enjoyable, but it’s also not fast,” Renikoff says.

For smarter pacing, Renikoff suggests progression runs: Start by running the first mile of your tempo run at a moderate pace, then increase your speed each mile or half mile (depending on the distance of your run) by about 10 seconds, finishing significantly faster than you started. This requires you to start slow enough that you can continue to run faster as the workout progresses.

While some runners start their runs too fast, others struggle to run faster than their easy pace at all. “If you’re aiming to run a fast 5K and you have not spent any time in those paces by doing some hard intervals, it’s really easy to give up in the race,” says Renikoff.

The key to not giving up at the first sign of fatigue? Implement one to two days per week of some form of speed training, including intervals and tempo runs, Woodruff says.

Seasoned runners may benefit from track intervals, like 200- to 400-meter repeats at 95-percent effort or goal 5K pace with equal recovery, she explains. Another option is a tempo or threshold run, where you sustain your 5K pace for a prolonged period of time sandwiched by a few easy miles.

A fartlek workout introduces newbie runners to interval training, Woodruff explains, by alternating one to two minutes at a hard effort with one to two minutes at an easy effort, essentially practicing interval training without the need for specific metrics.

If your most recent PR is a 24-minute 5K and you’re trying to run your next one in 19 minutes, you might need to readjust your goal setting, at least for now. Ellison explains that runners sometimes set overly ambitious goals, when in reality, true growth takes time.

Instead of looking to drop five minutes in your next race—which requires you to run nearly two minutes faster per mile—try setting a smaller goal like dropping 30 seconds to one minute from your finish time, Ellison explains. This requires about a 10- to 20-second pace difference per mile, making your PR more manageable to achieve.

A beginner 5K runner may not know how to properly warm up and cool down, explains Ellison, which is especially important for each workout, but also for race day.

Warmups can help you sustain a harder effort for longer periods of time, while cooldowns give your body a chance to actively recover after hard efforts. A solid warmup typically includes dynamic stretching, drills like high knees and butt kicks, along with a five-minute jog, Woodruff explains, while a cooldown should include a mile or two of easy jogging and static stretching.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#8786. My Shimano Pedals Are Nearly 10 Years Old—This 10-Minute Service Saved Me From Spending $200 on a New Set

A quick SPD-SL pedal service can revive old Shimano pedals—and help you avoid a costly update.

My longest-lasting pedals are a roughly 10-year-old pair of Shimano SPD XT pedals that have admittedly seen zero maintenance. Those pedals have been effectively abused on everything from getting bashed through rock gardens to long dusty or muddy days on the gravel bike. A few years ago I got my first road bike and switched to a pair of Shimano SPD-SL pedals. Since then I’ve put that bike (and those pedals) through the wringer.

I tend to stress test gear, even prior to having this job, so I enjoy taking my road bike out on everything from light gravel to singletrack that I have no business on. This means my road pedals have seen similar abuse to my mountain bike and gravel pedals. They’re still in great shape, but they could use a little love. Even pedals only used for road riding will start to get gritty over time.

Then I saw Shimano’s pedal release—not only are the old cleats not compatible with the new pedals, but the price of the new Shimano pedals starts at $200 for the Ultegra model and go up to $300 for the Dura-Ace model.

After I saw the rollout, it felt like a good time to bring my old generation SPD-SL pedals back to life and while I’m at it, give you a few tips on the process. Here we’ll run through how to service your SPD-SL pedals in under 10 minutes and save you a few hundred dollars in the process.

A quick note on reinstalling the pedals back on the bike: make sure you put the right pedal on the right side and the left pedal on the left side. I know, this sounds obvious. I’ve seen the wrong pedal get forced into the wrong side of the crank too many times, damaging the crank and the pedals to the point that sometimes both need to be replaced. Sometimes pedals are marked with an “L” for left and “R” for right, but you can always double-check to see which way the threads go. Left pedal threads will go up to the left and right pedal threads go up to the right. Then when it is time to reattach the pedals, put some grease on the threads of the crank arm and begin to thread them on by hand instead of starting with the wrench. If you can’t begin to thread the pedal onto the crank threads by hand, double-check the pedal is on the correct side, make sure it’s going into the crank arm straight, and make sure there is no debris in the hole of the crank arm preventing it from threading.

#8785. The Top 11 Women’s Running Shoes That Have the Comfiest Fit, Coziest Cushioning, and Most Responsive Ride

These are the current road and trail favorites of our women’s wear-test team.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 12, 2026: End-of-year sales have already taken off. Our Best Stability Shoe, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, is now on sale with 19% off. (We are currently testing the newest model, the Adrenaline GTS 26.) Our Best for Speedwork Shoe, the Adidas Adizero Evo SL, is also discounted with 20% off.

We are in a new era of running shoes, from stacked super trainers to plated racers to gravel models decked out with bike-inspired treads.

The industry formerly criticized for “shrink it and pink it,” i.e., the practice of making smaller-size men’s shoes and slapping pink on them and calling them women’s shoes, has gone to great lengths crafting footwear that’s women-specific.

Brands are taking care to produce shoes that accommodate the average woman’s foot shape: wider in the midfoot area, narrower around the heel. But don’t think this list is free of pink shoes. The traditionally feminine colors have been reclaimed by brands like Nike (turns out it’s flashy and easier to spot neon pink Alphaflys). Here you’ll find trainers of every color for all types of women’s feet and women runners.

Shopping for a daily trainer → Brooks Glycerin 23On a budget → New Balance EllipseMostly a run/walker → Hoka Clifton 11On the path to recovery → Hoka Bondi 9Adding in speedwork → Adidas Adizero Evo SLLogging long runs → Nike Vomero 18Racing a marathon → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3An overpronator → Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25Suffering from bunions → Altra Torin 9Running on rail trails → lululemon WildfeelNew to technical terrain → Altra Experience Wild 3

Runner’s World has been around for almost 60 years, providing news, fitness tips, and, of course, gear recommendations for runners. Our product guides for essentials like running shoes and shorts come from our hardworking test team, who put the latest and greatest running gear through their paces day in and day out. These selections come from Senior Reviews Editor Cat Bowen, who blazes the trails and is an ultramarathon beast, and me, Running Reviews Editor Amanda Furrer. I have written about running gear for a decade and hold an even longer Boston Marathon streak, beginning in 2013.

We picked these shoes based on feedback from the runners who are part of our 300-runner-strong team of local wear-testers and the expertise of our editors. We evaluated every shoe over the course of at least 100 miles, paying attention to overall performance, comfort, ride, longevity, and value.

To ensure our shoe recommendations are truly comprehensive and trustworthy, we grabbed a wide array of shoe types to put through our rigorous testing. This involved evaluating them across diverse terrains, including challenging trails, smooth tracks, varied road surfaces, and—of course—treadmills. Our massive wear-test team allows us to gather feedback from individuals ranging from sprinters to marathoners, runners of different weights and body types, those with different foot strikes, shoe needs, and biomechanics. By combining varied surface testing with a diverse runner pool, we learn a ton about each shoe’s performance and suitability for a wide range of users and individual experiences. Based on our extensive testing, the options below are currently the best running shoes for women.

In our testing, we found the Glycerin 23 excelled as a daily trainer over the Ghost 18 among women testers. The formerly max-cushioned Glycerin has evolved into an everyday shoe that you can take out on easy days to long runs. Our women testers preferred the Glycerin 23 over the Ghost 18 because of the shoes’ fit. Several testers reported hot spots in the Ghost 18’s bunion-prone area. The Glycerin 23, on the other hand, was praised for its broad platform, soft and plush knit upper, and ample wiggle room in the toebox.

“The shoe is cushioned in a way that makes me want to do all my long runs in them,” said tester and Senior Features Editor Pavlína Černá. “It doesn’t drag as some cushioned shoes do, but feels responsive. My go-to comparison of a cushioned shoe is the Saucony Echelon which I love for walking/hiking, but which I cannot do long miles in because the shoe drags, makes me work too hard. In comparison, the Glycerin is plushy but responds well to my moods and the corresponding pace changes.”

The shoe has Brooks’s DNA Tuned midsole foam, which was introduced in the even cushier Glycerin Max. The experience running on DNA Tuned is just like Černá described: plush, supportive, responsive, ideal for running long.

One of our women testers described the Ellipse v1 as “nearly perfect.”

New Balance’s intent with the shoe was to provide a high-cushioned, trampoline-like bounce experience for recreation. It’s the kind of shoe you can wear for daily training, while you lace up in it for a casual, conversationally paced group run. The Ellipse was specifically made to make runs easier.

Fresh Foam X is dialed in to produce a foamy, high-rebound ride with reliable shock absorption. It’s a ride that makes me look forward to lacing up the Ellipse and taking it out for whatever kind of run my heart desires on the spot. The tweaked foam makes running in the soft, springy shoe feel like a treat.

“The best word to describe the cushion is plush,” said tester Laura Parks. “It has the extreme cushion sensation of a Hoka Bondi without feeling the weight.” She described the ride as unlike any she’s had running in other Fresh Foam X models.

We’re still in the process of testing the Clifton 11, but the team is already loving the shoe weeks into testing. Everything we love about Hoka—plush cushioning, cozy fit, responsive midsole—is usually encapsulated in each iteration of the Clifton. The 11 is no exception. It was a hard follow after the ClifTEN, but the Clifton 11 makes runs feel effortless, thanks to the compression-molded EVA midsole foam, which provides high rebound and a comfy platform that pillows your foot.

The shoe has Hoka’s Meta-Rocker geometry to promote smooth transitions. Sidewalls make the fit snug but not too narrow as the Hoka Bondi 9.

The Clifton 11 is also excellent for run/walking because of that cushioned support and rocker geometry. These elements make the Clifton reliable at any pace.

The Bondi 9, one of Hoka’s plushest daily trainers, is somehow cushier and sleeker with this update. Hoka added 10 mm to the midsole—but this shoe is no chonk. We even tested it sprinting on the treadmill; the supercritically foamed EVA provides high energy return and soft support. But we especially like using the shoe for run/walking and recovery.

“The Bondi 9 delivers great protection with an amazingly smooth roll,” said tester Tiffany Volpe. “I can see why there is so much hype behind the Hoka and [why it’s called] the Queen of Cushion. I felt like I was sitting down in the midsole. I felt locked in with ample protection especially in the tongue and collar.

“I found the Bondi a perfect recovery day shoe and one that I reach for when I just want to head out for a long slow run to clear my head.”

The shoe was also rated high in stability among testers, and they appreciated the reflective, as well.

Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate boldly dubbed the Adizero Evo SL Shoe of the Year merely a month into 2025. That sentiment is upheld and shared; the shoe is Best Overall on our list of Best Running Shoes. For $150 (and frequently on sale), just above the cost of the New Balance Ellipse, you could also say it’s Best Value. And because of its secret sauce, Adidas’s Lightstrike Pro midsole, which is featured in the brand’s super shoes, you could also say it’s Best for Speedwork, too.

One woman tester gamely raced in the Adizero Evo SL, and experienced excellent results. “The coolest thing about these to me was the weight and cushion,” said that tester, Caroline Lennon. “It was a perfect balance of being light and springy but still feeling well-cushioned and supported. They were so comfortable at all paces and let me feel faster than I was anticipating. They felt best at a harder effort. My 5K race was surprisingly fast given that there was no carbon plate!”

Breaking: A Nike shoe with Hoka-plush cushioning. The Vomero 18 is unlike any Nike we’ve tested. It has a dual-density midsole with 46 mm of ZoomX and ReactX foam, which puts this shoe in the super trainer category. What you get is a bouncy, soft ride that makes long runs an energized quest instead of a Saturday (or Sunday) morning slog.

“I didn’t expect to love this shoe as much as I do!” said Associate Health and Fitness Editor Kristine Kearns, a self-described loyal Brooks Ghost fan. “I wasn’t sure if I would like the Vomero 18 because of how much heel cushioning there is, and how it kind of elevates me forward in that way. But it turns out the shoe provides so much stability, even on the side.”

The source of the stability Kearns is referring to: the wider platform. Nike collected input from women testers, who wanted a wider fit in the midfoot. The result is a more accommodating foot shape that provides midrun support.

The Endorphin Elite 3 makes good with super adjustments after a strong reception with the Endorphin Elite 2. Several testers loved the previous model’s aggressive bounce, becoming inspired to race in it at their next marathon. Others, like me, had difficulty troubleshooting the squishy TPEE foam. It was volatile, pogo stick-like bounce that required mastering before you went all out on this somewhat unstable super shoe.

Saucony tamed the shoe this go-around. That pogo stick bounce is still there, but the ride is more stable with a connected heel and midfoot (not the slightly decoupled heel that made it more likely to turn your foot inward navigating sharp turns). The PwrTrac outsole also adds more support by providing grippy traction.

The Adrenaline GTS 25 is pumped with even more foam for a comfier, more supportive ride. Brooks added 1 mm of DNA Loft v3 foam in the heel and 3 mm in the forefoot, resulting in a slightly higher stack height, lower heel drop, and more responsive ride.

Dense guide rails on the lateral and medial sides of the shoe act as bumpers to help with ankle and knee alignment while running. The support aids overpronators and late-onset overpronators alike.

“One of the shoe’s best features is the sense of security it provides,” said tester Kylie Rodriguez. “The Adrenaline series is known for its stability, and this model is no exception. I felt confident and secure on every surface, from slick sidewalks to uneven dirt paths.

“This blend of comfort, stability, and a lightweight feel makes the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 a fantastic and reliable choice for any runner looking for a do-it-all shoe. It’s a solid, dependable performer that won’t let you down. Another solid key component to the shoe was the cupping support the heel gave my strong heel striking steps even more confidence and support.”

We’re still getting in Torin 9 feedback, but it’s safe to say early on that the shoe is a worthy follow-up to the Torin 8. When Altra was founded in 2009, its core values were balanced zero-drop cushioning, an accommodating toebox for toe-splaying, and a women-specific fit. The brand has evolved with a 4mm-drop shoe line but its values haven’t changed.

The Torin, basically the Ghost version of a zero-drop shoe, is a terrific cushioned entry into running a no-drop shoe. Dual-density foam provides a moderate but supportive bed of cushioning to help you transition into zero-drop running. Runners with wide feet and bunions will also appreciate Altra’s wide toebox, which not only allows your toes to wiggle but also helps with your biomechanics (squeezed toes help you run faster, said no one ever).

The updated outsole is Vibram XS Dura, which is grippier than the rubber on the Torin 8. I like how the shoe can dabble off road and not have to worry about falling face-first when I traverse onto a trail—which is rare.

The lululemon shoe team has made it its mission to produce women-specific trainers since the release of the brand’s first running shoe, the Blissfeel, in 2022. Their latest model, the Wildfeel, provides the same comfy, secure fit with a responsive, high-rebound ride off-road.

The shoe has men’s and women’s editions, which are tweaked to support each sex’s anatomical differences and distinct biomechanics. For instance, the forefoot of the women’s shoe is slightly more flexible than the men’s to complement the shorter toes, longer arch, and shorter instep typical of women’s feet.

Our testers appreciated the Wildfeel’s flexibility and overall comfort. It’s a good choice for runners new to the trail who want more of a hybrid option that can take on some technical track.

“I loved the flexibility of the Wildfeels!” said tester Jenny Stump. “I am primarily a road runner. These felt comfortable enough that I could do some easy miles on the road as well as tackle some trails with uneven surfaces. All the trail runners I have previously tried felt more stiff and had such a thick sole that I wouldn’t even want to warm up on the road with them.”

What I love most about the Experience Wild 3 is that it’s a trail shoe that feels like a road shoe. The fit is accommodating in the midfoot and toe area—Altra is known for its spacious toeboxes that allow your toes to splay—and the collar and tongue are padded and cushioned.

The Altra Ego P35 foam is responsive on the trail and provides a nice balance of support and ground feel. Another win for me, the mostly road runner: the shoe is incredibly flexible. No stiffness or hot spots that cause my feet a world of hurt the first couple of runs before they’re broken in.

The shoes have gaiter attachments to provide even more protection and a toe sweep. The drop is a low 4 mm, which isn’t as intimidating as going full zero (though if you’re game, the Lone Peak 9 is a good place to start).

The shoe is also available as the Experience Wild 3+, which has a Vibram Megagrip outsole. It’s a little more expensive at $165. If you want tackier grip, go for it. But the 3.5mm lugs on the MaxTrac outsole suit me and fellow testers just fine on slush, mud, and icy snow.

Women’s feet have distinct structural differences than men’s feet. From shape to proportions to biomechanics, all of these things significantly impact shoe fit and comfort. For example, while men’s feet typically present a more uniform width from heel to forefoot, women’s feet tend to be wider in the forefoot relative to the heel. Any lady who has felt their toes get squished as their heel slips right out of the shoe knows this issue.

Recognizing these anatomical differences, and responding to the hoards of women runners clamoring for something better, running shoe manufacturers have (finally) started to incorporate more gender-specific design elements into their products. This means crafting shoes with distinct features tailored to the unique shape and biomechanics of women’s feet. For instance, a women’s running shoe might feature a wider toebox to accommodate the broader ball of the foot, while a narrower heel counter secures the back of the foot and prevents slippage.

Additionally, the materials used in the heel construction might differ between men’s and women’s versions to account for variations in where we strike our foot when we land. Women and men obviously have different centers of gravity—especially when we’re pregnant—and that changes how we strike and the wear pattern of our soles.

Brands are not just shrinking and pinking the shoes anymore. Their aim is to enhance performance and prevent running-related aches and pains. A shoe that fits properly and supports the foot’s natural movement can improve running efficiency and reduce the risk of common running-related injuries, such as blisters, plantar fasciitis, the pedi-ick black toenails, and shin splints.

Researchers have also found that, because women tend to have wider hips than men, women’s feet are more likely to strike the ground toward the outside of their shoe soles. The inward rolling of the foot, called pronation, that results from this explains why more women are believed to overpronate than men (aka, walk a bit duck-footed.). Some women’s running shoes account for this increased tendency with stability features in the sole, such as guide rails and medial posts, to provide more support.

This list includes what we regard as the best shoe in its category. But there are still plenty of other shoes for you to choose from.

For the plushest ride and more foam underfoot, check out the Best Cushioned Running Shoes.

If you’re an overpronator or think you need more support, take a look at the Best Stability Shoes.

And if you want more of a selection of non-road shoes, visit the Best Trail Shoes.

No matter the distance or your shoe preferences, there’s a great shoe for you on our lists.

What’s the size difference between men’s and women’s running shoes?

If you prefer wearing men’s running shoes, size down 1.5. For example: A women’s size 10 would equal a men’s size 8.5.

When should you change out your running shoes?

Running shoe shelf life is dependent on the runner. Some runners wear down their shoes after only a couple weeks, others have their shoes well past several months. The standard mileage on everyday trainers is 350 to 500 miles, 250 to 300 for lightweight shoes, and 100 to 250 for racing or minimalist shoes.

If you don’t keep track of mileage, a good rule of thumb is switching out shoes twice a year. For racing shoes, two to three races.

You can put your shoes in the washing machine with some detergent, set on cold. Never put your shoes in the dryer—it will melt the glue and make them degrade faster.

Instead, remove the insoles and allow them to air dry. Stuff wads of newspaper inside your shoes and leave them to sit for a couple hours so the paper can absorb the moisture.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Garmin GPS head units are one of the smartest upgrades you can make to your road, gravel, mountain, or electric bike, and a much safer alternative than strapping your phone to the bars to see your route. Cycling computers also capture, process, and display data from accessories like heart rate monitors, power meters, and even electronic shifting to help you ride better, train smarter, and stay connected. And because Garmin lets you customize nearly everything—from data fields to navigation screens—you can tailor exactly what shows up.

Buying Tip: Buying previous-generation cycling computers is a great way to save money. Older models usually have almost the same performance at a big discount. Cyclists often even prefer the old models if they’re lighterweight or have better battery life.

Cycling radar is one of the most important pieces of bicycle technology released in the last decade. On-bike radar systems mount to the rear of your bike and feature an integrated taillight. Paired with a cycling computer or smartwatch, they notify you about vehicles approaching from behind so you can move out of the way. They are a must-have item for road and gravel riders.

Buying Tip: Garmin is a pioneer in cycling radar tech and makes the most reliable, consistent systems. The Varia RTL515 is our benchmark and best-value pick, while the RearVue 820 is newer and more powerful; it’s our choice for best performance. The RCT715 is the 515 with an integrated rear-facing camera.

While dedicated cycling computers are the go-to choice for road, gravel, and data-heavy training, many riders prefer Garmin’s smartwatches because they keep everything in one place, especially when they track more than bike rides—anyone who mixes riding with running, hiking, paddling, strength training, or even walking the dog. Garmin watches have powerful GPS, workout metrics, and daily health data in a streamlined device that’s always with you (and they even tell time).

Buying Tip: Mountain bikers often appreciate the simplicity and safety of recording their rides from the wrist rather than risking a pricey head unit in a crash. Triathletes, duathletes, and cyclocross racers love the seamless transitions a watch allows. There’s no need to swap devices or merge files after an event.

Most riders know Garmin from its computers, smartwatches, and cycling radar. But Garmin also owns the indoor trainer brand Tacx. Its smart trainers and indoor bikes are highly regarded for their excellent performance, integration, and useful features. One cool feature we love—especially if you live somewhere prone to winter power outages—is that the Neo 2T generates its own resistance electromagnetically. That means you don’t have to scrap your workout plans just because the lights go out.

Buying Tip: Smart trainers are great for riding in virtual worlds like Zwift. For a deep dive into more great indoor trainers and buying info, check out my story “Ready to Ride Indoors? Here’s How to Pick the Best Trainer.”

Garmin Tacx Neo 2T with Zwift Cog and Click

Want to step up your training for next season? The best way to measure cycling gains is by training with power—and for that, you need a power meter. Power pedals, like Garmin’s Rally series, are easier to install than crank-based power meter options. Plus, you can swap power pedals easily between bikes. This not only saves cost, but it also gives you consistent data from bike to bike.

Buying Tip: Garmin offers a handy option to buy its power meter in a package including two pedal styles (road and mountain bike/gravel) with swappable spindles. This way you can measure power across riding disciplines.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8783. The Arizona Experiment!

The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.

Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.

Eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right. Early retirement has proved to be the most amazing, worthwhile adventure and it’s still just getting started. It was an astonishing thirteen years ago that I wrote to you about Little MM starting kindergarten, and now he’s done with high school.

It has given me the space to enjoy so many new experiences, working hard and playing hard sometimes, but also slowing things way down when necessary, to deal with and grow through some real hardships.

But now, with that child-raising phase finally almost done, I’m cashing in a few of those Freedom Chips for a particularly big change: moving to a warm sunny place for the winter to try out a new life in the walkable, bikeable, car-free community you’ve probably heard me raving about in the past: Culdesac Tempe.

So on the first of December I’ll be packing up the essential clothes, tools and gadgets, and throwing my very best mountain bike onto the Model Y to make the epic road trip across the mountains. Just in time to escape the incoming Colorado winter. And my son will be joining me for the trip!

Looking for updates? I have added a separate tracker page here.

We’ve booked ourselves a spacious two bedroom apartment there, for four full months. Little MM will be roughly alternating his months between Arizona and Colorado so he can still have time with both parents, while I’ll be there the whole time.

A big part of the fun is that this will force me to invent a whole new life for myself, away from the easy comforts of the big community and plentiful construction sites that keep me so busy here.  It will be both a big change and a significant challenge, which is exactly what all of us need on a regular basis to keep life full of meaning and joy.

The exact details are still in the works, and I’d love to hear your ideas and feedback (see the “get in touch” note below. But here’s what I’ve got so far:

Okay, you’re onto me. If I’m going to go to the trouble of typing shit into the computer and sharing it with you, there’s usually a purpose behind it other than just journaling my own personal life, and this another one of those cases.

First of all, there are the first-layer selfish goals: I want to have the best winter ever, meet a bunch of smart new people, and I also want Culdesac to be a huge success so they will build more neighborhoods like this around the country and set an example that permanently improves the way US cities build and expand themselves in the future.

But even if you don’t care about all that, I also want to use this as a little statement about trying deliberate life changes.

By throwing myself into a new community which aligns so nicely with my own values, I hope to serve as a reminder that maybe you might want to try the same thing. Or just try anything new.

In a comfortable, prosperous country like ours, some of the built in tendencies of Human nature tend to work against us, saying,

“Hey – I’ve noticed we have plenty of food and reasonable shelter and that’s good enough. So let’s just double down on the Netflix, comfort foods, and occasional luxury purchases and that will keep us safe.”

Instead, I want you to set your life treadmill to just a bit of a steeper, healthier incline setting.

That means questioning the status quo and doing your best to keep at least one little experiment on the go in the background. Maybe that means forcing yourself to move to a better place, or taking steps towards getting a new job that gives you a better work-life balance.

The biggest move I ever made was leaving family and friends and my old job behind to move to the US, alone, at age 24. Looking back, I’m shocked I had the courage (and the organizational skills) to pull that off back then. I’ve become older and a bit slower, and so comfortable that it’s hard to imagine doing something so bold now.

But even today 24 years later, I thank my past self every single day for doing it. My present life is an incredibly different and better thing because of that past bit of courage.

The spirit of positive experimentation might also mean starting to challenge your body more regularly – giving it harder work and exposing it to a wider swath of temperatures and movements. Or joining new Meetup groups to expand your circle of friends and experiences.

It doesn’t really matter exactly what you do, as long as you point your feet in what feels like a good direction and just start moving. Create some purposeful change, which will surely feel a bit difficult, simply because change is hard. And hard things are good.

Future Arizona Neighbors: I’ll see you in four weeks!

Further reading: I’ve been reading books, doing life experiments, and writing about the value of strategic hardship for a while now. But the latest is a book called Dopamine Nation by the talented psychiatrist/author named Dr. Anna Lembke.

To summarize: your brain creates a baseline for happiness based on the HARDEST thing you do, and then compares everything else to that. So if you do hard things, life in general seems fantastic because of this perspective. If you eliminate all hardship, suddenly even the pleasures of life seem bland, and you live a spoiled and unmotivated life.

Interested in stopping by for your own Mini Culdesac Experiment? They have a few short-term rentals available at rather reasonable rates (less than nearby hotels) – check em out at book.culdesac.com

I’m bringing the car just as a convenient electric moving truck to carry two people and four months of living supplies. Once I get there, I’ll find a safe place to park it offsite and live the full car-free lifestyle of Culdesac, much like I do when I’m here at home. I typically only use cars to carry really heavy stuff or for trips to other cities and states, but it’s even easier to accomplish this in Tempe with its location right on the light rail and with their onsite bike, scooter and even car sharing lots.

My place in Colorado is currently set up as a two bedroom house on the main floor, plus an apartment with a separate entrance on the walkout lower level. When I’m at home, I use the whole thing as one home – the apartment just makes a great place to host a fairly constant stream of visiting friends. But for the winter I’m hoping to rent out one of these spaces to a friend or trusted acquaintance who will take good care of everything, while I leave the other section free for the occasional visits I’ll be paying to this area over the winter. Aside from keeping an eye on the place, it will be a great way to practice the age-old Mustachian technique of making money while taking vacations!

As it stands, I have no plans beyond this point. I’ll head back to Colorado for my home base, but with this being a new phase of life I’ll be layering on new adventures. Aside from the two mountain properties that I’ve been helping to build out, I may end up with an MMM Mountain Retreat of my own someday. Conclusion: ongoing thoughts on the Culdesac experiment are here: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/

I’m a fellow Canadian (Newfoundlander to be precise) who’s been reading your blog from the very beginning. Mostly it’s a case of “preaching to the converted”.

I’ve been spending winters in Arizona for the last 10 years because my partner (also from Newfoundland) lives in Chandler. And literally, no joke, the first item that I have written down on my list of things to do in Arizona this coming winter is “go check out Cul De Sac”.

Maybe if I go and wander around there, I’ll spot your facial hair

I don’t know if it’s weird to say this, but I’d be up for a coffee or a bike ride or some hang time or whatever if you feel so inclined. It would definitely be the weirdest way that I’ve ever made a friend. In a good way.

Anyway, obviously the desert has lots of beautiful hikes and bike rides. But do yourself a favour (note the “u” in favour LoL) and go check out The Desert Botanical Gardens. It’s one of the absolute gems in The Valley. It can sometimes have lots of tourists there … particularly us Canucks. But it’s for good reason. It is spectacular. And they have lots of cool events there too. We take all our visitors there. And if you’re so inclined, the library offers free passes to DBG and lots of other local attractions too.

(1) The Musical Instrument Museum is pretty huge and unique

(2) The drive out to Tortilla Flats is really beautiful. It literally is an old stage coach trail that was turned into a twisty 2 lane highway.  And you can go boating or kayaking in Canyon lake, which is pretty sweet.

(3) Sedona is obviously one of the most gorgeous places in the US and a reasonably short drive. If you’re going to go to the Grand Canyon from Sedona (or even if you’re just going to Flagstaff), there’s this fabulous older highway called 89A that takes you to Flagstaff. It’s so much more fun than taking the freeway.

(4) There are oodles and oodles of free Disc Golf courses (my new obsession and the price is right)

(5) South Mountain has a thing called “Silent Sunday” where they close the mountain to cars. So you can ride your bike up (obviously challenging) but then down (woo hoo!)

(6) There’s a cool thing downtown called “First Friday Art Walk” every month. Google it.

(7) Most importantly, my favourite place to ride my bike is in the Northern part of The McDowell Sonoran Preserve. Specifically, I like the trail called “The Long Way Around”. It’s just the right length (around 25 km). The ground is very beginner friendly. In fact, I have a hybrid, not a mountain bike and it does fine. But the trail still has lots of ups and downs and twists and turns, so it’s a blast. So much so, that the first time I rode there, I was giggling like a kid, even though I’m 55. It’s as easy or hard as you want it to be, based on how fast you go. And also it’s one of the nicest parks in the area.

(8) Taliesin West is super cool. Particularly if you get a good guide. It was Frank Lloyd Wright’s personal project. His winter home. So he was free to do whatever crazy things he could dream up, without having to account to a client. The handyman in you will love it!

I could go on, but that’s off the top of my head.

One last note. If you wear something Canadian; like for example, I wear a CBC logo on my hat or my partner wears something from the Leafs … a zillion snowbird Canadians will approach you and ask what part of Canada you’re from.

Anyway, here’s to a great time in Arizona.
