#8782. 6 Budget Running Watches That Deliver Accurate GPS, Long Battery Life, and Much More

Not-so-average watches for the average runner.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I’ve spent the last several years testing running watches, from the $800 flagships with topographical maps and training-readiness scores to the ones that do almost nothing except tell you how fast you’re going. Both have their place.

“Basic” has become an insult, and I’d like us to cut that right the heck out. A basic running watch isn’t a cheap, crappy watch—it’s a watch that does what it was meant for. Pace, distance, splits, a lap button you can hit with sweaty or frozen fingers, a battery that won’t quit at mile 20, and a screen you can read no matter how tired. That’s the job. These do the job.

They’re also—and this surprises people—what a lot of very fast runners wear. Stand near the front of a starting corral sometime and count the watches that cost less than the shoes. Elites don’t need a wrist device to tell them they’re tired. They need accurate splits.

If you’re new, that’s the biggest thing you need. Nothing kills a running habit faster than forty metrics you don’t understand that insist you’re doing it wrong. Same goes if you’re kitting out a kid for their first track or cross-country season: buy the simple device. It’ll survive the school bus, the mud, and the whole season. And they’ll learn to run by feel, which is the entire point. My first Garmin was essentially a pace-watching brick on my wrist and I still managed PRs. Here’s what I’d actually put on your wrist.

Our Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate tested the Pace 4 and came away calling it a fast, accurate, lightweight GPS watch that nails the basics without charging laptop-level prices. The Coros Pace 4 adds a sharp, always-on AMOLED display and significantly improved battery life over the Pace 3, offering up to 31 hours in max GPS mode (about 24 with the screen always on), all while keeping the case compact and comfortable on the wrist.

It tracks advanced run-specific metrics like running power, ground contact time, and left/right strength balance: That might not be necessary for new and casual runners, but they are useful measurements for training. (There’s a reason why RW Senior Reviews Editor Cat Bowen named it “Best Value” in our overall Best Running Watches guide.)

GPS performance is a standout, with dual-frequency technology delivering smooth, reliable tracks even in neighborhoods and city environments that can throw cheaper chips off course. Dengate also highlights the new voice log feature, which lets you record post-run thoughts that automatically transcribe into the Coros app, making training logs easier to maintain.

At 40 grams with the silicone band (32 grams with nylon), the watch feels barely there in daily use and workouts, though Dengate dislikes the finicky digital dial—especially with gloves—and finds notification text too small to read easily mid-run. For runners who value turn-by-turn, full-color maps, the Pace 4’s breadcrumb-only navigation may be a limitation, but for most no-frills runners wanting accurate tracking, solid battery life, and a modern screen at an entry-level price, it is a compelling choice.

Look, I’ve spent more money on a pair of running shoes than this watch costs. And, honestly? That’s a little embarrassing for the shoes. At $170, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium is wildly outperforming its price tag, and in the words of Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate, if you can find better (for the price) I’ll eat it.

For new runners, this watch is a gift. There’s a whole training library that walks you through what a tempo run or a fartlek actually is, instead of assuming you already know. You get pace, cadence, heart rate zones, running power, and form metrics like ground contact time, which is stuff I did not have on watches costing three times as much. It also has free offline maps with turn-by-turn navigation, so you can leave your phone in your pocket. The cheapest Garmin with offline mapping is over $700.

The recovery metrics are right up there with Garmin and Apple: Training load, VO2 Max, readiness recommendations, sleep and HRV tracking that’s detailed enough to make you rethink that 5 p.m. Diet Coke. It nudges you toward rest days with a little less guilt than Garmin.

The nitpicks: The user experience needs polish—do not disturb is fiddlier than it should be, and the four buttons are sensitive. I’ve paused mid-run more than once with an errant sleeve. Still, for the money? Nothing touches it.

At just around $300, the Polar Pacer has some great training specific features that make it especially useful for competitive runners training on a budget.

Its built-in running program can help you create a training plan to get ready for a 5K, 10K, half marathon, or marathon. Using the Polar Flow app, you can select your race type and date (or the name of the race) and it will create specific workouts to follow within the app that are synched to your watch to follow along. It also provides comprehensive training insights after intervals and long runs, and tracks your long-term fitness trends outside of training.

There are also niche, but useful features like fueling and hydration reminders, and “Training Load Pro,” which monitors strain and recovery. As someone who isn’t great at taking cues from my body when it’s time to take a break, having an active reminder was helpful. (And something you can usually expect in an affordable running watch.)

Although I generally liked Polar’s hardware and software design, I felt that Polar could have used the space of its 1.2-inch MIP display a bit more effectively. Much of the text was small, and the screen had lots of unnecessary white space that could have been used to support more specs, or at least a larger font.

I also found it a bit unintuitive that the “red” button was used for intervals, rather than a start/stop button. It ended up working out great–it’s a helpful button–but there was a bit of a learning curve.

For race runners who want support to help them train, but may not be able to afford a coach or training program, the Pacer feels about as close to having a coach on your wrist as possible at this price point.

The Garmin Forerunner 70 is Garmin’s new entry-level running watch, priced at $250, and it’s a great pick for beginners.

It has a 1.2-inch AMOLED touchscreen, which is the same panel tech found on watches costing twice as much, so it looks and feels more premium than you’d expect at this price. More importantly, it includes Training Readiness and Training Status, features that used to be reserved for watches costing $400 or more, plus an on-device Quick Workouts generator and free Garmin Coach plans for 5K, 10K, and half-marathon training—no subscription needed.

The five buttons make it easy to navigate menus, and it’s light and comfortable for daily wear. Battery life is boss too: they say it’s up to 13 days in smartwatch mode and 23 hours in GPS mode, but in real life? You’re getting a full week. It skips extras like multi-band GPS and NFC payments, but for a new runner focused on building a habit and understanding their training, that’s an easy trade.

Before I switched to a “proper” running watch, I started my wearable tech journey by tracking runs on an Apple Watch. I trained for my first marathon using one, and I actually still wear an Apple Watch SE between runs because of its effective multi-sport fitness tracking and quality of life features like setting voice-activated timers.

Though the Apple Watch is generally beloved, we generally steer runners towards brands like Garmin and Coros, which offer more robust tracking features and better battery life, often at lower prices than Apple’s generalist counterparts. That said, Apple Watches still work well for casual runners, tracking the basics and giving you lifestyle features that you won’t find on other watches in this price range.

To keep it to $300 with GPS and cellular, we recommend the smaller of the SE’s two sizes, 40mm, which translates to a 1.57-inch display. (The larger 44mm version starts at $280 without cellular, though you can sometimes find it for less.) Both versions are far larger than any of my other basic recommendations, which is great if you have a larger wrist or need a large screen for visibility. I personally like the smaller version, which keeps the watch light but still easy to read.

Apple Watches also generally feature a wider range of wrist band options, first- and third-party, and the SE’s bands come in two sizes: If comfort has been an issue for you, this watch gives you the best chance of finding something that feels good.

Apple offers two related apps that utilize your run data–the fitness focused Apple Fitness and the more metrics-minded Apple Health. Fitness allows you to create workouts and segments for training, while charting deep metrics. You can see a lot of information at a glance, too, including time elapsed, heart rate, rolling mile (pace over the last mile), average pace, and distance. That said, I didn’t love the way Apple organized my workout data, you need to search by date rather than just checking an activity log. (Of course, you can always switch to Strava or Nike Run Club if you don’t like the system.)

If you have a child who is starting to exercise and wants to track their steps like mom and dad, the Garmin Bounce is a special smartwatch designed for kids that covers basic fitness tracking and serves as a controlled way for parents to keep tabs, both via texting and GPS tracking.

The Bounce is designed for kids, which is to say that it’s built to withstand them. It’s durable and water-resistant with an IP68 rating, so it can go anywhere with them. The battery lasts up to two days, minimizing the chance that it’ll run dry on them. It also has a colorful UI that encourages kids to engage with the watch and their metrics, and activities and games to help get them moving.

In terms of tracking, the Bounce falls short of my usual standards for tracking: It just shows time and distance. For a kid–not a teen or even a tween, but a kid–that’s about as much as they can handle or care about. That data syncs with the Garmin Jr. app, which parents can access remotely.

It’s worth noting that both the parenting and games features have elements that require mobile WiFi (LTE) support, so you will likely want to add it to your mobile data plan, which will add about $10/month to your monthly bill.

Overall, this is a great way to help kids start to move around more and start thinking about the concept of exercise.

Every watch on this list costs $300 or less. That’s the line I drew, and I drew it on purpose: you shouldn’t have to spend a car payment to find out whether you like running.

I’ve spent my running career strapping these things to my wrist—testing, logging miles, and digging through what’s actually worth buying right now. What made the cut are watches that nail the fundamentals: speed, heart rate, and location, tracked with reasonable accuracy. (If the gap between 155 and 156 bpm matters to you, you need a pricier watch or, better yet, a dedicated HRM. For everyone else, this is plenty.) From there, they earn their spots with battery life that won’t leave you hunting for a charger, multi-sport modes, advanced biometrics like blood oxygen, and built-in coaching programs.

Here’s the part nobody says out loud: a basic watch is the best way to figure out what you actually want. It shows you real data, real proof that the hard work is working. And by the time you’re ready to shell out for something flashier, you’ll know exactly which features you really need.

At the bare minimum, an affordable running watch needs to track your pace, heart rate, route, distance, and time—with at least moderate precision, and displayed in a way you can read at mile 9 when your eyes are glazing over. It should have GPS, so you can map your routes and find your way home, and it should be accurate.

But basic doesn’t mean bare-bones. Plenty of watches in this range monitor more nuanced heart rate data, like your body’s ability to use oxygen during exercise (VO2 max). Most throw in sleep tracking and multi-sport modes, and many will synthesize your training data into insights that can help you get faster.

Spend more and you’ll get mid-tier and high-end watches with features that are nice to have but almost never essential: bigger and more precise sensors, LTE and WiFi support, contactless payment, onboard music storage. Worth knowing: some of the most elite runners in the world train and race in shockingly basic watches. The watch doesn’t run the miles. You do.

Checking your stats mid-run on a sunny day is miserable if the display is small and dim. The best running watches use an AMOLED display which is the same tech found in high-end smartphones and it has brighter colors and deeper contrast, so your numbers stay legible in full daylight.

An AMOLED screen isn’t a guarantee at $250, but that doesn’t mean you’re stuck squinting. Several watches I recommend use a transflective Memory-in-Pixel (MIP) display, which trades vibrant color for battery efficiency and stays highly visible outdoors. Pixel density matters just as much as the panel type, as does maximum brightness, measured in nits.

Most running watches have an auto-off backlight to conserve battery, but the screen should snap on the instant you raise your arm. You should never be standing there waiting for your own watch.

Size-wise, basic running watches run small. They’re roughly 1 to 1.6 inches. A bigger screen makes it easier to see your route map and stats, and gives you room to fit more data on screen if you customize your workout display.

Every smartwatch brand makes a companion app for iOS and Android that stores and analyzes your run data. Because the watch display is tiny, your phone is almost always the better place to adjust settings, rearrange screens, and build workouts.

If you have an iPhone, you already know Apple Fitness. Garmin, Coros, and Polar all offer companion apps with similar functionality, though some are meaningfully easier to live with than others. And any running watch worth buying should support the big third-party apps like Strava and Runna.

Aside from Apple’s watches, even the budget-friendly models I recommend only need charging every week or so, and they juice back up fast. The best of the best go over a fortnight on a single charge.

Keep your expectations calibrated, though: manufacturer battery estimates are best-case scenarios, and your watch probably won’t hit them. Real-world battery life varies charge to charge, and your mileage depends on, well, your mileage. Continuous GPS tracking during workouts is the biggest drain by far. You can switch features off to stretch the time between charges, but a good watch gives you plenty of run time either way.

A good running watch should feel light enough that you forget it’s there. At this price you rarely find something heavy and bulky, but check how it sits on your wrist before you take it out for miles. Some of my picks come in multiple sizes, which helps if you have smaller or larger wrists.

Make sure the band is highly adjustable and can feel secure without being too tight. And remember that many watch bands are replaceable, so if the stock strap isn’t working for you—comfort-wise or style-wise—you have options.

Known as a “social network for athletes,” Strava has become increasingly popular since its launch in 2009. By connecting your running watch to the app, you can upload your runs to the platform for your “friends” to see and give each other “kudos”. The app also tracks PR for different distances and frequent segments that you can get badges for.

It can be an easy way for you to keep all your running data in the same place, especially if you’re using different brands of running watches to track your runs. Plus, you can unlock more features, such as advanced training metrics, with the full paid membership.

What heart rate do I need to hit to get faster?

According to Mayo Clinic, runners should aim for a target heart rate zone of 70- to 85 percent of their maximum heart rate to improve speed over time. This is also known as Zone 2, which some runners tout as the ultimate training metric. A running watch can help you figure out your max heart rate and will allow you to monitor your heart rate during and after the run.

Do basic running watches track distance and heart rate accurately?

For both mapping and logging distance, smartwatches rely on a Global Position System (GPS), which uses satellites to precisely track your location. The quality of your specific watch’s tracking can vary, both based on the quality of the GPS system and on environmental factors like tall buildings and crowds.

That said, the quality of GPS tracking in smartwatches is quite high across the board: Nothing’s perfect, but you can expect your location to be accurate to within a few feet, and your movement to be captured precisely.

Running watches are set to connect with US GPS systems, but you can also opt to connect with other systems like Galileo (European Union) and GLONASS (Russia) to try to improve your accuracy, something I recommend for those experiencing disruptions.

For heart rate, smartwatches rely on optical heart rate sensors that use light (those green beams coming out of the bottom of your watch) to measure blood flow changes in the skin's capillaries and determine your heart rate. They are fairly accurate, generally to within a few beats per minute (BPM). That said, a dedicated heart rate monitor that you strap to your chest will generally provide more accurate readings.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

#8781. Canyon’s PACE Cockpit Has a Clever Answer to One of Integrated Bars’ Biggest Problems

Five drop shapes and three width settings add flexibility to a proprietary cockpit.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Integrated cockpits can be light, aerodynamic, and good-looking. They can also make simple jobs harder than they need to be. Adjusting your position can mean cutting a steerer tube. Replacing a broken handlebar can mean buying a whole new cockpit. And routing brake hoses through everything can turn a small change into a long afternoon.

I’ve given Canyon’s PACE system plenty of criticism in my reviews. It’s proprietary, and integrated systems come with real compromises. But after swapping the drops on the Endurace CF SLX 9 I have in for review, I want to give Canyon credit for a thoughtful design choice.

The main section of the PACE cockpit is called the T-Bar. Canyon’s system lets you adjust cockpit height by up to 20 mm in 5mm increments, without cutting the steerer. The cockpit is also made up of three pieces, with the drop sections bolted to the T-Bar. That offers a couple of advantages.

First, it makes the bar width adjustable. The T-Bar has three width positions, 25 mm apart, for a total range of 50 mm. The actual widths depend on the drop shape. See the table below.

The bolt-on drops also let Canyon offer five shapes with different dimensions. If the drops that come on your new Canyon don’t suit you, you can swap them for another option.

My Endurace review bike came with the Compact drops. They have a 108mm drop, width settings from 390 to 440 mm, and 8 degrees of flare. I prefer a narrower bar with a deeper drop and more flare, so I switched to Canyon’s Control drops. They have a 120mm drop, adjust from 370 to 420 mm, and feature 17 degrees of flare.

*U.S. prices at the time of writing. Bar tape and fixing screws are included.

Here’s what I needed to do to make the swap: unwrap the bar, loosen and slide off the controls, remove the old drops, install the new ones, then tighten everything and rewrap the bar. Canyon includes fresh bar tape with the replacement drops.

Canyon also includes a clever cardboard tool that helps you evenly align your controls. I loved it!

With most one-piece integrated cockpits, switching to a different bar shape or replacing a broken drop means replacing the whole assembly. Depending on the bike’s routing, that may also mean disconnecting or replacing brake hoses and bleeding the brakes.

On the PACE, the brake hoses run behind the drop sections rather than through them, so I didn’t have to disconnect or cut them. That meant no brake bleed, no risk of ending up with a hose that’s too short, and no replacing the entire cockpit.

That also matters if you crash and break a drop. With a one-piece handlebar and stem, a broken bar can mean replacing the whole assembly. With PACE, you can replace the damaged section.*

*If you break a drop, check the PACE T-Bar, or stem, for damage, too. Replace it if necessary.

The system can also make bike travel less nerve-racking. If your bar tape is set up so the controls can slide on and off without rewrapping, you can unbolt the drops and let them hang out of the way. The bike packs a little narrower, and the handlebar ends are less exposed to side impacts. I’ve had bars damaged in transit more times than I can count, so I appreciate this feature.

PACE is still proprietary, and those concerns don’t disappear because one part of the system is clever. But integrated cockpits often force riders to accept limited adjustability, few shape options, and costly replacements. Canyon has found a useful way to make its handlebar easier to fit, repair, and travel with. For that, it deserves some credit.

#8780. ‘At 60, I Went From Zero Running Experience to Finishing the NYC Marathon Within a Year. These 5 Strategies Got Me to the Finish.’

A first-time marathoner over 50 shares the training, mindset, and support that carried him 26.2 miles.

I’ve never been a runner. Before this past year, the last time I ran was a local 5K on a whim with my daughter about a decade ago. I didn’t prepare for it at all, so it was challenging, and I never ran again after that.

Then, this past May, I signed up to run another local 5K, two months before I turned 60. Working in an office full of runners—I’m an editor at Popular Mechanics and we share an office with Runner’s World—I just wanted to prove that I could do it.

I went on a handful of runs before the race in an attempt to prepare, but I couldn't really make it past 1.5 miles. I got really frustrated. Leading up to race day, I saw how hilly the course was and decided to just wing it. If I had to walk at some points, I’d walk… and that’s what I did on most hills, because I didn’t quite have the stamina to make it through.

But all the runners around me were so inspiring; it felt like we could all make it through together. I saw someone in front of me going about the same pace, and that helped pull me to the finish line. I finished in 35:16, averaging an 11:20 pace.

A few months later, I got the opportunity to run the New York City Marathon. I was hesitant to accept, because I didn’t think I could run that far, but a few of my colleagues pushed me to say yes and really believed in me. So I signed up.

GET YOUR ZERO-TO-MARATHON TRAINING PLAN HERE

When I started marathon training, I followed the Runner’s World six-month zero-to-marathon training plan. I skipped a few weeks ahead because I had already worked up to running five miles and the plan starts with walking.

My training experience was far from perfect, but I learned that as a beginner, you have to just start and go from there.

To be totally honest, I didn’t train for the marathon as much as I probably should have. I started training around early August by running three times a week on local trails in the evenings, averaging three- to five-mile easy runs. I also made sure to add hills to most of my runs to get my quads ready for the hills in New York.

My training came to a bit of a halt after the first few weeks of training, when I realized I probably needed to contact my cardiologist. A couple of years ago, the doctors told me I have an enlarged aorta (the largest artery in your body that carries blood from your heart to the rest of your body), which the doctor attributed to my physically demanding years as an ironworker.

The problem with an enlarged aorta is that if it ruptures, you could have a fatal heart attack with little to no warning signs. Thinking about this made me nervous to train out of fear I might put too much stress on my heart.

So I called the doctor and scheduled an appointment, but they had to reschedule it for the last week of October and I wouldn’t be able to do imaging until November. But I told the nurse practitioner about my marathon training, and the doctor gave me the go-ahead to continue running with caution. I decided to stick with it knowing I didn’t have any symptoms or immediate concerns.

However, I did miss many of my long runs and I was pretty stressed that I wasn’t keeping up with the training plan. Once race day got closer, I grew tired of being hesitant and ran a 15-mile long run, which is the minimum distance run coaches recommend to cover in marathon training. Thankfully, I felt really strong through every mile and fueled well, which gave me reassurance for race day.

I also did about four of the threshold interval workouts in the beginning of the zero-to-marathon training plan, naively thinking they would be easier than easy runs because they included two-minute breaks…but they were not. I remember one workout in particular: eight sets of one-minute threshold efforts with one minute of recovery between each, along with a two-mile warmup and cooldown and some 30-second pre-workout strides. It was harder than I thought, but I got through it.

Toward the end of my training block, I noticed my pace naturally getting faster, which boosted my confidence and made me think I could potentially aim for sub-five hours on race day.

I also have a very basic strength routine that I do three to four times a week with a 35-pound kettlebell, which I kept up with throughout training, and I think that helped keep me strong and durable enough for the race.

I typically do a combination of 20 to 50 kettlebell swings, 10 weighted goblet squats, and 10 push-ups. I think the kettlebell is one of the greatest weight tools there is; I don’t have to go to a crowded gym and I can fit in a sufficient strength workout at home. The key with my strength routine is to not stop and complete the reps continuously.

I also incorporated two to three sets of five to 10 minutes of continuous jump rope between some of my strength sets at least once a week. This meant I snuck in some plyometric work to build my power and durability.

For people out there who think that they can’t train for and run a marathon, you can. I loved reading Runner’s World articles and training plans. If you follow a plan, even loosely, you can get to the finish.

The morning of the race, I felt very anxious. I traveled from Princeton, New Jersey, that morning, making a stack of six large pancakes (my go-to fuel source) and ate three before I left my house, saving the rest for the bus ride to the start line.

I felt a sense of imposter syndrome at the starting line, which I think goes hand in hand with being a writer. Whether it was my early years of being a screenwriter or adjusting to a new job at Popular Mechanics, I constantly dance with a feeling of “why am I here?” Those feelings came flooding back at the marathon. I thought to myself, “I’m not a runner…what am I doing here?” But I’ve learned the only way to work through that is to just do it, and take the first step.

With 12 gels on me and a 17-ounce handheld bottle of electrolyte mix, I made my way through the race, maintaining an easy effort. I felt like I could breathe through my nose if I wanted to for most of the time.

Some of my favorite parts of the race were running past buildings I’ve worked on and listening to the crowds. I didn’t turn on my music once during the whole race because the cheering was so loud and gave me so much energy.

There’s something particularly special about the creative, weird, and wonderful energy in the New York City Marathon. It was touching to see how such a big city comes together on this day, and not out of tragedy. I had never even been to a marathon before this, so that part felt really powerful. We’re living in a time of uncertainty, so it’s nice to know that people are still there for each other in the way they should be.

By the time I got past the halfway mark of the race, I realized sub-five was out of reach and I adjusted to sticking to my goal of simply finishing. I found my family around mile 17, which gave me the courage to keep going despite miles 19 and 20 hitting me hard.

I finished in 5:18:56, greeted by my colleagues holding my medal for me at the finish line. I felt like I proved that you can do anything you put your mind to, and I was so glad that my family was there to watch me finish, too.

The same thing that pulled me through my 5K happened around mile 18 or 19 of the marathon. I looked up and saw a woman wearing a hydration vest with a sign on her back printed in pink that read, “22 weeks pregnant.” I thought to myself, “Oh my god. I’m following you because you’re my new inspiration.” If she was running this race pregnant, there was no way I was giving up.

At mile 20, I knew I wasn’t going to be able to break five hours, but I’m grateful and proud I made it past mile 15 because that was the farthest distance I’d gone. I saw my family spectating at mile 17, and I think if I had seen them at an earlier mile, I would’ve struggled more to keep going.

My family really believed in me along the way. They made “Team Smith” shirts, and a bunch of my friends and family members came in to watch, including my son FaceTiming in from Paris. I only got to see them for a minute, but that’s what carried me for the last nine miles.

For me, half the battle of the race was mental. I thought to myself that anything after 15 miles would feel like driving at night: Your headlights only show you 50 feet in front of you, so only focus on that. You can’t see the whole road out to where you’re going, but you can keep going bit by bit. I told myself I could go another two miles at a time, and before I knew it, I was at the 23-mile mark.

My marathon experience brought me back to an early point in my career, when I graduated from film school in Ithaca, New York in 1988, lived in Los Angeles for a little while, then moved back home to New Jersey. People told me I would never sell a script living in New Jersey, but I sold four. Then, people told me I would never get a movie made, but I did. I really wanted to prove these things to myself, and I treated 26.2 miles the same way.

I also have three kids in their early and mid-20s. I wanted to set an example for them that you can do anything you set your mind to, and to reiterate a value that holds up in our family: to never, ever give up.

When I think about what my kids experience, I notice a lot of pressure on their generation on social media to not fail at a goal they set. In my work life, the only way I ever learned anything new with tools or construction was by trying, messing something up, and then trying to do it better. The entire marathon experience emulated that belief for me: The only way to succeed at anything is to fail a lot. That’s how you learn, grow, and get better.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#8779. Garmin’s Best Cycling Radars Are Discounted for Black Friday—Here’s How the RearVue 820 and RTL515 Compare, and Which Is Best for Your Rides

The benchmark Varia RTL515 is cheaper, but the RearVue 820 adds range, battery, and smarter tracking.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Cycling radar entirely changed my bike rides. After a speeding pickup passed dangerously close to me on a ride in June 2025, I installed a radar system on my road bike. Since getting a radar, I have ridden over 7,500 miles on paved and gravel roads, and I’ve had a radar mounted on my bike for almost all of them—I cannot imagine riding without it. It’s the best safety upgrade I’ve made in more than three decades of riding and something every road and gravel rider should try.

For Black Friday, Garmin—the market leader in cycling radar—has its two top-performing Varia radar systems on sale. This includes the benchmark RTL515 and the new RearVue 820 released earlier this year. Both are exceptional radar units, and our top-tested models—but which one is best for you, or as a holiday gift for a cyclist in your life?

SHOP MORE GARMIN DEALS SHOP MORE GEAR DEALS

Above: Test Editor Dan Chabanov digs into all of the details in this video.

All cycling radar systems work essentially the same. The radar unit emits pulses of electromagnetic radio waves that bounce off vehicles approaching from behind before returning to the device. Using the reflected beams, the device calculates and tracks vehicles’ distance, direction, and relative speed, and sends that tracking data to your cycling computer. The head unit then provides an audible warning and graphically displays vehicles’ relative location and speed, giving you time to react accordingly. Most devices also integrate the radar with an LED taillight to alert drivers to your presence.

What separates good radar units from bad ones is the proprietary algorithms each brand uses to tune sensitivity and detection for their respective devices. A good radar consistently provides clear warnings of approaching vehicles, but bad ones can provide frequent false alarms, or worse, fail to warn of an approaching vehicle.

In the year and a half since I started using a radar light on my rides, I’ve ridden a dozen radar systems from nine brands. Several work well and I use them on my bikes, and a few of them were duds. However, of all of the cycling radars we’ve tried, none are as consistently reliable as Garmin’s Varia models.

Picking the Varia model that’s best for you (or a rider whose safety you care about) depends on a few factors. Both are excellent units, but why overpay for tech you can’t use or don’t need on your rides?

The RTL515 is the benchmark cycling radar system, and we judge all others against it. The 515 works more reliably than any other radar we tested—Other systems might have longer battery life, weigh less, or pack a brighter light, but none are as well-rounded or as easy to use as this Garmin. It detects vehicles up to 153 yards away, and its 65-lumen flash is visible to drivers from 1.2 miles.

The 515 packs up to 8 hours of battery life per charge, and weighs 72 grams (without a mount). It connects to most cycling computers featuring Bluetooth or ANT+ compatibility, but Garmin’s Varia radar phone app is also stellar. If you ride with your phone on your bar, it can serve as a display, and it can deliver audio notifications through headphones even if you’re not listening to music or a podcast.

Garmin’s newest cycling radar improves on the Varia RTL515’s greatness. Compared to the 515, the RearVue 820 has more battery life (up to 15 hours), a brighter flashing light (100 lumens), and greater vehicle-detection range (up to 191 yards). Plus, the 820 adds a brake-light feature that increases rear light intensity as you slow.

Crucially, the RearVue 820 incorporates features found on no other radars (from Garmin or any other brand). While other radars often drop vehicles when they slow down behind you, the 820 tracks vehicles traveling at your same speed; it’s a handy feature you don’t know you need until you try it. Additionally, if you use a Garmin Edge X40- or X50-series computer, the radar tracks a vehicle that changes lanes behind you. It also shows icons to indicate each vehicle’s size (small, medium, or large).

The RCT715 is basically the RTL515 with a rear-facing camera. However, it is larger, heavier, and has a shorter battery life than the 515. It’s so heavy (148 grams) that it requires a proprietary mount. The camera also greatly reduces battery life—in continuous video mode, it might not last through long rides. However, the 715 is worth considering for bike commuters, riders who advocate for better cycling infrastructure, or those who want peace of mind.

#8778. After Hitting Rock Bottom, an Army Veteran Went for a Run With a Plan to End His Life. Then He Heard a Familiar Military Command He Couldn’t Ignore.

For years, Jeremy Hurtt asked himself: “Why should I be alive when better people weren’t?”

Editor’s Note: This story contains a mention of suicide. If you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or self-harming behaviors, call or text 988 to get help from the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

Jeremy Hurtt woke up that winter morning in 2014, and after staring at the ceiling for a few minutes, headed out for a run, thinking it may be his last.

He headed toward the spot where the run—and everything else—could end. An overpass above an interstate in the town of Benton, Arkansas, a mile from the house he had been crashing in for the past few weeks, sleeping on a cold floor, getting by on the generosity of a friend. Money had troubled Jeremy for years. He did odd jobs around town for a few bucks but mostly was bumming $10 and $20 from friends just to get by. He was 34 years old, with nothing in the bank, no home, no car, not even a driver’s license. All these little indignities, piling up, had started to bury him.

Since finishing a deployment in Iraq in 2008, there’d been lots of days when Jeremy felt down, depressed—and seemed different from the playful, clownish, upbeat guy his Army pals and others had come to know. “He was no longer good-time Jeremy,” one friend says. “He was withdrawn, reclusive.” But he never seriously thought about hurting himself. Until that morning when the indignities were too many, and his mind couldn’t stop wondering why he was still alive and better people weren’t.

The overpass was a destination he had crossed before. On walks and runs when he was up for it. At that early-morning hour, semitrucks would be rushing below. He, on the other hand, wasn’t rushing, running at his usual 8- to 9-minute pace, which let his mind race ahead. Running was something he had done occasionally, a means to an end after his return home from Iraq, a way to stay somewhat fit. That morning, running was the means to get where he needed to go.

He thought of what would happen if he decided to jump. About the driver whose vehicle would likely strike him once he landed on the road. He didn’t want to cause another person pain. He knew from his time in Iraq the pain that comes with sudden death. But even this good intention couldn’t deter him from running ahead.

He gave little thought to what might happen if he didn’t jump.

He neared the overpass. A short way to go. The sound of semis intensified. Just a little farther. A railing on the overpass to climb over. The poor driver. One more step.

And then he heard something else. Words in his head.

If you’ve been in the military, you know Charlie-Mike. You may have heard the call, the command. Jeremy followed it often when stationed in Iraq in the mid–to-late aughts. It was a time when improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and explosively formed penetrators (EFPs) got mentioned on the nightly news as often as sports scores and tomorrow’s forecast. When American troops tried to end chaos in a country exacerbated by American miscalculation.

Charlie-Mike is military code: Continue the Mission. Move forward. In the face of adversity. No matter what.

There was no shortage of adversity in Iraq, which the U.S. invaded in 2003. By the time the U.S. Central Command announced the final withdrawal of troops this past September, more than 4,300 American troops had been killed. Jeremy Hurtt served there for 15 months, during the 2006–2008 surge. What he saw and heard, and those he met and those he lost, remain fresh in his mind. He and his troop—Alpha 3/61—were fired upon often; sometimes they stopped until they heard the command. Like the memories of friends who didn’t come home from their deployment, he’s never forgotten Charlie-Mike.

At that moment atop the overpass, Charlie-Mike dominated his thoughts—pushing out all others. It triggered, he says now, “a moment of clarity.” Everything is a mission. “You’re not done,” he recalls thinking that morning. “You’re not done until you get to where you’re supposed to be.” To him, that meant he couldn’t stop running—or living.

Jeremy ran until he was back at his friend’s house. He had a plan, one he put into action a couple of days later. And as the plan unfolded in the weeks and months that followed, the running intensified. Longer and longer distances. Not fast miles, just miles.

But as much as he’s run in the years since that January morning, Jeremy has never outrun what ultimately brought him to the overpass in the first place.

Jeremy Hurtt comes from Harrison, Arkansas, a town in the Ozarks. When he was a kid, the town had maybe 9,000 residents. “It’s big,” Jeremy, now 47, says with a slight chuckle. “There’s not a town that size for 90 minutes in any direction. Growing up, my cousins called me a city boy because I was from Harrison.”

In many ways, it had the comforts—and trappings—of the South. Like nearby Bull Shoals Lake, filled with smallmouth bass that made for easy fishing. Jeremy’s dad, a semipro fisherman, showed him all the tricks. Come the fall, football ruled. University of Arkansas Razorbacks, with their wishbone offense. When he wasn’t watching them on TV, Jeremy played ball himself. Even though he was barely 5 feet when he got to high school, he earned a spot as a wide receiver and safety on the school’s team. But for all the fun, at home his mom, Frances, kept priorities in order. “She was definitely one of those Bible-thumpin’ Southern Christian Baptists,” says Jeremy’s older brother, Jason. “We were raised in the church, and we always had that voice in our head, even when she wasn’t around.”

After high school, Jeremy followed many of his classmates to the University of Arkansas. He liked being away from home, living in the bigger city of Fayetteville, far from his mother’s rules. He was social, made friends easily, and bonded with many over his love of the Razorbacks. He attended games, as well as the pre- and postgame tailgates. He could go out on a Saturday night, and Friday and Thursday, too. The parties and the drinking came easy for the garrulous kid from Harrison. But his grades suffered, and by the end of his freshman year, his time in college had ended. Jeremy, who friends say was one of the smartest guys they knew, was “asked not to come back” for year two.

That summer, back in Harrison, he kept drinking, hanging out, working a dead-end job at a local newspaper. It was leading nowhere, and that didn’t sit well with Frances. One night he returned home to some tough talk. “My mom basically came to me,” he remembers, “and was like, ‘You’ve got a decision to make; you’re not going to sit here forever. You’re gonna figure out what you’re doing next.’” She’d already done some groundwork for him, talking with a local Army office. Jeremy followed up with a recruiter, thinking it would “get her off my back.” Instead, he was tantalized by prospects of a steady paycheck and career options following his service time. And, the recruiter told Jeremy, it was peacetime. There was no war to worry about. Jeremy enlisted right away and within days was headed to basic training.

It was September 1998. Peace wouldn’t last forever.

These days, Jeremy Hurtt loves to run hills. He’ll track his runs, aiming to hit 2,000 feet of elevation gain during a 13-miler. The effort calms him, lets him think. “The feeling of pushing yourself,” he says, “and trying to improve yourself.”

Running and hillwork weren’t always his forte, though, especially in boot camp where, as a college dropout, he was learning what discipline was all about. “I never was a huge running fan,” he says, “and I hated hills. I just couldn’t stand it, you know? I’d get halfway up a hill and just want to quit.”

After basic training, he was first stationed in South Korea and then assigned to a communications role in Washington, D.C. Some days he worked in the Pentagon. Life was good. He made friends with the other enlisted soldiers, who got to know Jeremy as the quick-witted guy from the Ozarks. The one who’d send his buddies off-color emails to get a chuckle or impress them by demonstrating how to download music for free. “I was always trying to make people laugh,” he says. They loved hanging out with him, especially after a cocktail or two. “He was a really smart guy, really funny, and he definitely enjoyed the world he was in,” says Dillon Cunningham, who was stationed with Jeremy at the time. He pauses a moment. “And then, you know, 9/11 happened.”

Jeremy was not in the Pentagon on September 11, 2001, when a hijacked American Airlines plane crashed into the building, killing the 64 passengers on board and 125 military personnel and civilians; he was doing fieldwork a few miles away. Amid the horrors and chaos of the events unfolding, it would take days before he could contact his mother and tell her he was okay.

Until 9/11, Jeremy’s path in the Army had gone according to plan. “My idea was [not] to go anywhere near combat,” he says. But the terrorist attacks that took nearly 3,000 lives changed his mind. One of his grandfathers had served in World War II. Jason, his brother, was already stationed in Turkey with the Air Force. Jeremy no longer wanted to serve within the relatively safe confines of his communications posting, testing radios and satellite switches. In 2003, he asked to be assigned to a cavalry unit so he could prep for deployment. He was 25 years old. “It was just a feeling that this is the moment for my generation,” Jeremy says. “I wanted to be directly involved in whatever came next.”

It would take three years before Sgt. Jeremy Hurtt learned what next involved—and how it would test him like no hill ever could.

As fall arrives in the Ozarks, the Buffalo River, where Jeremy and his friends used to raft in the summer, is still just deep enough for one last excursion. And the Arkansas Razorbacks are back on the field, offering once more a promise to their diehard fans.

But in the fall of 2006, Jeremy was in Iraq and missed all that. Home was 7,000 miles away—and somehow felt even farther. On his first full night in Baghdad, a rocket struck his barrack. It didn’t explode, and no one was injured, but Jeremy now had firsthand experience of combat life. “It wasn’t like that all the time,” he says. But it was clear to him that “there are people who want me dead. They are going to try to kill me.”

For much of his time, Jeremy and his troop were on security detail. They patrolled sectors in Sadr City and East Baghdad, scanning rooftops and street corners, searching for “high-value targets” to capture or kill. “There’s some combat; occasionally people shoot at you,” he says. “It’s a lot more common for them to try to blow you up.”

He recalls just one of many incidents. One afternoon in 2007, Alpha 3/61 was southwest of Sadr City. They were in six armored vehicles, Jeremy with his M240 machine gun on lookout in the third Humvee. Without warning, an EFP, the most lethal form of homemade explosive used against Coalition troops during the war, tore through the backside of the lead Humvee. The warhead narrowly missed Sgt. Matt Haeffner, Jeremy’s roommate, who sustained a concussion in the blast.

As Haeffner recalls, Jeremy was one of the first in his troop to check on him. “We’ll be friends forever because we shared crazy moments like that,” says Haeffner, who was awarded a Purple Heart following the EFP attack. “My wife calls it trauma bonding.”

Not all of Jeremy’s friends in Iraq made it home. Sgt. Eric Snell, a father of two, was killed during a small-arms fire in Baghdad. He was charismatic, Jeremy remembers, a former pro baseball player with the looks of a model. And there was Sgt. Alexander Fuller, who died when his Humvee struck an improvised bomb. “His wife was pregnant with their first child,” Jeremy says. Jeremy knew both Snell and Fuller from his earliest days in the cavalry. And then there were the eight men from his troop who died in a vicious battle in Afghanistan. That was hard on Jeremy, who, by then, had finished his deployment and was back in Arkansas, a world away from the fighting.

The distance added to his sense of guilt. Should he have re-upped for another tour and gone with his former troop to Afghanistan? Why did Snell and Fuller die, and not him? Why did the dumb drunk, as Jeremy thought of himself, get to live and those men did not?

“I always thought it’s a trade that anybody would have made. If you could trade me for Fuller and he gets to see his daughter grow up—I think people would make that trade,” Jeremy says. “And keep Snell around for his kid; that trade would make sense.” He pauses for a second. “To me, it just always seemed like a cruel joke—those people didn’t get to experience their lives, and I was still here.”

So he’d keep asking himself, “Why should I be alive when better people weren’t?”

Back in Arkansas, Jeremy didn’t forget what he saw and what he was missing. He couldn’t find much work but found plenty to drink. Within a year of returning home, his weight went from 170 pounds to 230. In Iraq, he ran occasionally, when the situation allowed, sweating in the desert heat. So when he got prodded by friends to enter a local weight-loss competition, he turned to running to peel the pounds away. “I was running up and down hills and in the heat and humidity of Arkansas,” he says, “so it came off pretty quickly.”

Bringing order and routine to other parts of life proved more challenging. For a time, he returned to the University of Arkansas, starting fresh. He tried majoring in broadcasting but never made it to graduation. He found a variety of part-time jobs, including production work at an ESPN radio affiliate. Nothing stuck. A girlfriend came and went. Alcohol was the only constant.

Fireworks on the Fourth of July or at a football game made him edgy. He’d drive through an underpass, see trash on the side of the road, and wonder if it was concealing an IED. He’d suddenly remember Snell. “He was my favorite soldier ever and got killed the day I went on leave,” he says, his eyes watering. He waits a moment. “That all rolled up into the guilt, everything, I felt for a lot of years afterward.”

Friends and family noticed a different Jeremy from the one they knew before deployment. “I remember linking up with him a few times, catching up, and it was like a shell,” Dillon Cunningham recalls. “He was there, but there wasn’t anything solid in there. You could quickly tell he was not operating at the specs we used to expect from him.”

Once they began to notice the changes, his friends and family began to worry.

Twenty-two. It’s a number “that really sticks heavily in most military guys’ heads,” Jason says. For nearly a decade, 22 referred to the number of deaths by suicide among U.S. military veterans each day. Several suicide prevention organizations have 22 in their names. The number is on flags and tattoos to promote awareness. Various versions of a 22 Push-Up Challenge ask participants to do 22 daily push-ups for 22 days. Even though the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs downgraded the number of suicides to 17.7 per day in 2024, 22 remains code for those in the know.

Jason worried his brother might become a statistic.

“The power that the brain has when you get yourself in certain situations—if you don’t have those people to talk to, you do just fall down a drain,” Jason says. “And the unfortunate thing is, so many people don’t know who to talk to. A perfect example is Jeremy; he lost his buddies. Those may have been the guys he talked to and that he felt good with. Well, they’re gone, and so he starts going down that drain.”

Jason became Jeremy’s lifeline. On that morning in 2014, when Jeremy didn’t jump from the overpass, he got back to his friend’s house and called his brother, who was living outside of St. Louis, several hundred miles away. He didn’t talk about his suicidal thoughts, but asked for help finding work, getting back on track. Jason didn’t hesitate. He got Jeremy a job on his crew that worked on upgrading cell towers. He’d be on the road a lot, and the hours would be unpredictable, but the work would be steady and bring in a paycheck—and a group of coworkers to be around. And after his shifts, Jeremy could go for a run, which he often did, in the same pair of basketball sneakers he wore to work.

Jeremy never sought professional counseling, but he suspects he was suffering from PTSD. Getting psychological help is not something many veterans choose to pursue, his brother says. “When you come home, and you go talk to someone that has the sheepskin on the wall,” Jason says, “they say they know how a brain works. [But] you start talking to them, and there’s a major disconnect. These people have no idea what you’re talking about.”

Jeremy found a different kind of help, a different way to cope. The simple act of putting one foot in front of the other that brought clarity to his mind like nothing else. It interrupted the repetitive negative thoughts rumbling in his head. “So many troops find things to soothe their pain—if that’s gentlemen’s clubs, beer, drugs, whatever,” says Jason, who now works as a helicopter pilot for the FAA. “Jeremy was smart enough to channel that into running, and running was that savior for him.”

Jeremy started paying off debts. With the technical skills acquired from his past communication job, he eventually got a job with a company doing software testing. By 2018, he had saved enough to buy a place in a wooded, secluded area back in the Ozarks. Hills were nearby. That was when his love for accumulating elevation kicked in. He entered some races—he’s run the Little Rock Marathon three times, with a PR of 4:55:58—but preferred running solo.

And on those solo runs, he could finally start processing what he lived through in Iraq.

Jeremy has never mentioned his run to the overpass to Jason or Matt Haeffner or Dillon Cunningham. In fact, the only person he’s told is his wife, Stacie. They met online before his deployment to Iraq and stayed in touch for nearly a decade. In 2014, they reconnected. Stacie was living in Nashville at the time, and Jeremy was in the area working on a cell tower job. They went on a few dates, kept texting and calling when Jeremy’s job was done and he was back in Arkansas. Then, at the end of 2019, when Jeremy was living alone in his house in the woods, he texted Stacie that he wanted to be more serious. “He had been running,” she remembers, “and he was like, ‘I really think we’re supposed to give this a real shot.’ I was like, ‘Okay, let’s figure this out.’” She packed up and moved to Arkansas. “We were engaged in a few months,” she says with a smile.

And by 2021, they were married. Friends from around the country came to the wedding. They saw the Jeremy they remembered from before Iraq. Sort of. The night before the wedding, a group of Army friends got together in his house. The laughter was flowing, and so were the drinks. But before it got too late, Jeremy told his buddies he was headed to bed. “You can imagine military guys—we were like, ‘Oh, come on, man. You’re getting married. Screw that,’” Dillon says. “And he was like, ‘I gotta run a half marathon in the morning. I run a half marathon every Saturday.’” On the morning of his wedding, Jeremy ran, showered, and made it to the ceremony with time to spare.

This past June, Stacie and Jeremy welcomed a new member to the family. Baby Josephine. She keeps Mom and Dad busy, so Jeremy has cut back on running. He might get a short one in during the workweek. Come the weekend, though, Stacie gives him the green light and lets him go long. And at an 11-minute pace, he runs his half marathon.

“I don’t think it was trivial that I ran to that overpass,” he says, sitting in the den of their home outside of Houston, where they moved just before Josephine was born. “There’s something that happens in a run where, like, I have breakthroughs and insight. And I think that’s what happened that day. The mile I took to run to that overpass gave me just enough to be in a moment. It all kind of clicked into place.” Jeremy waits a second. He thinks back a dozen years. “I was—excuse my frankness—bullshitting away the opportunity. I had to be here, in this experience of being alive.”

Just then, Josephine starts stirring. Jeremy Hurtt has to go. He has a mission to get back to.

Charles Butler, a former editor at Runner's World, now teaches journalism at the University of Oregon. With Matt Long, he wrote The Long Run: A New York City Firefighter's Triumphant Comeback from Crash Victim to Elite Athlete.

#8777. Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X Review (2025): Assault’s Best Bike Yet?

Written by Joseph Lucero, MS, CSCS Last updated on Jan 12, 2024

The Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines currently offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity. Popular in the CrossFit community, this fan bike consists of a belt-driven system and a heavy-duty steel frame, making it a great tool to build both endurance and strength.

Here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike. We put it through hours of strenuous cardio workouts to see if it could take on the challenge. In this Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X review, we’ll highlight our results, how well the bike ranked in testing, and how it compares to other fan bikes.

At Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment. We have a product testing team that has put hundreds of machines through the wringer, using them for everything from gentle warm-ups to high-intensity interval training (HIIT) workouts. Many of our staff members are home gym owners themselves and use these products nearly every day.

With the knowledge we’ve gained over the years, we created a proprietary scoring system that we used to rank the AssaultBike ProX in various categories. Not only did we evaluate how the bike performed on its own, but we also compared it with nearly 30 other exercise bikes to see how it stacked up against the competition.

From the founders of the AssaultRunner (one of the best treadmills to train with), the Assault Bike ProX is made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat that helps keep it corrosion-resistant and capable of standing the test of time. It is a top-tier fan bike that can provide a brutal workout for any athlete.

In addition to its tough and durable frame, it incorporates a belt-driven system for a quiet, smooth training experience. It also requires less upkeep than chain-driven systems, which should come as a relief to busy individuals who can’t be bothered with complicated maintenance protocols.

At the time of writing, the Assault Bike ProX costs $899. Fortunately, there is also an option to finance it at around $82 a month through Affirm. For comparison, the Assault Bike ProX is more expensive than the AssaultBike Classic at $699 but cheaper than the Concept2 BikeErg, which costs around $1,100.

The Assault Bike ProX also provides free shipping, which is a big deal for equipment this size. Buying an air bike from another brand could set you back another $100 in shipping costs.

All of the above considered, we’ve rated this bike 4 out of 5 stars for its shipping rate, finance options, and value.

The Assault Bike ProX weighs 125 pounds, has a max user weight of 330 pounds, and boasts a heavy-duty steel frame with a corrosion-resistant black powder coating finish.  We love this type of frame and finish because it means less maintenance over time.

It’s also similar to what you would see with the Rogue Echo Bike, which has a black powder coating and almost looks like it was built from scraps of a heavy-duty squat rack! But the Assault Bike ProX isn’t as bulky as the Rogue Echo Bike, making it more compatible with small spaces, which our product testers enjoyed. For comparison, the ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high, while the Echo Bike is 55 inches long, 29.5 inches wide, and 52.25 inches high.

The Assault Bike ProX provides a wide padded seat that can adjust to 11 different heights and six different directions either forward or backward. These adjustments were the same on the Assault Bike Pro, which the ProX replaces. The rubber handles on the ProX help you maintain your grip and keep your hands comfortable throughout the workout as well.

This fan bike also comes with footpegs at the base of the handlebars for you to place your feet. This gives you the option to do an upper body-only workout, which is great for injury recovery or arm day.

Based on the quality and construction of the Assault Bike ProX, we rated it 5 out of 5 stars.

We gave the AssaultBike Pro X 5 out of 5 stars for delivery and assembly because of how straightforward it was to build. The bikes arrived at our testing facility 75 percent built, so all we had to do was attach the LCD console, pedals, handlebars, seat post, and saddle. Assault Fitness provides all the tools needed to build your air bike, and it should take roughly 35 to 45 minutes.

When testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a smoother and quieter ride than what we’ve experienced with other air bikes, like the Titan Fan Bike or the AssaultBike Classic. This is predominantly thanks to the belt-driven system. A belt-driven system requires less maintenance than a chain-driven system, but it is also harder to use. When you pedal, the steel fan wheel generates resistance based on your effort. The harder you pedal, the more resistance is applied.

However, once you stop pedaling, the fan wheel will stop moving, requiring more effort to get it started again. This might be tough if you’re not prepared for a high-intensity workout. Due to this, we gave the Assault Bike ProX a 4 out of 5-star rating for performance.

The Assault Bike ProX’s LCD monitor provides seven built-in training programs and a competition mode for those ready to take on the challenge. Through the Assault Fitness App, which we’ll review below, there is also an option to follow instructor-led programs or create customized workouts.

All in all, we give it a 3 out of 5 star rating in this category. The included workouts aren’t as robust as what you’d see in a more interactive bike like the Peloton. However, we do appreciate having them and think they can be valuable for people who may not know where to start.

While the AssaultBike Classic was only compatible with the Polar T34 heart rate chest strap, the Assault Bike ProX is compatible with other brands, like Garmin. You can link a heart rate monitor through the bike’s Bluetooth features. However, you need to purchase a compatible one separately, which is why we only rated it 4 out of 5 stars here (though to be fair, this is common for most exercise bikes).

The Assault Bike ProX comes with a five-inch by eight-inch monitor, which is a common size amongst other fan bikes. This high-quality LCD monitor is powered by four AA batteries, which Assault includes with your purchase. The console is great for tracking stats such as calories, distance, heart rate, speed, watts, and RPM. It also connects to the Assault Fitness App.

Our product testers loved that it could track power output in addition to distance and speed, which is a great measure of energy expenditure to quantify workout intensity. The Rogue Echo Bike monitor doesn’t provide feedback such as watts and RPM on its monitor, which gives the Assault Bike ProX the edge.

All things considered, we’ve given this bike 5 out of 5 stars for its display and tracking capabilities.

When testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a ton of conveniences. First, the air bike requires no electric outlet, and we loved being able to use it anywhere. This feature is also a welcome benefit for commercial CrossFit gym owners, as you don’t have to worry about your members tripping over power cords.

Other conveniences include a device holder and a water bottle holder. Some fan bikes like the Titan Fan Bike also include these conveniences. Others, like the Rogue Echo Bike, don’t (though they are available to purchase separately). We always appreciate it when a brand throws in little extras like this. They allow you to have all your workout essentials within reach. Plus, you don’t have to worry about potentially placing multiple orders or paying extra shipping fees to get them.

Overall, our product testers rated the conveniences 4 out of 5 stars. The only reason we docked a point is that we wish the bike came with a wind guard to prevent cold air from blowing in our faces when training in a cold garage. There is one available on the Assault Fitness website, but you have to buy it separately for an additional $39.

The Assault Bike ProX is a part of the Assault Fitness line of exercise machines that operate using the Assault Fitness app. The app was one of our product testers’ favorite features.

Free to download from the App Store and Google Play, the Assault Fitness App provides you with a multitude of instructor-driven workouts. You can do these workouts on your own or compete against other athletes virtually. Many of the workouts also integrate other types of equipment, such as dumbbells and kettlebells, to help you get more well-rounded programming.

While we enjoyed the app, we only gave it 4 out of 5 stars. As of this writing, it’s not available on the most recent version of Android. Athletes with newer Android phones may not be able to use it.

The Assault Bike ProX is Bluetooth-enabled. We don’t necessarily consider Bluetooth connectivity a standout feature, as dozens of cardio machines we’ve tested now come with it. But we’ve also tried inexpensive cardio equipment that doesn’t have this feature, and even Assault Fitness’s classic AssaultBike lacks Bluetooth capabilities. As such, we rated the ProX 5 out of 5 stars here.

When comparing other fan bikes we tested, the Assault Bike ProX generated less noise due to its belt-driven system. The belt-driven system operates more smoothly than chain-drive systems such as those on the Schwinn Airdyne. A noisier system can make it tough to perform workouts at home, especially if you train early in the morning or late at night when others are sleeping.

That said, no fan bike will be completely silent, so you should still expect some noise as air travels through the flywheel. Due to this, we give the noise level of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

The Assault Bike ProX offers some portability, thanks to two small transport wheels at the front. To move it, all you need to do is tilt it onto its wheels to help glide it across the floor. However, although it might be easy for some athletes to move this fan bike, others might struggle to relocate it because it weighs 125 pounds. Based on these findings, we give the portability of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

The Assault Bike ProX has a three-year non-wear parts warranty and a seven-year frame warranty. The three-year non-wear parts warranty doesn’t cover normal wear and tear on parts like the seat, pedals, and handle grips. This may seem like a drawback, but in our experience, this is common in warranties on other brands’ fan bikes. But the length of Assault’s warranty is longer compared to Rogue, who only offers a two-year warranty on their Echo Bike, and Titan, who only offers a one-year warranty on their fan bike. We gave the warranty of the Assault Bike ProX 5 out of 5 stars for this reason.

The Assault Bike ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high. Compared to the classic AssaultBike, these dimensions are one to two inches bigger in each category. If you’re between the two, we definitely recommend measuring carefully to ensure you choose the one that will best fit your space.

The Assault Bike ProX is a fan bike, meaning it builds resistance based on how much air you recruit in the fan wheel as you work. The harder you pedal, the more air resistance is applied, making your workout more challenging.

In addition to air resistance, the ProX uses a belt-driven system, meaning it only operates when you begin to pedal. If you stop pedaling, the machine stops moving. This makes it harder to operate compared to a chair-driven system, like what you’d see with the AssaultBike Classic.

The weight capacity of the Assault Bike ProX is 330 pounds. This is more than the Classic bike, which holds 300 pounds, but less than the Elite, which holds up to 350 pounds.

The Assault Bike ProX can accommodate most body sizes with 11 different height settings and six front-to-back settings. These adjustment levels are relatively standard based on what we’ve seen on other fan bikes. However, some competitors like the Rogue Echo Bike only have five front-to-back seat settings.

Because the Assault Bike ProX does not require an electrical outlet, you can transport it wherever you want to go —outdoors or indoors. The monitor, however, does require AA batteries to operate.

At first glance, it seems the Assault Bike ProX and Rogue Echo Bike have many similarities. When you analyze them more closely, you’ll find that there are several key differences between the two.

Below are the dimensions of both fan bikes:

Even though the Rogue Echo Bike is bulkier in material and dimensions, it has the same 330-pound weight capacity as the AssaultBike ProX. Both of these fan bikes are also powered by movement, so no electrical outlet is needed. Further, weighing in at 123 and 125 pounds, respectively, the Rogue Echo Bike and the Assault Bike ProX are equally portable, especially given they both have wheels.

Finally, both products use belt-driven mechanics, providing a smooth and quiet riding experience. But the Assault Bike ProX gives more metrics on the monitor, such as watts and RPM. This feature alone could make or break your decision, depending on how important tracking is to your training.

The Assault Bike ProX comes in with a strong 4.6 out of 5-star rating on the Assault Fitness website. Many users claim that it is super easy to set up, requires low maintenance, and is a favorite piece of equipment in their home gyms. Customers also praise its sturdiness and its ability to handle a tough workout.

One user mentioned that the left peg became loose during their workout. Another buyer mentioned that the Assault Bike ProX was very noisy and didn’t think it was as stable as other reviews might suggest — note, however, that complaints like this are in the minority.

After extensive research and testing of the Assault Bike ProX, we can say that this air bike is worth it. Made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat, it can take on the toughest workouts. It’s ideal for anyone looking for a full-body, high-intensity interval training machine for improving both endurance and strength.

The smoother and quieter experience you get with the Assault Bike ProX is thanks to the belt-driven system integrated into the design. Although this system might require more effort to operate, this bike can still be a great purchase for everyone from CrossFitters to health and fitness enthusiasts.

The Assault Bike provides a great workout, combining air resistance and a belt-driven system for a tough cardio and muscular endurance workout. You can use both the foot pedals and the arm handles to get a full-body workout. Or you can just use the arm handles to work out your upper body exclusively.

The Assault Bike Pro X is a belt-driven system. The fan bike only works when you operate the pedals and/or handlebars. The belt-driven system also offers a smoother and quieter workout.

The AssaultBike alone may not aid fat loss if you’re eating too many calories. However,  it can provide a strong enough stimulus for an intense enough workout to help you burn more calories and hit multiple health and fitness goals.

Because the AssaultBike Pro X requires a full-body effort and utilizes a belt-driven system, you could potentially build a small amount of muscle by using it consistently. However, resistance training with implements like dumbbells or barbells (and following a diet that supports muscle growth) will be your best bet if you want to pack on as much muscle as possible.

Joseph Lucero is a strength and conditioning specialist who owns his online coaching business, Harvesting Strength. He earned his master’s degree from the University of Texas at San Antonio and has his Certified Strength and Conditioning Specialist Certification (CSCS) from the NSCA. He coaches all types of strength athletes, including powerlifters and strongmen, and has authored many books on Amazon regarding different topics in strength training.

#8776. I’m Anti-Fitness Tracker—But Google’s Fitbit Air Changed My Mind

A low-profile tracker for runners who want health data without the wristwatch overload.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I loathe running watches. They bastardize one of the most lasting examples of single-function elegance—the wristwatch—and turn it into an omnipresent reminder that your health is declining in some way at all times: too fast, too slow, not enough rest, not enough quality sleep, you’re 34 only in years—your body is a wheezing 78, etc. I’m aware of my mortality and run to forget it.

Fitness trackers combat most of my grievances. They don't offer real-time notifications, and many don’t even have screens. However, many are also obtrusive, have subscription fees to see the full scope of health data, or are just ugly. The Oura Ring messed with my grip on pretty much every lift while strength training, and though the Whoop Band is covert (but still bulkier than I’d like), you’re on the hook for a 12-month subscription. Both devices also cost well over $200. It's steep for something I want to use only while lifting or running, not in my civilian life.

I wanted to try Google’s Fitbit Air after reading how simple it was to use. After weeks of testing, it’s stayed out of the way, gives me the health metrics I want, and is priced right at $100.

The Fitbit Air gives me heart rate, steps, and estimated calories burned through the paired Google Health app. It has a simple interface that lets me go as deep (or not) as I want in data, and it's delightful to use. I only use it for fitness, but you can also track food and water intake.

I wanted a fitness tracker to record running, lifting, and the occasional rowing or cycling workout. I’ve run four marathons and one half marathon, relying only on my phone and Strava to tell me how far I ran, how long it took, and pace breakdowns. Running is how I turn on, tune in, and drop out. A running watch would have me constantly worrying about my pace or anxiously waiting for a notification that my heart rate has gone above Zone 2. I want heart rate data from my runs, but I don’t want it to bother me in the moment.

Linking the Fitbit Air to Strava was easy and straightforward. I’m still used to manually starting a run in the Strava app, but the device automatically detects them and loads the data into the Google Health app. It also tracks lifting sessions, giving me an idea of cardio load and time spent in different heart rate zones. I’ve only needed to charge it once in about two and a half weeks, but I don’t wear it every day.

The Fitbit Air is so pleasantly small and lightweight that I forget I’m wearing it. I don’t even clock it on runs, and it doesn’t hinder gripping dumbbells or the handlebars on my spin bike and rowing machine. I’m using the Performance Loop wristband that it comes with and see no need for another—it’s comfortable, inconspicuous, and easy to adjust. Call me shallow, but how a fitness tracker looks is generally where they lose me. The device reads more like a wristband from the night before or a NATO strap of a field watch; I’m fine with either interpretation. If people ask, I say it’s a Kabbalah bracelet.

The Fitbit Air tracks heart rate variability, blood oxygen, skin temperature variation, sleep stages, and irregular heart rhythm alerts for atrial fibrillation. You can also upgrade your Google Health membership to Premium for adaptive AI coaching that breaks down health metrics and suggests workouts. These are features more expensive fitness trackers tout, and I’m not interested in them. I’m not using the device to its full potential. That’s the beauty of the Fitbit Air—capable tracking that lets you tap into the info you want without bombarding you with data.
